summary: 2018-10-30: Mahmut Nazli conveyed 2601 Greenmount Ave to Matthew Kelley and Gregory J. Bowen, financed by a deed of trust to PrimeLending (Allan B. Polunsky, trustee) (DEED, Book 20617 pp.476-481). ★★ READ IN FULL (MB 20617/476-481 + purchase-money deed of trust at 482-500, made 10/25/2018, rec. 10/30/2018): Mahmut Nazli conveys to MATTHEW KELLEY and GREGORY JAMES BOWEN, joint tenants, for ONE HUNDRED NINE THOUSAND DOLLARS ($109,000.00) — $93,437 of it a new PrimeLending purchase-money note (Fannie/Freddie uniform DOT, trustee Allan B. Polunsky, MERS nominee, maturity 11/1/2048). OCCUPANCY AFFIDAVIT: the property is 'residentially improved, owner-occupied... will be occupied by me/us for at least 7 of the next 12 months' — A HABITABLE BUILDING STOOD HERE thirteen months after the city's 'full demo' record (the demo was the adjacent lot). Tenant's Right of First Refusal compliance certified; taxes: state recordation $870, state transfer $545, county transfer $1,305. THE FREDDY'S ARC RESOLVES: Nazli, gifted the building for $0 in 2009, asked $119,000 in 2014 at peak House of Cards fame and sold for $109,000 in 2018 — fame arguably DID convert, for the owner whose basis was nothing. BUYERS IDENTIFIED (2026-07-15): Kelley and Bowen were the co-founders of Human Being Productions LLC (est. 2013) — the production company bought its own home.

summary: The block sits in the old village of Huntingdon on the York Turnpike (York Rd = later Greenmount Ave). Baltimore City annexed Waverly in 1888 and converted its lanes to the numbered street grid — so by the 1901 city directory these buildings are already '443/445/447 E 25th St,' NOT 'Huntingdon Ave.' A SEPARATE Huntingdon Avenue survived on the west/Hampden side of the city (house numbers in the 800s–900s, meeting 25th at 221 W 25th) and still exists today.

summary: 'Treutlein, Edward L., 2452 Greenmount Ave ... 12' appears in a Baltimore civic name-list printed in the German-language Der Deutsche Correspondent (published July 2, 3 & 5, 1909): ~27 residents from across the city, each with an address, a ward number (Treutlein = Ward 12, Waverly), and some marked '(verheiratet)' married or '(Wittwe)' widow. Because the list includes WOMEN, it is NOT a 1909 jury venire; the format (names + address + marital status + ward, run three days) fits a naturalization or court/legal notice, though the column heading isn't legible in the scan and the LoC full-text blocked automated retrieval. NOTE: the 1909 Polk directory lists the Amos/Ward household at 2452, so Treutlein's exact tie to this house is unconfirmed (a short-term resident, or a contact address) — the value here is placing him, a German-American, at the address in the German community's paper.

summary: The building at 2602–2608 Greenmount (Block 3836A, a ~9,400 sq ft brick warehouse built 1910) was the home of GREENMOUNT MOVING & STORAGE CO., founded 1915 by George Roscoe Conklin (1887–1966) and run by the Conklin family for ~75 years, to 1990. George married Bertha Florence Callender in 1908; their sons worked the business — Herbert E. Conklin's 1940 WWII draft card names his employer as 'George R. Conklin / Green Mount Storage, 2608 Greenmount Ave' — and the 1950 U.S. Census lists George R. Conklin (62) at the address, occupation 'furniture moving.' The company's original hand-painted truck signage still survives. (The 1922–23 city directory also shows a small 'soft drinks' parlor in a corner bay of the complex, and the 2600 corner earlier held a veterinary surgeon then a blacksmith/auto shop.)

summary: The '2643 ball player' (Polk lists him as Robert W. MacLeary, occupation 'ballplayer,' 1915-17) is identified as minor-league pitcher 'CHALKY' McCLEARY (b. Jan 19, 1892; 'MacLeary'/'McCleary' spelling variant). His pro career ran 1913-1922: the Waterbury Contenders (Eastern Assn), the Portsmouth Truckers (Virginia League), and the Blue Ridge League - chiefly the HAGERSTOWN TERRIERS. His standout year was 1916 with Hagerstown: 18-8, 2.57 ERA over 235 innings - 3rd in the Blue Ridge League in wins and the best win-loss pct among the top starters, in the same Class-D league as future St. Louis Cardinals star Bill Sherdel. He played Class C/D ball out of town but kept his Baltimore home at 2643 Greenmount with his widowed mother Jessie (which is why the off-season Polk directory lists him here). His Waverly neighbor and 1915-16 Portsmouth/Hagerstown TEAMMATE was catcher Krozer 'Doc' Milliman (b. Feb 13, 1886, Baltimore; 2449 Greenmount; a 10-season minor-leaguer, 1906-16, who caught for the 1912 Anderson Electricians in the Carolina Association of Charlotte-Hornets-game-fixing infamy) - the two of them part of a documented cluster of men who listed 'ballplayer' as their occupation along Greenmount within a few blocks of Oriole Park, 1915-17 (2643, 2449, and 2825 Greenmount) - a grouping I've informally called 'ballplayers' row' (a descriptor, not a period name).

summary: The twin storefront at 2637-2639 Greenmount was HARVEY'S ORIOLE TAVERN (Harvey's Oriole Tavern Inc, by 1972). The 'Oriole' name comes from the neighborhood ballpark: Terrapin Park / 'Old' Oriole Park stood two blocks north (29th-30th & Greenmount), built 1914 for the Federal League Terrapins, renamed Oriole Park by Jack Dunn in 1916 (the International League club — Lefty Grove pitched at this park in the 1920s; Babe Ruth's 1914 Orioles stint was at the adjacent, earlier Oriole Park across 29th St, a common conflation), and burned July 3-4, 1944. From 1977-1985 the tavern's real estate and license were held by the SAPPERSTEIN family — Gilbert Sapperstein (1932-2016), Baltimore's best-known liquor-license broker (secured creditor to failing bars via his Star Coin Machine Co. and Allstate Boiler Service; later tangled in gambling charges and a 2005 city-schools bribery case; father of developer Mark Sapperstein of Silo Point/McHenry Row), his wife Sondra, and his brother Jerome 'Jerry' Sapperstein (1938-2023) and Rita. Later McKinley H. Waites (1985) -> Bessey Ikem & Odile Koudou (2004) -> Caring Hands Health Solutions (2016). ('Harvey' himself — the pre-1972 namesake — is not yet identified.)

summary: George Roscoe Conklin, founder of the Greenmount storage business, was born in 1887 in Sunnybrook (rural Baltimore County near Phoenix), attended Sunnybrook School and Baltimore Polytechnic Institute, and worked as a contractor and builder before entering the warehouse business ~1910. Per his Evening Sun obituary, 'both of his warehouses at 2604 Greenmount avenue were built by his construction firm' - he literally built the buildings his moving-and-storage company ran from. A member of Chestnut Grove Presbyterian Church (Sunnybrook) and the Junior Order of United American Mechanics, he died of a heart attack at his home on Merrymans Mill Road on Feb. 7, 1966, and is buried in Chestnut Grove Presbyterian Church Cemetery, Phoenix, alongside his parents Walter H. Conklin (1853-1936) and Barbara Brown Conklin (1852-1892). Wife: Bertha Florence Callender (1883-1967).

summary: 3130 Greenmount Avenue was the general offices of THE HOOPER FOOD CO., Inc., a Baltimore seafood-restaurant chain. It began with G. Carroll Hooper, a stockbroker ruined by the 1929 crash, who in December 1932 opened a seafood restaurant in a converted one-car garage at 511 Gorsuch Ave in Waverly. 'Hooper's' grew into a small chain: restaurants at 511 Gorsuch Ave, 415 E 32nd St, and 3 W Chesapeake Ave (Towson), plus seafood stores at 3200 Old York Rd and the North Avenue Market - a food business strung right along the York Road/Greenmount spine. Its menus survive in the Enoch Pratt Free Library's 'Maryland Menus' collection (Digital Maryland). Its flagship 511 Gorsuch Ave location later became Eddie & Brooks Robinson's Gorsuch House restaurant (near Memorial Stadium) - so one corner carried a Depression-era seafood chain and, later, an Orioles Hall of Famer's restaurant.

summary: An Evening Sun 'Mr. Peep's Diary' column (Aug 24, 1966) caught Charles R. 'Bull' Robinson between his day job and his mat career: the boys at the John Eager Howard Recreation Center (Linden Ave & Konig St), where he was director, were startled to learn their director was a pro-wrestling 'baby face' (hero). The piece confirms he was an all-American guard at Morgan State (1947-51) and a pro lineman for the Green Bay Packers (1951) and Baltimore Colts (1954), and adds color: he learned that a lineman could 'pick up some nice change' wrestling from his Packers teammate 'Dick the Bruiser' (Dick Debruser), trained with wrestler Frank Veney at the YMCA, went on the road as a 'clean' grappler in 1955, and won some 70 matches from 'villains' before his first loss - beating the 234-pound Angelo Savoldi at the Baltimore Civic Center. He'd been a Bureau of Recreation athletic teacher ~9 years (earlier at the Lafayette Rec Center) and, at 225 lbs, still taught wrestling to teenaged boys 'only for body building and muscle coordination, never for competition.' In 1966 he lived at 2313 N. Monroe St.

summary: 2736 Greenmount Ave (the SE corner of Greenmount & 28th) was BULL ROBINSON'S LIQUORS, opened in the late 1960s and run for about 20 years by Charles Rogers 'Bull' Robinson until he sold it in 1989. Robinson (May 30, 1925 - Feb. 3, 2007) was a Lester Manor, Virginia native and a Morgan State College star - a physical-education graduate who captained both the football and boxing teams (two unbeaten football squads, 1949-50; All-CIAA; heavyweight boxing champion; Morgan State Athletic Hall of Fame, 1974). Drafted by the Green Bay Packers in 1951 as an offensive tackle (on the Packers' integrated roster), he played defensive middle guard for the BALTIMORE COLTS in 1953-54 - scoring his only NFL touchdown on Oct. 10, 1954, recovering a fumble in the end zone against the Chicago Bears. He then wrestled professionally in the 1960s (some 70 wins, debuting at the Baltimore Civic Center) and worked for the Baltimore Department of Recreation and Parks, directing the John Eager Howard Recreation Center in Reservoir Hill and coaching semipro football and basketball while steering his athletes to college scholarships. His wife of 23 years, Mazie Price, died in 1973; he died of cancer at 81 in Towson in 2007.

summary: Dr. Bertha E. Tapman kept her physician's home office at 2733 Greenmount (1915-23). A Baltimore native, she graduated the Woman's Medical College of Baltimore in 1906, worked at Johns Hopkins' Harriet Lane Clinic and as physical examiner at the Baltimore City Juvenile Court (1907-12), then ran a general practice specializing in obstetrics & gynecology — 'delivered babies at home and in Baltimore hospitals' — keeping the Greenmount office plus a second on W. North Ave. She married Dr. Maurice E. Shamer; their daughter Miriam Shamer Daly also became a physician, and living descendants still hold Dr. Tapman's diploma. She was socially close to the art-collecting Cone sisters.

summary: The physician who kept a home office at 2733 Greenmount (listed 1915-1923) was Dr. Bertha Tapman Shamer, one of Baltimore's longtime woman gynecologist-obstetricians. She graduated cum laude from the Women's Medical College of Baltimore in 1907 at just 20 - too young to be licensed in Maryland, so she worked a year in the Johns Hopkins pharmacy until old enough. She was associated with Johns Hopkins Hospital 1909-14 and served as an examiner for the Juvenile Court 1915-22 (overlapping her 2733 practice), then spent most of her life in private practice, delivering babies in homes and hospitals and seeing patients into her 80s. She married Dr. Maurice E. Shamer, a fellow obstetrician-gynecologist (they met at Church Home & Hospital); their children Dr. Miriam S. Daly, Margaret S. Petersen, and Dr. David H. Shamer largely followed into medicine. A charter member of the Maryland branch of the Women's American Medical Association. She moved to Albion, Michigan in 1974 and died there May 15, 1978, aged 91.

summary: 2825 Greenmount was the 1910s home of the Russell baseball family: father Charles A. Russell (carpenter), mother Mary K., five sons and three daughters (per SABR). Three sons pitched professionally - Clarence 'Lefty' Russell, Allan E. 'Rubberarm' Russell (1924 World Series champ; see other entries), and Frank Russell (Roanoke, Virginia League, 1911). The 1914 Polk lists Allen and Frank as 'ballplayer' at 2825 with their carpenter father. The family MOVED NORTH within the corridor to reach this block: the 1901 Polk lists Charles Russell at '2650 York Rd' = '2650 Greenmount' - the SAME house under both the old road-name and the new grid number (in the lower corridor the York Rd and Greenmount numbers coincided, unlike the 3200s where York Rd kept its own 1000s numbering) - and by 1914 they had moved about two blocks north to 2825 Greenmount, at 28th St directly across from Oriole Park.

summary: 2841 Greenmount (pre-1919 '2833'; earlier '2829 York Rd') was the Coggins home, near neighbors of the ballplaying Russells at 2825. Father Edward R. Coggins ran an express/transfer business; sons were Edward R. Coggins Jr. (clerk), Howard R. (lineman/foreman), David (a Baltimore Sun paper carrier), and daughter Grace (stenographer). The family held 2841 Greenmount into the 1940s (all the parents and Edward Jr. died there - an earlier note that they 'left ~1922-23' was WRONG). The baseball tie is DOCUMENTED and now corroborated by age: SABR says Hagerstown 'sent their second baseman, Eddie Coggins, a neighbor of Russell's,' to sign 18-year-old Lefty in 1908, and the Baltimore Sun box score of Sept 5 1908 shows 'Coggins, 2b ... Russell, p' together. Edward R. Coggins Jr. died Dec 30 1946 AGED 63 - i.e. born ~1883 - exactly the right age for the ~25-year-old Hagerstown second baseman of 1908, confirming he is the 'Eddie Coggins' who signed his neighbor Lefty.

summary: Clarence 'Lefty' Russell (b.1890-d.1962) came up on corridor sandlots: the Frisby Stars and the 25th Street Christian Church Sunday-school nine, which he led to consecutive league titles in 1906-07 (the church stood on the north side of E 25th St between Calvert and Guilford Ave). Baltimore church baseball was a thriving world then - a Catholic League (St. Andrew's, Holy Cross, St. Gerard's, St. John's, St. Clement's, St. Michael's), an Episcopal 'Church League' (Church of the Messiah, St. Paul's), and the Sunday-school circuit Russell's team won. In June 1908, at 18, he signed with Hagerstown (Sunset League); the man the club sent to sign him was its second baseman EDDIE COGGINS - his own Greenmount neighbor from up the block (2833/2841) - and the two then played together (Baltimore Sun box score, Sept 5 1908: 'Coggins, 2b ... Russell, p'). Two years later his 24-14, 219-K season for the IL Orioles - at the park across from 2825 - made him Connie Mack's record $12,000 purchase.

summary: 2900 Greenmount, the NW corner of 29th directly at Terrapin/Oriole Park's gate, was J. Firman's SALOON (1914-18; 'J Firman saloon 2900 Greenmount av h do', with a live-in bartender) - a ballpark corner tavern. The Sanborn shows the corner as 'Hardw./Rest.' A textbook saloon-to-dry-era pivot right at the ballpark gate.

summary: The west (even) side of the 2900 block, between E 29th and E 30th, WAS the ballpark. The 1915 Sanborn (sheet 710, Block 3) labels it 'TERRAPIN PARK - FEDERAL LEAGUE BASEBALL GROUNDS - CLOSED AT TIME OF SURVEY' - an all-FRAME (wood) grandstand ~22 ft high with a main Grand Stand and Pavilions A & B, and a run of OPEN BLEACHERS fronting directly on Greenmount across the mid-block (roughly 2906-2928, where the Polk shows no houses). Built for the Federal League Baltimore Terrapins (1914-15); the Polk lists it as 'Balto Baseball Co / Federal League Baseball Co, Greenmount av c 29th' (1914-15). After the Federal League folded, Jack Dunn's International League Orioles moved in and it became 'Oriole Baseball Park' (Polk, 1918) - the park where the IL Orioles won seven straight pennants (1919-25) and the Negro-NL Elite Giants played (1938-42), until it burned July 3-4, 1944. This parcel (2920) sits on the old bleacher frontage.

summary: A full-page Baltimore Sun Sunday feature (Feb 26 1911, by C. Starr Matthews) profiled the corridor's Lefty Russell as a clean-living local boy - 'a star athlete who leads simple life,' with 'no bad habit,' a 'model man for a team,' who as a boy 'did not care much about attending school' and instead 'regularly went frog shooting… on the banks of the brickyard pond' with a little rifle ('Lefty was a crack shot'), a hobby the paper credits for his batting eye ('a good batter, a clever pool player and a splendid bowler'). It fixes his boyhood haunts on the corridor: he swam 'on the banks of Herring Run, near the famous old race course,' and 'hooked school regularly to go swimming.' It notes he toughened up 'in the winter of 1909 in a lumber camp,' then 'made good in the Eastern League and… was bought by Connie Mack,' with a debut for the Athletics against the Boston Red Sox in which he 'twice fanned Tris Speaker' and 'became a hero.' The piece gives his real name as Clarence Dixon Russell (this paper's spelling; SABR has 'Dickson') and notes he would turn 21 on July 8, 1911.

summary: The feature traces Lefty's climb. Hagerstown's Eddie Coggins - a York Road neighbor - saw 'the making of a great twirler' and tipped his manager to sign the boy in 1908: 'that is the way those York road boys take care of each other.' Lefty in turn got his Sunday-school catcher Will Callahan signed. Oriole VP Moses N. Frank re-signed Lefty for Baltimore by meeting him on the street and beating Savannah's offer by $50/month to keep him home; Lefty picked up his 'spitter' at Wilkes-Barre under Mal Kittridge (1909). To toughen up for 1910 he and three companions - Tommy Bell, CHALKY McCLEARY (a fellow corridor ballplayer, 2643 Greenmount up the block), and his own brother Howard Russell - spent the winter of 1909 chopping wood at a lumber camp just north of Towson (up York Road); the shy Lefty's only recorded dinner-table words were 'I think I will, please' to an offer of lemon pie. His Athletics debut against Boston, twice fanning Tris Speaker, made him a hero - though, not knowing Speaker, he told Eddie Collins 'they all look alike to me.'

summary: The 1911 Sun feature explains how the Russell boys became ballplayers: 'they learned to play the game with the balls that were hit over the fences of Oriole Park, for they have lived near the ballpark for years,' and were on the professional diamond 'before they had cast aside short trousers.' All THREE brothers pitched for the same 25th Street Christian Sunday-school team - Lefty, Allen ('mastered the art of twirling with both hands' - AMBIDEXTROUS), and Frank (a right-hander bound for Roanoke) - 'two more prospects for $12,000 beauties in the Russell family.' Lefty's first team was the Frisby Stars, a Frisby-street sandlot nine (ages 10-13) that played 'on grounds back of Oriole Park' (a May 11 1906 Sun notice names its manager as George Annan of Mount St, Waverly). Its neighborhood rivals were the Boone Rippers and the Oxford Sluggers, the Russell and Bonthron families fighting 'running down the York road.'

summary: The Frisby-street sandlot world that produced Lefty Russell had a documented cast. The Frisby Stars' rivals were the BOONE RIPPERS - a real Waverly youth nine advertising for games as early as 1903 (Baltimore Sun, Aug 6 1903, contacts Norfleet Mercer & C.E. Harris) - and the OXFORD SLUGGERS, named for Oxford Avenue (the Waverly street that became modern E 27th St). The 'other' ballplaying family the 1911 feature paired with the Russells, the BONTHRONS, were real ballplayers: Harry L. Bonthron is listed by occupation as 'ballplyr' in the 1909 Polk directory (400 Lorraine Ave, off the 2600 block of York Rd/Greenmount) and starred that same August for the Westminster semipro club - 'BONTHRON'S FINE WORK: He Makes Homers And Figures In Fast Double Plays' (Baltimore Sun, Aug 11 1909, p.9). The Scottish-descended Bonthron clan (stonecutters, machinists, printers) clustered just east of Greenmount (David C. at 412 Oxford Ave = ~411 E 27th St; Henry at 55 Gutman Ave). So the corridor's sandlot war centered on TWO ballplaying families a few blocks apart - Russells and Bonthrons. (Not related to the 1930s Princeton runner Bill Bonthron, a separate Detroit family.)

summary: The 'famous old race course' near Herring Run where the boy Lefty swam (per the 1911 Sun feature) is the documented HERRING RUN RACE COURSE - a 19th-century Baltimore track along Herring Run in NE Baltimore (named in the Baltimore Sun as early as Oct 8 1855, 'strayed or stolen from Herring Run race course,' and still a live reference in an 1889 classified). It sat in what is now the Herring Run Park / Clifton Park - Lake Montebello area, about 1.5-2 miles ENE of the Greenmount corridor; omnibuses carried gamblers out to it. It is a DIFFERENT track from the Govane's Town (York Road) course up in Govans (an earlier note that guessed 'Govans' is corrected here). Lefty's boyhood haunts thus reached NE toward Herring Run. [Map check, 2026-07-11: the 1877 Hopkins Waverly plate and the early-1900s Baltimore City Archives ownership plat (both now in the Data Room) were examined; both cover the York Road village core and stop short of Herring Run, so neither pins the course. Its precise footprint remains documented by name only — NE Baltimore, Herring Run corridor.]

summary: Harry L. Bonthron (b. ~1883, Baltimore) - the ballplaying son of the Bonthron family in the Frisby-street sandlot world - was a genuine minor-league professional, and a decade older than Lefty Russell. His Baseball-Reference register shows FIVE pro seasons, 1901-1905: Harrisburg and Reading of the Pennsylvania State League (Class D, 1901-02); Fargo of the Northern League (Class D, 1903 - 84 games, .200); Coatesville of the Pennsylvania League (independent, 1904); and the Norwich Reds of the Connecticut State League (Class B, 1905, his highest level). By 1909 he was back home, listed by occupation as 'ballplyr' (400 Lorraine Ave, off the 2600 block) and starring for the Westminster semipro club - 'Bonthron's Fine Work: He Makes Homers And Figures In Fast Double Plays' (Baltimore Sun, Aug 11 1909). So the corridor's 'other' ballplaying family, the Bonthrons, produced a real Class-B professional - a generation ahead of the Russell boys next door.

summary: The Russell parents were Charles A. Russell (carpenter) and Mary K. Russell, nee MILLS. Per SABR the 1900 census put nine children at 1906 York Road - SIX sons and three daughters (beyond Lefty, Allen, Frank, and Howard, two more sons remain unidentified). Charles A. Russell died suddenly Nov 4 1928, aged 76 (b. ~1852), and was buried at Loudon Park Cemetery; his wife Mary K. (nee Mills) had already predeceased him. His funeral was held from the home of his daughter, Mrs. James H. Strain, at 610 East 31st Street - the only one of the three Russell daughters yet identified (by married name). Allan 'Rubberarm' Russell died Oct 20 1972 (of 21 N Wickham Rd; Loudon Park, Spruce 46; survived by daughter Janette Russell); Lefty had died Jan 22 1962 (Dulaney Valley). The three sisters' given names still require the 1900/1910 census (login-gated).

summary: The Coggins were a serious ballplaying family a full decade before Eddie signed Lefty. In 1897 'Edward Coggins, c.' and 'Lawrence Coggins, c.f.' played for the youth nine the 'Lilies of the Valley' (ages 11-14; Baltimore Sun 'New Organizations' amateur-club directory, May 11 1897) - Edward at ~14 fits his ~1883 birth. By 1903 THREE Coggins brothers - William Coggins (1b), Edward Coggins (ss), and Lawrence (lf) - played for the Maryland Athletic Club, a nine the Amateur Athletic Union's Thomas K. Barrett declared PROFESSIONAL (because ex-pro Frank Bevans played on it); the M.A.C. played its games at ORIOLE PARK, the corridor ballpark blocks from the Coggins home (Baltimore Sun, 'Shock to M.A.C. Players,' May 30 1903). So Edward R. Coggins Jr.'s arc runs 1897 sandlot -> 1903 semipro at Oriole Park -> 1908 Hagerstown pro (where he signed his neighbor Lefty Russell).

summary: An Oct 1906 court docket (Court of Common Pleas) lists 'Daniel Coggins vs. United Railways and Electric Company' and 'Edward Coggins vs. same' - two Coggins family members with pending suits against Baltimore's streetcar monopoly (typical streetcar-accident/damage actions of the era), adding a Daniel Coggins to the family roster. CAUTION - two same-surname items are NOT this corridor family: (1) Hannah Henton Coggins, a Philadelphia artist who died in New York in 1902 (father Edward H. Coggins killed at Antietam) is a separate Philadelphia family; (2) an 1867 Baltimore County divorce, Mary Amanda Coggins vs. Edward Coggins (he abandoned her in 1862 and left Maryland), is an earlier Baltimore Coggins of unconfirmed relation. Do not conflate either with the 2841 Greenmount Cogginses.

summary: After the bakery era, 3213-3215 (Block 4076, Lot 7) was owned by Kang Jung Yi and Kyung Cha Yi, Korean-American merchants who ran Dandy Men's Store (its storefront listed at 3219 Greenmount). A Sept 23 1985 $60,000 purchase-money deed of trust to First National Bank of Maryland (SEB 658/574) also encumbered 902 Sibley Road in the county; a Nov 14 1985 confirmatory agreement (SEB 707/336) corrected the owners' names after their naturalization — Kang Jung Yi became Dandy Kangjung Lee and Kyung Cha Yi became June Kyungcha Lee (the husband adopting the store's own name, 'Dandy'). A 1997 intra-spousal deed put title in June Kyung Cha Lee alone (Liber 658/570), secured by a Korea Exchange Bank indemnity mortgage (Book 6291/113, satisfied 2001, FMC 1889/357). By 2001 she had moved to Allentown, PA; on Dec 30 2003 she and So Cheung Lee refinanced with a $202,500 Wachovia Bank deed of trust (FMC 4871/350), paying off a prior $128,671 balance. The lender succession — First National → Korea Exchange → Wachovia — tracks the corridor's Korean-immigrant merchant thread.

summary: Alan and Janet Wurtzburger were among the Baltimore Museum of Art's greatest benefactors. In two phases they gave the museum its foundational non-Western holdings — 400+ African, Oceanic, and Pre-Columbian sculptures (major African gift 1954-55; Pre-Columbian core 1958), establishing the Wurtzburger Gallery of the Primitive Arts (1958; catalogued by Paul S. Wingert, 'The Alan Wurtzburger Collection of African Sculpture,' BMA 1958) — and they assembled a landmark modern-sculpture collection: a Rodin (a 'Balzac'), Bourdelle, Maillol, Henry Moore, Jacob Epstein, Marino Marini, Jacques Lipchitz, Ossip Zadkine, Alexander Calder, Isamu Noguchi, and José de Rivera. The sculpture was first displayed on the grounds of their Stevenson (Baltimore County) estate 'Timberlane' (landscaped by James Rose and Thomas Church); the 1.1-acre Alan and Janet Wurtzburger Sculpture Garden opened at the BMA in 1980 (landscape architect George Patton). The Wurtzburgers belong to the same German-Jewish art-collecting-and-philanthropy tradition as Baltimore's Cone sisters.

summary: In Sept 1927 federal 'dry agents' raided a saloon in the 2500 block of Greenmount Avenue and arrested eight men ('Dry Agents Raid Saloon And Arrest Eight Men'); no liquor was found. Among those arrested was EDWARD R. COGGINS (then of the 2300 block Greenmount) — the corridor Coggins family later at 2841 who signed pitcher 'Lefty' Russell — alongside John F. Emerick and saloon figure Louis A. Saylor of the 2500 block. Days later U.S. Commissioner J. Frank Supplee condemned the wholesale arrests (attorney R. Palmer Ingram); Saylor was released on $100 bail. In March 1928 William Brown of the 2500 block drew sixty days on a sale-and-possession charge.

summary: 2711 Greenmount was VINCENT'S 2711 MEAT MARKET — an "American and Italian Grocery" (as the storefront signage reads) — run by the Sicilian-immigrant Bongiorno family from Calascibetta, Enna: Vincent (Vincenzo) Bongiorno and his wife Pietrina (Scavuzzo). Established after the Colgan/Weidner era (exact founding year undocumented; the family was in Baltimore by 1940) and run into the 1960s; Vincent died 1963, Pietrina 1968.

summary: 2709 Greenmount was a family bakery and confectionery run by the Weidners — a long-settled German-American Roman Catholic family (St. Ann's parish, New Cathedral Cemetery). It was a father-and-son operation: Edward Paul Weidner Sr. (b. 1873, Baltimore) the candymaker/confectioner, and his son Leo Edward Weidner (b. 1891) the baker, both living over the store, with kin John (carpenter) and Paul A. (ironworker) in the household. The bakery opened around 1916 and is documented in the 1917 and 1918–19 Polk directories, including the classified 'Retail Bakers' trade section — whose OCR garbled the surname to 'Weldinger,' the source of the long-standing 'Weidinger' misreading. Leo, a WWI veteran, never married and died in 1949 (buried at Baltimore National Cemetery); Edward Sr. died in 1929 (New Cathedral Cemetery).

summary: After the Weidners, 2709 turned into a high-turnover rental. For a single directory year — 1922 — it was the home of May Tillet, widow of Robert Tillet, who kept the household, with Charles Currie, an awning erector, boarding there. Both are near-ghosts: neither appears at 2709 (or traceably anywhere in Baltimore) in any other year. Robert Tillet was already dead and never shows up alive in a city directory, so May likely arrived on Greenmount already widowed. Currie's trade ties him to the corridor's small awning industry — most plausibly the Jefferson awning works six blocks up at 3332–3337 Greenmount — though no employment record confirms it.

summary: Weeks after her husband Vincent died (Feb 10, 1963), the widow Pietrina Bongiorno acquired the leasehold to 2709 Greenmount — the parcel next door to the family store at 2711 — on March 27, 1963 (JFC 1461/477). It was structured as a life estate to Pietrina with remainder to her daughter Frances (Bongiorno) Thalwitzer, a classic Baltimore ground-rent leasehold (1c annual rent). The fee/ground rent had just been created that same day by Charles J. Novak Jr., who leased to Clayton W. Bordley, Inc. (JFC 1461/474); Bordley conveyed the leasehold to Pietrina. When Pietrina died in 1968 the leasehold vested in Frances Thalwitzer.

summary: In 1915 the east side of the 1900 block of Greenmount (block 7) was a continuous row of 2-story brick buildings numbered 1901-1919: a 3-story brick saloon at the 1901 corner, a plumber (1903-05), 2-story brick dwellings (1907-1915), and a store (1917-19), with a brick 'Play Ho.' summary: The 2700 Greenmount block sits in Harwood, which was originally the pre-1888 Baltimore County hamlet of 'OXFORD' — a country village annexed to Baltimore City in 1888 alongside Waverly, Peabody Heights, Homestead and Friendship along the York Road/Greenmount spine. E 27th St at this corner was 'OXFORD AVENUE' until the 1908 Brune street-renaming (primary source: Report of Commissioner William H. Brune, Apr 30 1908 — Oxford Ave → E 27th St; Huntingdon Ave → 25th; Barnum/Brady Ave → 28th; Waverly Ave → 31st). The nearby Oxford Club (2837) and 'Oxford Sluggers' ballclub took their name from this Oxford Avenue. The rowhouses (built c.1910-13) stand on the 1688 Huntington/Stansbury land patent, a few blocks from the original Oriole Park (25th & Greenmount, 1882-89) that gave the Orioles their name; rowhouse developer James Keelty began his career building at 25th & Greenmount c.1904. 'Harwood' is a 20th-c. community name (Harwood Improvement Association organized 1972) of undocumented origin — no Harwood estate is documented.

summary: Louis Rabai (b. Italy ~1902-03) came to the United States in 1923 to join his brother, John B. Rabai, in the baking business. About a decade later he went into business for himself — the bakery he ran on Greenmount Avenue.

Rabai in the Baltimore baking business","image_id":"wp-1923-louis-rabai-arrives","relevance":"Documents the proprietor of Rabai's Bakery at 3215 Greenmount and his relationship to the wider Rabai baking family.","confidence":"documented","source_document":"The Baltimore Sun 1957-03-15 p.11 (Louis Rabai obituary; Newspapers.com img 56705892)"}

summary: Rabai's Bakery, an Art Deco shop, opened at 3215 Greenmount Ave in 1937, run by Louis Rabai. A neighborhood retail bakery ('For Those Who Want the Best') known for coconut sticks, meringue pies, gingerbread cookies and peach cake.
data: {"evidence":"Better Waverly 'Village Life Walking Tour': 'Just south of Mr. Nifty was an Art Deco bakery called Rabai's which opened in 1937. The bakery later became a Butter Crisp before closing in 1987.' Proprietor per the 1957 Louis Rabai obituary.","headline":"Rabai's Bakery — the Art Deco bakery — opens at 3215 Greenmount (1937)","image_id":"wp-1937-rabais-opens","relevance":"The signature use of the parcel — a beloved mid-century Waverly bakery on the Greenmount 'Avenue'.","confidence":"documented","source_document":"Better Waverly Village Life Walking Tour (betterwaverly.org); The Baltimore Sun 1957-03-15 (Louis Rabai obituary)"}

summary: A mid-century Rabai's Bakery matchbook (Maryland Match Co.) advertises the slogan 'For Those Who Want the Best' and two locations: 3215 Greenmount Ave (University 5800) and 5110 Park Heights Ave (Liberty 4880) — a two-store retail bakery.
data: {"evidence":"Rabai's Bakery matchbook (Maryland Match Co., Baltimore): 'RABAI'S BAKERY / For Those Who Want the Best / 3215 GREENMOUNT AVE, University 5800 / 5110 PARK HEIGHTS AVE, Liberty 4880'.","headline":"Rabai's Bakery matchbook — 'For Those Who Want the Best' — 3215 Greenmount + a 5110 Park Heights branch","image_id":"wp-matchbook-two-locations","relevance":"Documentary confirmation of Rabai's Bakery at 3215 Greenmount and its Park Heights branch, with the slogan and phone exchanges.","confidence":"documented","source_document":"Rabai's Bakery matchbook (Maryland Match Co.); Jeff Jetton collection / matchcovercollector.com"}

summary: Louis Rabai ran his Greenmount Avenue bakery until he sold it in 1952, after roughly two decades of ownership.
data: {"evidence":"Baltimore Sun, 1957-03-15 (Louis Rabai obituary): '[he] ran [his] shop until he sold out in 1952.'","headline":"Louis Rabai sells the Greenmount bakery (1952)","image_id":"wp-1952-louis-sells","relevance":"Marks the end of Rabai-family ownership at 3215; the shop continued under the Rabai's name and later as Burri's, then Butter Crisp.","confidence":"documented","source_document":"The Baltimore Sun 1957-03-15 (Louis Rabai obituary)"}

summary: After Louis Rabai sold the Greenmount shop (1952), it is reported operating by the mid-1950s as 'Burri's French Bakery' — 'Burri' almost certainly the Brusini family name (the co-founding branch, related to the Rabais by the Vicarini-sisters marriages) continuing the bakery before its later Butter Crisp era.
data: {"evidence":"Jeff Jetton's 3213-3215 Greenmount monograph (city-directory citation); the Brusini/Rabai family link (1918 Brusini-Vicarini marriage; Mary Rabai's sister Rose Brusini).","headline":"Continues as Burri's (Brusini) French Bakery (~1956)","image_id":"wp-1956-burris","relevance":"Ties the mid-century bakery succession back to the founding Brusini family.","confidence":"verify","source_document":"Jeff Jetton monograph; Brusini-Vicarini-Rabai family records"}

summary: Michael Gotti incorporated Butter Crisp Bakery, Inc. at 3215 Greenmount Ave on March 21, 1977 (MD entity D00740985; Articles of Incorporation Film F2378/Folio 461), taking over the former Rabai's/Burri's storefront and continuing the parcel's ~50 years of bakery use. Gotti (an Italian surname; home at 5900 Benton Heights Rd, NE Baltimore) was the resident agent/proprietor. The bakery hired an 'all-around baker, morning shift' in 1978 and advertised through the 1980s. (Michael Gotti the baker is thinly documented — no obituary or grave found online, and he is NOT the New York crime-family John Gotti.)

summary: 3215 Greenmount today is Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart. The consolidated parcel is recorded under 3213 (Block 4076 Lot 7).

summary: Louis Rabai, 'long the proprietor of a bakery [on] Greenmount avenue' and 'a leader in the Italo-American community,' died at 54 after a long illness. He came from Italy in 1923 to join his brother John B. Rabai in baking, went into business for himself ~1933, and sold his shop in 1952. He served ten years (three terms) on the Baltimore City Jail Board and was for a time chairman of Italy's own Boys Town in Rome.

summary: Mary Vicarini Rabai, who with her husband John B. Rabai ran a series of businesses called Rabai's French Bakery (downtown stores supplying French bread and hard dinner rolls to restaurants), died at 93. Born in Paris in 1896 to Italian parents, she came to Baltimore's Little Italy at age 8 and married John B. Rabai in 1914. Their children included Ermine (DePasquale) — pictured working at the Greenmount store in 1938 — Edith Segraves, and Cmdr. John F. Rabai. (The Rabai's French Bakery was the family's downtown/wholesale line, distinct from Louis Rabai's Greenmount retail shop.)

summary: The bakery family had TWO men named Louis, often conflated: (1) Louis RABAI (b.1902 Italy, immigrated 1923 to join his brother John, ran the Greenmount store, City Jail Board, d. Mar 14 1957) — buried New Cathedral Cemetery Plot VV-714, beside brother John B. Rabai (1896-1961) at VV-704; and (2) Louis BRUSINI, who married Rosa Vicarini (sister of John's wife Mary), making him John's brother-in-law and bakery co-founder. John B. Rabai m. Mary Vicarini (b. Paris 1896, d.1990) in 1914; their children were Ermine (DePasquale), Edith (Segraves), and John Frank Rabai (1921-2013, ran the bakery after WWII). Living descendants include grandson Peter DePasquale (Ermine's son) and Amy Brusini. A charming coda: the widowed Mary Rabai sailed on the RMS Caronia's Mediterranean cruise from New York on May 6, 1965.

summary: Rabai's Bakery was founded in the 1920s by Louis (Luigi) Brusini and his brother-in-law John B. Rabai — the two men had married the Vicarini sisters (John m. Mary Vicarini 1914; Louis Brusini m. Rosa Vicarini 1918). The original location was on Edmondson Avenue in West Baltimore; the business grew to multiple stores, including the Greenmount Avenue retail bakery (run by John's brother Louis Rabai) and a Park Heights Ave branch.

summary: In Waverly memory Rabai's was a beloved fixture a couple of doors from the Waverly Theater (near Zales): people stopped after church or after a movie. Remembered for yeast doughnuts, sticky pecan buns, crumb cake, milk bread, coconut sticks, meringue pies, and a peach cake called 'the unofficial taste of Baltimore summers.' A neighborhood boy traded his Morning Sun paper for a bun at the back door; delivery driver Jim Frizzera brought fresh rolls to the neighbors. 'Some of the nicest people in the world.'

summary: After the Rabai's/Burri's bakery era, the same storefront at 3215 Greenmount Avenue carried on as the Butter Crisp Bakery (incorporated 1977 under Michael Gotti). A July 3, 1978 Evening Sun help-wanted ad — 'BAKER. All around, morning shift, apply in person only. Butter Crisp Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Ave.' — confirms it operated at Rabai's exact address and was actively hiring its own bakers. Butter Crisp has a substantial newspaper footprint (~39 Baltimore Sun/Evening Sun matches), running from 1978 through a cluster of mentions in September 1987 (its apparent closing, amid the wave of 1980s Avenue store closings that alarmed the community) and a final trace into July 1988 — roughly a decade at the corner before the storefront's later conversion (today Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart, the Art Deco front lost).

summary: A late-1930s streetscape photograph of the Greenmount & E 32nd St node (the Old York Rd wedge) captures the commercial cluster 3201's corner store anchored. Legible businesses include a White Coffee Pot restaurant, the Family Finance Corporation, Brandau's / 'Marlboro' Clothes, and a W.L. Douglas 'Cinderella Shoe Shop' selling Weather Bird Shoes, with a large HEINZ OVEN-BAKED BEANS billboard mounted atop the corner building. On the sidewalk at the corner stands an open-air fruit-and-flower stand — crates of produce and potted flowers — the kind of outdoor display the 3201 corner grocery ran. A 1960s color view of the same stretch shows the block's later tenants (Nifty Cleaners, Roberts Jewelers) with the Waverly Theatre marquee and a streetcar beyond.

summary: The mid-to-late-20th-century owner of 3201 Greenmount was Matthew Swerdloff, a colorful Baltimore figure. Reared in Forest Park, he graduated City College (1944, lacrosse attackman), took a B.A. (1952) and law degree (1955) at the University of Baltimore, played lacrosse there (1952 North-South Game at NY's Polo Grounds, All-American honorable mention). In 1958-59 he was GENERAL MANAGER of the (Eastern Basketball League) Baltimore Bullets — a struggling minor-league pro basketball team he kept afloat by scrounging backers, doing front-office work unpaid while practicing law (the club ran ~$15,000 in the red, drew 500-600 fans a game, sat 6th at 7-11). He was also head coach of the Maryland Lacrosse Club and became a legendary lacrosse referee ('the Charley Eckman of lacrosse') — refereeing 1953-73 and 1986-95, president of the Southern Lacrosse Officials Assn, co-founder of the National Intercollegiate Lacrosse Officials Assn, teacher of youth lacrosse at the JCC (1960), and founder of the Heroes summer lacrosse leagues (1965) that gave players scholarships. He later worked in real estate (owning this Greenmount corner). A Mount Washington resident, he died Feb 25, 1995 (age 64) of a heart attack while refereeing a scrimmage at Anne Arundel Community College; his estate sold 3201 in July 1996.

summary: The Waverly Theatre at 3211 Greenmount Ave opened in 1909 as a neighborhood movie house, designed by architect Alfred 'A.' Lowther Forrest in partnership with Oliver Birkhead Wight. Its façade was a classical temple-style front with a large arched window and a decorative 'W' monogram — a scaled-down echo of the Beaux-Arts elegance the pair brought to Baltimore's downtown picture palaces. The Waverly is the project that ties Forrest and Wight together; its success led to Wight's involvement in their subsequent commissions. The building survives today as a retail store, still recognizable by its original theatre front.

summary: Alfred Lowther Forrest was born 1862 in Notting Hill, London, trained in architecture in London from age 19, and emigrated to the U.S. in 1898 (Boston/New York) before settling in Baltimore by 1907 — a city rebuilding after the 1904 Great Fire. He briefly worked for Baldwin & Pennington (B&O Railroad architects) before opening his own North Charles St office. A prolific theatre architect — 'he designed more than a dozen theaters, most of them in Baltimore' (Headley) — his works include the Victoria/Embassy Theatre (1908), the New Theatre (1910, co-designed with Wight), the Second-Empire Macht Building (1908, an early post-fire landmark), and Roland Avenue M.E. Church (1912). He left Baltimore for Rochester, NY ca.1928 and died in 1951, age 89.

summary: Oliver Birkhead Wight was a Baltimore-born architect (b. ca.1876–1880) who became one of the city's principal theatre designers of the 1910s–1930s. His early collaboration with Forrest on the Waverly (1909) and the New Theatre (1910) gave him his start in cinema architecture; by 1915 he was a registered AIA architect. His masterpiece was the Parkway Theatre (1915), modeled on London's West End and now restored as the SNF Parkway Film Center in Station North. He also remodeled the Howard Theatre (1920), designed the Arcade (1928) and Avon (1933) in Hamilton, the Irvington (1925), and the Carroll Theatre in Westminster (now the Carroll Arts Center) — collectively shaping Baltimore's neighborhood-cinema landscape.

summary: By the 1980s the Waverly had closed as a theatre and its front converted to retail — a 'SHOE CITY / The Family Shoe Store' occupied the storefront. Per a kilduffs.com account, the decorative 'W' was still visible atop the building into the 1980s before a new coat of siding hid it; the building's front remained 'easy to spot,' and the old sloped theatre floor survived in the stockroom. A new food store was later built in the rear of the old theatre. The Waverly was remembered as the neighborhood's favorite movie house, one block south of the more upscale Boulevard Theatre.

summary: The original 1909 iron-front picture-show-and-billiards was extensively renovated in 1919 and reopened in 1921 under the name 'the New Waverly Theatre.' The rebuilt brick-and-concrete house seated more than 1,300 people and featured a gold fiber screen and a five-piece orchestra to accompany the pictures — a major upgrade from the storefront nickelodeon. The reopening coincided with the 1919 opening of the Olmsted-designed 33rd Street boulevard and the 1921 debut of the rival, larger Boulevard Theatre three blocks north; the Waverly remained the smaller neighborhood 'community theatre' while the Boulevard drew the Guilford/Peabody Heights crowd.

summary: In the decades before air conditioning, theatres commonly closed in the summer heat. Waverly manager Harry Kahn worked around this by creating an open-air theatre in the open lot behind the building — a bed-sheet screen, wooden folding chairs, and a piano player — so the Waverly could keep showing pictures through the summer. A small, human detail of how a neighborhood movie house survived the season.

summary: Like the other movie theatres on Greenmount Avenue, the Waverly operated under racial segregation for much of its life. The National Register nomination notes the pointed contrast that while the Avenue's movie theatres were segregated, its 'refined stores' were open to everyone and employed Black workers — a marker of the everyday geography of Jim Crow in a mixed commercial district. Part of the corridor's civil-rights-era social record.

summary: The Waverly Theatre — the first theatre in Waverly village, running from silent films through talkies — closed in 1969 after sixty continuous years (1909–1969). The building was converted to commercial retail ca.1970 and given a sheet-metal facade ca.1990; the decorative 'W' that long survived on the parapet was covered over. Part of the building had also housed the Knockblock (Knowblock) Brothers' grocery store (1937), and the storefront later became Shoe City, with today's Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart occupying the space. The terrazzo paving of the former ticket booth still survives at street level (at the 3203 entrance bay).

It passed to the CRYSTAL AMUSEMENT COMPANY in 1922 (SCL 3844/65, the era of the 1919-21 'New Waverly' rebuild) and on Nov 30 1929 to THE GRAND COMPANY (SCL 5069/562) — the theatre-operating enterprise of Frank H. Durkee III, whose Durkee circuit also ran the nearby Boulevard, explaining the jointly-printed 'Boulevard and Waverly Theatres' programs. In 1955 Beulah Bruehl conveyed a strip to Grand Co (MLP 10007/357) and Grand Co granted a revocable license to the adjoining CROWN 5-AND-10-CENT-TO-$1.00 STORES, INC. (MLP 10007/361) — the Crown store that appears beside the theatre in 1930s photographs.

summary: The primary-source grand-opening ad: 'We take great pleasure in notifying our patrons that the NEW WAVERLY THEATRE, Greenmount Avenue, at Gorsuch, Will Open Monday, February 21 at 6 P.M.' The opening bill was Jack Holt and Lois Wilson in 'Midsummer Madness' plus Larry Semon in 'Schooldays,' followed by a full week (Otis Skinner in 'Kismet,' Lois Weber's 'To Please One Woman,' 'Heliotrope,' Dorothy Phillips, and William Farnum in 'If I Were King'). The ad states 'DAILY PERFORMANCES — CONTINUOUS 2 TO 11 P.M.' and 'ADMISSIONS: MATINEE 11c; EVENINGS 11c AND 17c,' and displays the theatre's ornate 'W' monogram framed by classical columns. This fixes the exact reopening date of the rebuilt house (the NPS-cited '1921' reopening = Feb 21, 1921).

summary: By 1963 the Crown five-and-dime had wound down here: a Circuit Court trustee's sale in the matter of the Trust Estate of Crown 5c & 10c to $1.00 Stores, Inc. auctioned the property Monday, September 23, 1963. The Greenmount piece was described as '3203-3205-3207-3209 Greenmount Ave.' — a 2-story brick business property with 3 stores and separate-entrance offices above, fronting ~70 feet on Greenmount with an average depth of 175 feet and 'running from Greenmount Avenue to Old York Road' (a through-lot spanning the wedge between the two streets), zoned 1st commercial. Stores at 3203 and 3207-9 were rented ($10,200/yr gross); 3205 and the upstairs offices were vacant. The SAME trust estate also owned a separate property five miles north — 507-509-511 York Road in Towson (Baltimore County), leased to a well-known tenant — sold at the same auction. (The two 'York Road/Greenmount' addresses are the same historic road by lineage but different places: Greenmount Ave is the straightened city segment of the old York Turnpike, with 'Old York Road' surviving as the fork behind the 3200 block; the Towson store is a wholly separate location.) The Greenmount frontage later passed to Eli & Yetta Miller / The Miller Realty Corporation and the 1981 Princess Shops rehab.

summary: The Greenmount storefront was not just a Crown branch — it was the CHAIN'S ORIGIN. A full-page Aug 27, 1936 Evening Sun ad narrating 'THE STORY OF CROWN STORES' opens with 'CHAPTER ONE — The First Crown Store — 3207-09 Greenmount Ave.,' followed by Chapter Two (735-37 Washington Blvd), Chapter Three (517-19 York Rd, Towson — the 1932 'Store No. 3'), and Chapter Four, the newest unit being opened that night at 5118-20 Park Heights Ave ('The Ten-Cent Store Beautiful'). Crown billed itself as 'Maryland's Own Chain — Owned and Operated by Marylanders.' So the corridor birthed a homegrown Baltimore five-and-dime chain: from this 3207-09 Greenmount flagship (c.1930, predating the 1932 Towson store) the chain grew to four stores by 1936 and at least six by 1950. Crown's trust ultimately owned the entire 3203-3209 frontage before auctioning it in 1963.

summary: Rabai's Bakery's earliest documented Greenmount location was 3205 Greenmount Ave — a few doors south of its later signature Art Deco store at 3213-3215. summary: As the chain's founding store, 3207 Greenmount doubled as Crown's hiring office and headquarters. A long run of Baltimore Sun / Evening Sun help-wanted ads placed from '3207 Greenmount Ave.' (phone UNiversity 6880) recruited for the whole chain — an Aug 27 1941 ad sought 'young ladies… selling positions open in our various stores… Apply Miss Stricker' (naming the store's hiring manager); others sought receiving/stockroom young men (1941), a store manager and stock man (1943), 'girls 16 or over' to 'earn Xmas money… in your own neighborhood' (1943), window trimmers (1944), and sign-holders (1948). A Sept 1943 ad's segregated 'Porters — Colored. Steady work' reflects the era's Jim Crow hiring language. By Oct 1958 the firm advertised as the incorporated 'Crown 5c & 10c to $1 Stores, Inc.' of 'Baltimore 18, Maryland,' a self-described 'rapidly expanding chain' hiring assistant managers — 3207 Greenmount still its address.

summary: On the night of Nov 25, 1951, burglars used a 4-pound maul to batter open the large second-floor office safe at Rabai's Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Avenue, and escaped with $3,320 in cash — the noise drowned out by the dough-mixing machinery running in the basement as the bakers worked below. Owner Louis Rabai told police the thieves also took a solid gold cigarette lighter ($240) and a $300 pocket watch, and drank a bottle of the bakery's brandy (kept for use in the recipes). The robbers had scaled a light pole in the side alley, forced the second-floor window of chiropodist Dr. Jacob Ostroff, and crossed into the Rabai office; the break-in was discovered the next morning by attorney J. Philip Knapp, whose office was nearby. Sgt. Allen Berman of the Northeastern district investigated. A press photo shows 'Louis Rabai inspects battered safe in his bakery.'

summary: The proprietor of Rabai's Bakery was a fixture of Baltimore's Italian-American civic and political world. Louis Rabai chaired the arrangements committee of the Italian-American Civic Club of Maryland — organizing its Columbus Day banquet in Oct 1945 (with Anselm Sodaro as club president) and standing among the Little Italy families who feted Mayor Tommy D'Alesandro at the club's 1947 testimonial dinner. In July 1947 Mayor D'Alesandro appointed Rabai to the Baltimore City Jail Board (term to July 1, 1951), on which he served, through reappointment in 1955, until his death — a tenure that included the board's March 1957 vote to desegregate the jail's visiting system (removing the Jim Crow sign). He was also the 'third man' in the uncropped photograph State's Attorney Anselm Sodaro used to defend himself in the bitter 1954 primary. Rabai's Bakery itself made a wartime Red Cross War Fund honor roll of organizations that exceeded their campaign goals.

summary: The Waverly Tower Shopping Center opened October 30, 1957, dedicated by Mayor D'Alesandro as 'the city's first redevelopment project' completed — and, per the Urban Renewal agency, the second finished redevelopment area in the nation (the Waverly project was conceived 1950 and officially launched 1953). Its owner-developer was Community Research and Development, Inc., whose president was JAMES W. ROUSE (chairman Jack Meyerhoff) — the same James Rouse who would go on to build the Harundale Mall (one of the country's first enclosed malls, then CRD's 'third project'), the new town of Columbia, Maryland, and Baltimore's own Harborplace. The Waverly Tower thus stands at the very start of Rouse's shopping-center career, just after CRD's first center in Easton. Designed by Cochran, Stephenson and Wing and named for the WWIN radio tower rising from its parking lot (300-350 cars), the center had 17 stores and a ~77,000 sq ft shopping component with a 400-foot frontage on Greenmount; alongside it Harry Bart built 28 apartment buildings (320-321 units). Some 250 aging structures were razed across ~19 acres between Greenmount Ave and Mathews St and the extensions of E 28th and E 29th Streets — the west-side 2800-block frontage, the rowhouses that had risen after the old Oriole Park ballpark cleared.

summary: A July 1957 pre-opening feature by Sun business editor Carroll E. Williams detailed the Waverly Tower's 17 outlets and ~65,000 sq ft of store/storage space. The anchor was a Food Fair supermarket (22,000 sq ft); the next largest were Eagle's Store (9,000 sq ft — the first Baltimore outlet of the Charlotte, N.C. chain) and Sunray Drugs (7,000 sq ft). Other tenants, 'all of this city,' included National Shores, David's Credit Jewelers, Rabai's Bakery, and Adolph's Beauty Salon, with a White Tower Restaurant on the north side of the 29th St extension just east of Greenmount, plus Moore's Toy Stores, One-Hour Valet and Terry Shops. Community Research & Development had been formed in January 1957 to build shopping centers 'in scattered parts of the nation'; its first was in Easton, this its second, and its third — the regional Harundale center off Ritchie Highway near Glen Burnie — was about to break ground. The Baltimore Gas & Electric survey of the moment counted 30 completed shopping centers in the area with 495 outlets, of which 'Waverly, 13' was one — the corridor entering the postwar shopping-center age.

The Greenmount & 33rd corner thus sits on the corridor's deepest chain of title. (See the corridor's original land grants: Huntington/Stansbury 1688 and Merryman's Lot 1688.)

summary: East 33rd Street is one of Baltimore's Olmsted-designed parkways, the 'green ribbon' connecting the city's major parks. The 1903 Municipal Art Society call for new parks led the city to commission the Olmsted Brothers (OBLA), whose 1904 'Report Upon the Development of Public Grounds for Greater Baltimore' proposed the parkway system. In 1907 Baltimore spent $70,000 of a $1-million park-bond issue assembling a 60-acre parcel along the newly-authorized 33rd Street boulevard. Construction of 33rd Street and the Alameda — linking Wyman Park, Venable Park, Lake Montebello and Clifton Park — began in 1911; the roads were paved and opened to traffic in 1914, and the tree-and-shrub 'parking' of the median was completed in 1916. As originally designed the parkways were to be 120-foot curvaceous boulevards (a central drive, two ancillary drives, a bike path, a promenade, and planted medians); financial and land constraints yielded the straighter four-lane road with the wide grassy, tree-lined median that still defines 33rd Street at Greenmount.

summary: On August 31, 1972, about 100 Waverly residents took their battle against the paving-over of part of the grassy 33rd Street median to the city director of public works. The flashpoint was a proposed left-turn-lane at Greenmount & 33rd; residents charged it was part of a larger plan to divert heavy traffic out of the wealthier, less-populated Guilford section — 'the matter of the median strip had become somewhat of a class issue for the Waverly residents.' A vivid instance of the Greenmount/Waverly-vs-Guilford fault line playing out at this exact corner.

summary: One of 33rd Street's most storied living landmarks stands west of Greenmount at Union Memorial Hospital. In November 1939, after his release from Alcatraz (where he had served time for tax evasion), Al Capone came to Baltimore's Union Memorial Hospital to be treated for syphilis (paresis). In gratitude he gave the hospital two Japanese weeping cherry trees; one was later lost to a hospital-wing expansion, but the other still blooms each spring and is celebrated as a Baltimore landmark. A vivid piece of the 33rd Street boulevard's lore, on the same Olmsted parkway that runs through the Greenmount corridor's north edge. (Note: Union Memorial fronts 33rd St near Calvert/University Parkway, roughly a mile west of the Greenmount & 33rd corner; recorded here as 33rd-Street-corridor context. The popular retelling that Capone 'took over the entire 5th floor' is folklore-grade.)

summary: East 33rd Street hardened into a social boundary. It became the dividing line between Waverly (north) and Better Waverly (south) and between their two neighborhood associations — the Waverly Improvement Association (WIA) took the north side of 33rd as its southern border, and the Better Waverly Community Organization (BWCO) took the south side as its northern border. The 1940 Federal Home Loan Bank Board study 'Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation' selected the area north of 33rd for conservation while describing the area to its south as a 'slum district' — helping cement 33rd Street as a border. The line had a racial dimension too: the corridor's segregated schooling put the white school at Greenmount & Gorsuch (later up on 34th) and the 'colored' school near Brentwood, Barclay and Merryman (its site now the 32nd Street/Waverly Farmers' Market parking lot). The 1972 fight over paving the median for a left-turn lane at Greenmount & 33rd (Waverly vs 'wealthier Guilford') was the same fault line at the same corner.

summary: The most famous landmark on the 33rd Street boulevard east of Greenmount was the stadium at Venable Park. A predecessor 'new stadium' was erected in 1922 in the portion of Venable Park north of the 33rd Street boulevard (Baltimore/Municipal Stadium), later rebuilt as Memorial Stadium — home of the Baltimore Colts and Orioles, 'the old gray lady of 33rd Street.' The Colts left for Indianapolis in 1984 and the Orioles left for Camden Yards in 1992; the site was later redeveloped (with the old Eastern High School property) into Stadium Place and a community playground. Hundreds of thousands of fans passed through the Waverly/Greenmount commercial corridor to reach games here — the north-end counterpart to the corridor's earlier Oriole/Terrapin ballparks at 29th-30th.

summary: The hub of the old village was the York Turnpike toll gate, which stood at York Road and Gilmore Lane. Established with the turnpike (laid out 1741; toll road financed from ~1810), the Waverly toll gate and house served as a center of commerce and communication until the toll gates along the road were removed in 1894. Its recorded gate keepers were David Mumma, William Eaton, T. S. Bonsal, and T. Schoofield — the men who took the tolls from travelers, farmers driving livestock to market, and stagecoaches on Baltimore's main overland road to the north.

summary: The Aull family were among the founders of Waverly village. Jacob Aull kept a shoemaker's shop in the 1830s hamlet of Huntingdon (the pre-Waverly settlement), and his residence — a snow-capped gambrel-roofed frame cottage dated 1836 — stood on the west side of York Road near 31st Street. The Aulls put down deep roots along the road: a later Jacob H. Aull built the 'Eagle Nest' mansion (1884) on the west side of York Road near 25th Street, and the 'old Aull residence' at Brentwood and East 31st survives today as the Thir-Tea-First Street Café & Tea. The family name threads through a century of village life.

summary: Louis J. Aull, a builder of the next Aull generation, put up his own Victorian frame residence in 1888 at 414 Waverly Avenue, running his shop at 3101 Talbot Street. The house — photographed with a mounted policeman and the family on the porch — later had a commercial storefront added; from 1988 to 2001 it housed the 'Old Waverly History Exchange & Tea Room,' owned by Donna Beth Joy Shapiro and Fred Shoken, who restored parts of it (and used this very image on their sign) while wishing they could have removed the storefront and restored the original front porch. A neat closing of the loop: a founding builder's house became a shop celebrating the village's history.

summary: A first-person village census in prose. Verbatim highlights: OXFORD: 'numerous neat and cosy houses. Several of them are owned by Mr. John Knobloch. There is also a fine brick store... of which Mr. Theodore A. Bokel is proprietor... contains many fine and convenient residences. Several of these are owned by Mr. A. D. Clemens, the owner of most of the land.' TOLLGATE: 'Before reaching Waverly, a point commonly known as the "first tollgate," is the finely-situated place of Mr. Samuel Brady.' RAILROAD & BAPTIST CHURCH: 'The Peabody Heights and Waverley railroad, extending from the present Charles street terminus at Northern Boundary avenue to Waverley, will be completed... about the first of August... The route of this road will cause the tearing down of the old Baptist church, situated near the tollgate. Another site has been selected, and a new church will be erected at a cost of from $10,000 to $15,000. The pastor, Rev. John Berg, has already about $5,000... to be built of brick, and is to seat about 500 persons.' ESTATES: 'On the road running from the right of the tollgate... are the fine places of Messrs. Henry Taylor, A. Hoen, M. P. Smith, George Saunders, W. S. Thompson'; 'the fine Wilson estate, embracing several acres... adjoining which on the north is the magnificent McDonald estate, which binds both on the York road and Charles street avenue... The McDonald mansion is a model for convenience and comfort'; 'the elegant place of the late Mrs. Gen. McDonald... the elegant country residence of Mr. Charles Taylor, and the fine cottages of Dr. R. Sappington, Mr. Atkinson, Mr. Milholland, Mr. Savin... and the fine place of Mr. I. N. Steele.' HALL: 'Among the numerous attract[ions is] a fine public hall, erected re[cently at] $12,000' — the hall standing by JULY 1871. Explains booklet items 15/16 (the railroad forced the Baptist church move; the 1873 'new church' at Barclay & 31st is Rev. Berg's brick church).

summary: 'A requiem mass for Joseph Varsalona, a shoe repairman in Baltimore for 54 years, will be offered at 10 A.M. Friday at St. Ann's Church, Greenmount avenue and 22d streets. Mr. Varsalona died unexpectedly Monday at his summer home in Bowley's Quarters. He was 84. Born in Sicily, he came to Baltimore in 1919 and shortly afterwards opened Joe's Shoe Repair Shop at 2703 Greenmount avenue, which he operated until the time of his death. He was known to his customers and friends as Mr. Joe. He was a member of the Moose and the Sons of Italy. Survived by his wife, the former Josephine Domina; a daughter, Mrs. Concetta Carmen Meyls; three grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.' A 52-year single-proprietor storefront — one of the longest business tenures documented anywhere on the corridor. SSDI VERIFIED (2026-07-15): Joseph Varsalona b. December 25, 1885 (vs the obit's ~1887 — records variance), SSN issued Maryland, d. May 1971, last residence Baltimore 21218; Josephine b. April 25, 1897, d. September 1979. Burial not yet located — Most Holy Redeemer Cemetery (Belair Rd) is the lead for the Sicilian-Baltimore family.

summary: 'A requiem mass for John T. Hayes, a retired city worker and decorated Army veteran of World War II... Mr. Hayes, who was born in Baltimore, died unexpectedly Tuesday at his home, 2701 Greenmount avenue. He was 63.' Drafted June 1942; served in the African, Middle Eastern and European theaters with the 315th Infantry Regiment. Under barrage, he crawled to the crest of a hill, found a German tank, moved to within 50 yards and hit it with two phosphorous rifle grenades; returned through 'a gantlet of small arms and artillery fire,' located a bazooka, and — 'firing one well-aimed rocket,' per his Distinguished Service Cross citation — destroyed it. After discharge (Dec. 1945, Technical Sergeant, DSC + Purple Heart): shipyard worker at Sparrows Point, then ~15 years a city sanitation worker until 1970. Survived by sisters Mary Ellen O'Keefe (Edison, N.J.), Helen Dambrogi and Beatrice Hayden (Baltimore) and brother Martin R. Hayes. The corner's second front-line war story, thirty years after the Meyls valentine at 2703. THE AWARD RECORD FOUND (agent research 2026-07-15, homeofheroes.com valor database): Private John T. Hayes, Jr., U.S. Army — Distinguished Service Cross for action 24 OCTOBER 1944, awarded by Headquarters, Seventh U.S. Army, GENERAL ORDERS NO. 63 (1945). The date lands precisely on the 315th Infantry's celebrated fight east of EMBERMENIL, Lorraine (Foret de Parroy sector): Companies A and F of the 315th earned Presidential Unit Citations for repelling German armor there 20-24 October 1944 — a private killing a tank with a bazooka fits that action exactly (rank at action Private; the obit's Technical Sergeant = later rank). Identity match held PROBABLE: the online record carries no unit/hometown, and the 79th Division's 1946 history's awards appendix is ambiguous on OCR — full citation text lives in Seventh Army GO 63 (NARA RG 407/338 or Fold3), queued.

summary: READ IN FULL from the MSA image — and the 'Marguerite E. Wolf' mystery dissolves: she was a STRAW. The deed's own caption reads 'Marguerite E. Wolf, of Baltimore City... (straw-party).' September 28, 1973 (recorded October 31): Wolf conveys BOTH lots — 2701 (northeast corner of Twenty-seventh Street, formerly Oxford Avenue, and Greenmount Avenue, formerly the York Turnpike Road, 15 x 90 ft) and 2703 — for $1.00 to 'Josephine Varsalona, Concetta Meyls and Rosemarie M. Meyls, as joint tenants and not as tenants in common, the survivor of them.' The companion instrument, RHB 3074/881-883, recorded the same minute-stamp run (receipts 287468/287469), is the OUT leg: Josephine Varsalona to Wolf, same day, same notary (George Sempeles). Purpose: after Joseph Varsalona's death 'on or about May 31, 1971' vested the corner in Josephine alone, the widow used the straw round-trip to re-title into a JOINT TENANCY with her daughters, putting survivorship in place — estate planning by deed, the parcel's THIRD straw conveyance (Neuman 1916, Coughlin/Lovitt 1923, Varsalona/Wolf 1973). The out-leg recites the whole chain: 2701 from Catherine T. Kelly by deed of May 31, 1930 (SCL 5124/305); 'NO TITLE EXAMINATION MADE.' RECITAL-ERROR FINDING: the 1985 deed (SEB 487/238) cites this instrument as 'Liber 3072 folio 884' — WRONG; RHB 3072/884 is an unrelated Hamilton deed for a 409 E. North Avenue leasehold. The real liber is 3074, found by name-searching Varsalona: lesson — recitals can miscite; verify by party search.

summary: READ IN FULL from the MSA image: 'Marguerite E. Wolf... (straw-party)' — the deed itself says so. September 28, 1973 (recorded October 31): Wolf returns 2703 (with 2701) for $1.00 to 'Josephine Varsalona, Concetta Meyls and Rosemarie M. Meyls, as joint tenants and not as tenants in common, the survivor of them' — the return leg of a same-day round-trip whose out leg (RHB 3074/881-883, Josephine to Wolf, notary George Sempeles) recites 2703's full pedigree: fee by deed of May 29, 1942 from Monumental Life Insurance Company (MLP 6320/477), leasehold by assignment of July 27, 1921 from Max Stoler and Sophie Stoler (SCL 3762/310), 'the said Joseph Varsalona having since departed this life on or about May 31, 1971 thereby vesting title in the said Josephine Varsalona.' May 31, 1971 was a Monday — the Sun's obituary said Joe the shoemaker 'died unexpectedly Monday.' The widow re-titled into a joint tenancy with her Meyls daughters — survivorship planned by deed, which is exactly how the 1985 sellers (Concetta and Rosemarie, Josephine having died) came to convey without probate. summary: 'Mrs. Margaret C. Tarlton, of 1009 North Caroline street, was awarded $475 damages by a jury in the Superior Court, Part 2, this afternoon in her suit against Aaron Neuman, a tailor, of 2701 Grenemount avenue. It was said that on June 24, 1915, Mrs. Tarlton was standing looking in a store window on East Baltimore street. NEUMAN WAS TAKING HIS FIRST LESSON IN RUNNING HIS AUTOMOBILE. He lost control of it and the machine ran on the sidewalk, with Neuman and the man who was teaching him in it... smashed the window in which Mrs. Tarlton was looking and... struck her a glancing blow. Isidor Goldstrom represented Mrs. Tarlton and John G. Schilpp represented Neuman.' The Evening Sun's fuller account rewrites the farce: the 'Motor Car Company' crash of June 24, 1915 was literally lesson one. Trial ran Apr 14-17 (docket 'not concluded' Apr 15, img 373321149; 'verdict for plaintiff for $475' Apr 18, img 373322538).

summary: THE DEED READ IN FULL (SCL 3799/101, pulled 2026-07-15): dated November 14, 1921 — AARON AND IDA NEUMAN convey 2701 Greenmount IN FEE SIMPLE to THOMAS J. COUGHLIN AND CATHERINE KELLY, unmarried, AS JOINT TENANTS — roughly $12,000 per the Sun's transfer column. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS: the newspaper compressed the grantees to 'Thomas J. Coughlin, etc.,' but the deed shows CATHERINE KELLY — identified as Coughlin's NIECE — was a CO-PURCHASER FROM DAY ONE, not merely the executrix-legatee she appears as in 1929-30. The 1923 Lovitt straw round-trip consolidated title in Coughlin alone; his will (ERD 164/299) then devised the corner back to her, and she sold to the Varsalonas in 1930. Recital: the Neumans held under the 1916 Williams straw pair (SCL 3047/411-412), Aaron having merged the fee in 1915 (Mutual Life, SCL 2979/316) onto the leasehold he took from Jacob Klein in 1903. Signatures witnessed/notarized by Jeannette S. Fleischer — the same notary as the 1923 straw legs. The 19-year Neuman era ends; two weeks later Neuman bought 2705-2707 from Max Cohen.

summary: The vacant corner store at 2601 Greenmount played the EXTERIOR of Freddy's BBQ Joint — the hole-in-the-wall where Kevin Spacey's Frank Underwood eats ribs alone, run by his confidant Freddy Hayes (Reg E. Cathey, who won the 2015 Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama for the role). In the pilot Underwood dines on the side patio — the 26th St corner exposure; the production dressed the already-weathered storefront and removed the signage when filming wrapped (interior accounts conflict: re-dressed in place vs. a set at the Joppa, Md. soundstage — both claims recorded). In-universe the joint sits in a rough quarter of Washington; in fact it was Better Waverly, a storefront Google Street View shows vacant since at least 2007, earlier a fried-chicken restaurant, a bookstore and a community center (per iamnotastalker's location work). The location stayed a fan mystery until the owner's 2014 sale listing outed it. The corridor's biggest latent-IP fact: a flagship-series canon location, deed-anchored to this ground. A production still (supplied 2026-07-15) shows the dressed corner: hanging 'Freddy's BBQ JOINT' blade sign, painted sign over the corner door, the one-story wood-boarded storefront tight against the three-story row — with a laundromat sign visible up the block toward 2603. The dressed building is unmistakably the one-story corner standing today.

Phoebus & Sons' sold $99 gas water heaters from 2701 Greenmount in 1957 — was the son of Edgar D. Phoebus, owner of 2601 Greenmount until May 1961. The six children named ('& Sons' = John, David, Robert...) date the shop's second generation. summary: A Superintendent of Transportation Office photograph (shared by Marvin Welch, Baltimore Past and Present Photos, 10/13/2021): the vast low tabernacle built for evangelist BILLY SUNDAY's 1916 Baltimore campaign, at York Road and 29th Street — 'in the left center background is a sign that reads ORIOLE PARK circa 1915.' Streetcar No. 790 passes on York Road; crowds mill; a horse cart stands at the curb; new rowhouses rise behind. The block's sacred-and-profane double bill: the Federal League ballpark and the sawdust trail side by side. RENUMBERING EVIDENCE in the caption: 'it was situated in 1916 at York Road and 10TH STREET. Only later were these streets renamed Greenmount Avenue and 29th Street' (the cross-streets north of North Ave carried numbers from 9th upward before the 1919-era renumbering; Sun columnist Jacques Kelly, in the thread, disputes how current '10th street' ever was). GEOGRAPHY RESOLVED (agent research: SABR/Wikipedia): the tabernacle stood ACROSS 29th Street from this parcel — on the SOUTHWEST corner block (28th-29th/Greenmount/Barclay), the abandoned AMERICAN LEAGUE PARK site, Waverly's old 'York Road grounds' where professional baseball ran 1889-1914 (Oriole Park II of 1889; the 1901-02 American League Orioles; the International League Orioles through Babe Ruth's 1914 rookie season). The photo thus captures BOTH ballpark blocks at once: the revival shed on the dead park, the 'Oriole Park' sign on the living one (Terrapin, this parcel's block). THE CAMPAIGN (Sun retrospective 7/2/2005 + campaign histories): February 2 - April 23, 1916; the 15,000-seat 'Salvation Shed'; over a million hearers; 23,027 'trail hitters'; ~96,000 through the doors on the final day, when 'Home Run' Baker and four other Yankees hit the sawdust trail. Sunday was himself a former big-league ballplayer — the evangelist-outfielder preaching on a dead ballpark beside a live one.

summary: A color slide (Baltimore Memories collection; shared by baltimore.history, captioned 'The Boulevard Theatre located 3302 Greenmount Avenue. (1963)'): the Boulevard's marquee reads 'LEE RE[MICK] — THE RUNNING MAN — TECHNICOLOR' (Carol Reed's film, released October 1963); a yellow PCC streetcar No. 7105 loads passengers mid-avenue; 'NO LEFT TURN 6AM-9PM' on the mast arm. Across Greenmount, the east side's full midcentury lineup: the grand brick hall with green arched windows lettered BOULEVARD BOWLING LANES, KUSEN'S RESTAURANT — BAR, a Remington cards-and-gifts shop, MAB PAINTS, and the Save-A-Dollar market up the block. The 3300 block as complete entertainment district: movies, bowling, bar-restaurant, all trading at once in the streetcar system's final years. THE HOUSE (agent research, Cinema Treasures/Kilduffs/Sun): opened October 8, 1921 — 1,625 seats, architect Ewald J. Blanke, a Durkee house (sister to the Senator) with a Skinner organ; twinned 1984; closed 1989; gutted for retail with the auditorium ceiling still intact above the drop ceilings; the 1948 marquee came down in fall 2022; bought ~2016 for $1.2M by the CENTRAL BALTIMORE FUTURE FUND (the same fund that later helped Red Emma's land at 3128) with a 2020 reuse RFP pending. AND THE BOWLING HALL ACROSS THE STREET: the upstairs duckpin lanes ('the Boulevard,' 25 cents a game) sat one flight above HARRY W. SCHWAAB'S soda fountain and confectionery — homemade pistachio and coffee ice cream, wedding cakes — and F. SCOTT FITZGERALD kept Schwaab's number in his personal address book during his 1930s Baltimore years (Sun 7/1/1992; Sun 2/8/1998).

summary: A 7-inch 45: 'SWEENEY'S TWIST (Billy Martin) — BILLY MARTIN and his Corvairs — MONITOR RECORDS #1402-A, 45 R.P.M., Jalo Music, Inc. - BMI,' b/w 'I Found My Baby' (1962). Per collector documentation (Discogs r4207180; popsike auction notes), the record is a tribute to Sweeney's Lounge on Greenmount Avenue — the bar is named in the lyrics — produced by Baltimore DJ Jack Gale on the local Monitor label. A Greenmount corner bar with its own twist record at the height of the dance craze: place-made IP, pressed in vinyl, still trading among collectors sixty years on (Jeff holds a copy). The through-line from the 1942 amateur nights to the 1962 record is the venue's own: the stage that paid cash prizes eventually paid in canon. PRODUCER IDENTIFIED (agent research 2026-07-15): Jack Gale (1925-2018), Baltimore-born WITH-AM 1230 morning host 1957-63 and later Billboard DJ of the Year (1970), was recording local acts (Ronnie Dove, the Kings, the Combonaires) at Biddle Street Studios in exactly this period; 'JALO' = JAck + LOvey Gale (his wife's public records list The Jalo Corporation and Lovey Music Inc.), and Jalo Records 1406 (Ronnie Dove, June 1962) shares Monitor 1402's numbering series — Monitor was almost certainly a Gale imprint. 'Billy Martin' himself remains unidentified (a Montreal-trumpeter attribution on citizenfreak looks like name-collision; no Baltimore Jam band listing) — possibly a pickup band for the one-off. The side was later anthologized on the 'Buzzsaw Joint Cut 7' compilation LP.

summary: 'THE SUBURBAN LEAGUE — Waverly, Govans And Towson All Win From Opponents. ROLAND PARK GETS BUMPED... Waverly, 4; Roland Park, 2. Amid the cheers of 500 persons the Waverly White Sox of the Suburban League won their thirteenth straight victory by defeating the Roland Park Club... A. Bonthron started to pitch for Waverly and for four innings pitched great ball, but owing to a sore arm gave way to Green... a neat squeeze play pulled off by Kuzm and Sommer tied the score.' League standing: Waverly 13-0, 1.000. Five hundred fans for a Waverly nine in 1908 — the sandlot tradition that runs through the Loyalty Club (1923, from 2705) and the Rosebud A.C. (1930, from 2703), six years before the Terrapins built their park at 29th. HOME GROUNDS (probable, agent research): Waverly's diamond was the 'YORK ROAD GROUNDS' — the block at 28th-29th/Greenmount/Barclay, per SABR 'at the corner of York Road and Tenth Street (now 29th Street and Greenmount Avenue),' pro baseball's home 1889-1914 and the amateur showcase ground when the Orioles were away (Interclub championships drew 4,600 there). Deeper still: the WAVERLY BASE BALL CLUB of 1860, formed by lawyer William Clapham Pennington, merged into the Pastimes when its players left for the Civil War — Waverly's sandlot lineage runs 1860 -> White Sox 1908 -> Loyalty Club 1923 -> Rosebud A.C. 1930.
