summary: Michael A. Fletcher, Evening Sun: 'For 16 years, Tom Fannin drew customers to Early Attic, his Waverly antiques shop, by displaying a few pieces of fine wood furniture on the sidewalk out front... at 415 E. 32nd St.' A city inspector's violation notice (March) revealed that sidewalk-display permits were BANNED in the Waverly commercial district under the 'hard-fought urban renewal plan for the area in 1979' — city housing official Roseann Walsh: 'We have a history of people displaying used washing machines and dryers on the sidewalk.' The Board of Estimates split 2-2 (City Solicitor Neal M. Janey + Comptroller Hyman A. Pressman FOR — 'I think what is being asked for here is reasonable'; Council President Mary Pat Clarke + DPW Director George Balog AGAINST — 'The minute we [approve this] we might as well build shelves on 32nd Street'), Mayor Kurt L. Schmoke abroad and unable to break the tie. Dating ~1989-91 from the officeholders; Early Attic thus open since ~1974 — the building's second act after the Hooper's Restaurants general offices. Its painted EARLY ATTIC letters still clung to the facade in 2020 Street View (Dixon-for-Mayor banner era), letters falling, before Red Emma's took the building. OWNERSHIP CONFIRMED (2026-07-15): Thomas R. Fannin owned the building, selling it 7/1/2016 for $240,000 to 415 East 32nd Street, LLC — the assembler that sold the pair to Red Emma's in 2022.

summary: SCL 5124/305, read line-by-line. 'THIS DEED made this 31st day of May... 1930... between Catherine T Kelly unmarried of Baltimore City... and Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife... as tenants by the entireties' — consideration a nominal $5.00 (the real price rode the same-day purchase-money mortgage: at least $6,500). The recitals close two loops in one paragraph: 2701 came to Kelly 'by the last will and testament of Thomas J Coughlin recorded... in Liber E R D #164 folio 299... devised to the said Catherine T Kelly in fee simple,' and to Coughlin 'by deed dated December fifth 1923... Liber SCL No 4114 folio 511... conveyed by William Lovitt' — the return leg of the 1923 straw round-trip, now precisely cited. Witness/notary: Lennox B. Clemens, the Waverly Building Association's own attorney. Recorded May 31, 1930 at 11:11 A.M. — deed, mortgage and settlement all inside one Saturday morning. The Varsalonas, nine years at 2703 (Joe's Shoe Repair), now owned the corner next door; the family would hold both until April 1985. Coughlin bought for ~$12,000 in 1921; his estate let the corner go in the first Depression spring at roughly its $7,000 inventory value.

summary: Same page-run as the Kelly deed (SCL 5124/305-307), recorded minutes behind it: Joseph and Josephine Varsalona mortgage to the WAVERLY BUILDING ASSOCIATION OF BALTIMORE COUNTY, which had 'received therefrom an advance of Six Thousand and five Hundred ($6,500.00) Dollars on fifty (50) shares of stock standing in their names... Said sum so loaned being paid as part of the purchase money' for 2701. Security: THREE parcels — Block 4071's 2701 (the deed of even date) and 2703 (the 1921 Stoler assignment, ground rent $90), plus Block 3837's 319 EAST TWENTY-SEVENTH STREET, a third Varsalona holding acquired by assignment from Edgar N. Dinsmore, November 17, 1925 (SCL 4491/99), subject to $60 ground rent — the family compound wrapped around the corner. Terms are pure building-association mechanics: weekly dues of 25 cents per share plus 15 cents weekly interest per $130 share advanced, interest stepping down 15 cents with each $130 of principal retired; attorney Lennox B. Clemens. An immigrant shoemaker buying his corner with neighborhood mutual-society money — the Waverly Building Association underwrote the block it was named for.

summary: Recited in full in MLP 6320/478: 'by lease dated the twenty fourth day of May 1898 and recorded... in Liber RO No 1734 folio 497 etc was demised and leased by Charles C McColgan unto William L Dail for the term of ninety nine years renewable forever at and for the annual rent of ninety dollars ($90.00) payable in equal half yearly installments on the first days of June and December.' The creation of 2703's ground rent — the classic Baltimore two-estate split at the moment the east side of the York Turnpike Road was being cut into 15-foot storefront lots, when the cross street was still Oxford Avenue. Every subsequent leasehold paper on 2703 (Samuels 1915, Stoler 1915-21, Varsalona 1921-42) paid this $90 until the Varsalonas extinguished it in 1942.

summary: SCL 3762/310-312, read line-by-line: THREE instruments recorded back-to-back on the same afternoon (2:51, 2:53 o'clock stamps). (1) ASSIGNMENT: 'Max Stoler and Sophie Stoler his wife... and Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife' — the leasehold at 'Number 2703 York Turnpike Road or Greenmount Avenue' (east side, 15 ft north of the NE corner of the Turnpike and Oxford Avenue, 15 x 90 to the ten-foot alley), subject to the $90 annual ground rent; recites the Stolers took it by assignment from LOUIS SAMUELS, December 20, 1915 (SCL 3019/136). Notary: Rudolph M. Winterling. This is the deed behind the family legend: Joseph Varsalona, arrived from Sicily in 1919, opens Joe's Shoe Repair — and the Sun's shoemaker-wanted ad runs from 2703 exactly three weeks later (August 17, 1921). He would work this room 50 years, to the week of his death. The Jewish shoe-store family hands the shop to the Sicilian shoemaker — the corridor's succession pattern in a single page.

summary: Second instrument in the run (SCL 3762/310-312): 'Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona... justly indebted unto the said Giovannai [sic] Geppi in the full sum of thirty hundred ($3000.00) dollars... at the expiration of two years... with interest... at the rate of six per cent per annum payable half yearly... Said principal sum being part of the purchase money.' Named attorney: VINCENT J. DEMARCO. Geppi's oath that the consideration was bona fide came 'at the same time' — and both his oath and his 1924 release are signed 'Giovanni x his mark Geppi': the lender could not write, but he could fund a storefront. Release witnessed by Vincent J. Demarco and JOSEPH J. CULOTTA, recorded January 17, 1924 — paid off in two and a half years. Italian-community private credit doing what banks wouldn't for a 1919 arrival: with the Stolers' $1,500 take-back (next instrument), the whole ~$4,500 acquisition was financed within the community. (Same-surname note: the Geppi name later becomes Baltimore-famous via Diamond Comic Distributors' Steve Geppi — kinship unresearched.)

Vinson and Evelyn D. Vinson, his wife. THE SIGNATURE IS THE STORY: Edgar executed by mark — 'Edgar D. The lot runs 25 x 200, spanning 375-400 feet south of 27th Street, with a 20-foot reservation for BOONE STREET at the rear — the paper ghost of a street the plat promised. summary: Same run as the deed (Liber JFC 1070, folio 380, recording stamp JUL 20 1961): Robert L. and Evelyn D. Vinson give the YOLANDA BUILDING ASSOCIATION a $7,500 purchase-money mortgage on 2601 Greenmount, secured by 75 shares of the association's stock. The corner's fourth building-association purchase in the corridor pattern — Waverly Building Assn financed the Varsalonas' 2701 in 1930, Title Permanent their 2703 fee in 1942, Augusta the Phoebuses' own purchase of 2601 in 1947, and now Yolanda finances the Phoebuses' buyers. The share-accumulation loan (borrow the price, buy shares weekly until they retire the debt) was the immigrant and working-class mortgage machine of rowhouse Baltimore for a century, and 2601's title chain samples four different associations doing it.

summary: Deed dated June 25, 1962, recorded June 26 at 10 A.M. (Liber JFC 1302, folio 548): Mark Levy, widower, grants the 2705 Greenmount leasehold to PAUL VERNON MEYLS AND CONCETTA MEYLS, his wife, as tenants by the entireties — $5 'and other good and valuable considerations,' with U.S. documentary stamps of $4.40 implying an actual price near $4,000. The lot: east side of 'York turnpike road,' 30 feet north of the northeast corner at 27th Street ('formerly called Oxford Avenue'), 15 x 90 to a 10-foot alley — subject to the $90 annual ground rent payable May 17 and November 17, with benefit of renewal forever (recital: Nathan and Daisy Platt's lease to Levy, May 17, 1962, JFC 1281/7). THE CONVERGENCE: Concetta Meyls was Concetta Carmen Meyls née VARSALONA — daughter of Joseph and Josephine Varsalona of 2701-2703. Eighteen days after the on-premises auction (June 7), the family that had held the corner pair since 1921-30 took the third house in the row through the daughter's marriage. Eleven years later the 1973 Wolf straw deed would put Concetta on 2701-2703's title too; in 1985 the Meylses sold all three to Strucko as a single group. Witness and notary Mary Margaret Sloman; grantee-index stamp July 24, 1962, assignment code 52543.

summary: Lease dated and recorded May 24, 1898, 1:15 P.M. (Liber RO 1734, folio 497): Charles C. McColgan leases to WILLIAM L. summary: Deed dated and recorded December 2, 1898, 4:20 P.M. (Liber RO 1764, folio 209) — ten days after leasing the row to builder Dail, McColgan sells the REVERSIONS and $90 ground rents on the FIRST FOUR lots (2701, 2703, 2705, 2707) to the MUTUAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY OF BALTIMORE for $6,545.45 — exactly four times $1,636.36, a $90 rent capitalized at 5.5%. The insurer (later Monumental Life) would collect the corner's ground rents for decades: it sold 2701's fee to Aaron Neuman in 1915, 2703's to the Varsalonas in 1942 ('forever merged and extinguished'), and 2705's to the Levys by deed of redemption in 1945. summary: Deed dated May 28, 1915 (Liber SCL 2979, folios 316-317): the Mutual Life Insurance Company of Baltimore conveys the FEE — the reversion and $90 ground rent it had bought from McColgan in 1898 — to AARON NEUMAN, who had held 2701's leasehold since taking it from Jacob Klein in 1903. summary: Two deeds recorded back-to-back May 13, 1916, 12:21 P.M. (Liber SCL 3047, folios 411-412): Aaron Neuman conveys 2701 to John Williams, who immediately reconveys to AARON AND IDA NEUMAN AS TENANTS BY THE ENTIRETIES. A classic Baltimore straw round-trip — the corner's second (after the Stolers' 1915 trip next door at 2703) — done for no other purpose than converting Aaron's sole ownership into a marital tenancy a year after he bought the fee. The row's running straw-party count reaches FIVE by 1973: Stoler/Samuels 1915 (2703), Neuman/Williams 1916 (2701), Coughlin/Lovitt 1923 (2701), Levy/Bach 1947 (2705), Varsalona/Wolf 1973 (2701+2703) — every one an intra-family tenancy rearrangement.

So 2703's chain runs Neuman -> Max Stoler 1908 -> straw 1915 -> Varsalonas 1921.

The insurer (later Monumental Life) would collect the corner's ground rents for decades: it sold 2701's fee to Aaron Neuman in 1915, 2703's to the Varsalonas in 1942 ('forever merged and extinguished'), and 2705's to the Levys by deed of redemption in 1945. Witness/notary Jno. Spring Jr.; Robt Ogle, Clerk. Recites the Dail lease (RO 1734/497).

summary: Assignment dated April 12, 1923, recorded April 17 at 12:16 P.M. (Liber SCL 3996, folio 308): AARON AND IDA NEUMAN assign the 2705 Greenmount leasehold ($90 ground rent, June/December; '27th Street, formerly called Oxford Avenue') to MARK LEVY AND BESSIE LEVY, his wife, as tenants by the entireties. Nominal $5 consideration, but $9.50 in cancelled U.S. documentary stamps prices the sale near $8,600. RECITAL: the Neumans had held 2705 only sixteen months — they took it by assignment of December 2, 1921 (SCL 3805/141) from MAX COHEN, two weeks after selling 2701 to Coughlin and Kelly. The same run carries the Washington & Lafayette Building Association's release of the Neumans' 1921 purchase mortgage (SCL 3813/170) to clear title. Test/notary Lennox B. Clemens; Stephen C. Little, Clerk. The tailor's family exits the block's ownership; the Levy era (1923-1962) begins.

summary: Two purchase-money mortgages in the same April 12, 1923 run: (1) folios 309-311 — Mark and Bessie Levy to the WAVERLY BUILDING ASSOCIATION OF BALTIMORE COUNTY, $5,070 advanced on 39 shares of stock (George E. Leight, President; attorney Lennox B. Clemens; released February 28, 1929, liber 4977/436); (2) folios 311-312 — a $1,730 second mortgage back to AARON NEUMAN himself, a five-year note with ten $51.90 semiannual interest coupons (6%), expressly subordinate to the Waverly mortgage (released early, October 28, 1926, liber 4653/421). summary: Three deeds executed July 12, 1947, all notarized by HERBERT H. MILLER, recorded together July 18 at 1:50-1:51 P.M. (Liber MLP 7179, folios 374-378): (1) Mark and Bessie Levy convey 2705 Greenmount in fee to FRANCES BACH, unmarried — a straw. Its recitals give 2705's true chain: leasehold from Aaron Neuman by assignment of April 12, 1923 (SCL 3996/308); reversion from Monumental Life by Deed of Redemption, January 17, 1945 (MLP 6695/255), merging the fee. (2) Bach reconveys 2705 to MARK AND BESSIE FOR LIFE, tenants by the entireties, with full powers of sale, lease and mortgage — remainders: one half to ALFRED LEVY absolutely, the other half to LOUIS LEVY for life, then to Alfred. (3) Bach conveys a half-interest in 3910 FERNHILL AVENUE — the family HOME, furniture and furnishings included, 'excluding any and all cash and/or securities' — to Mark and Bessie for life, remainder to NATHAN AND DAISY PLATT. The plan in one sentence: the store to the sons, the house to the daughter. Fifteen years later the widowed Mark would use those reserved powers to redirect 2705's fee to Daisy instead (JFC 1281/5) — and in 1987 her children's gift of the ground rent to Alfred Levy quietly RESTORED the 1947 intent. A margin note on all three deeds — 'order filed 8/21/58' — marks some 1958 proceeding, an open thread. Miller notarized the family's paper in 1947, 1962 and 1987: forty years the Levys' lawyer.

summary: Fee-simple deed dated May 17, 1962, recorded May 18 at 12:45 P.M. (Liber JFC 1281, folio 5, 'PREPARED WITHOUT TITLE EXAMINATION — NO STAMPS'): MARK LEVY, widower, conveys 2705 Greenmount to NATHAN PLATT AND DAISY PLATT, his wife — identified in the deed itself as 'the son-in-law and daughter of the said Mark Levy' — for $5 'and of the natural love and affection which the party of the first part has for the parties of the second part,' exercising the powers reserved in the 1947 Bach deed. RECITALS: Frances Bach's deed of July 12, 1947 (MLP 7179/376) gave Mark and Bessie a life estate with full powers of sale; 'the said Bessie Levy having since departed this life on APRIL 27, 1961,' Mark conveys 'the entire fee simple interest, both life estate and remainders.' One minute later (12:46 P.M., folio 7) the Platts leased the lot back to him for 99 years at $90 — so the daughter got the fee and the rent, and the old man kept a leasehold he auctioned that June to the Meyls family. Test/notary Herbert H. Miller; James F. Carney, Clerk.

summary: Deed dated August 1, 1892, recorded the same day at 2:20 P.M. (Liber JB 1404, folio 446): ENOCH PRATT and Maria Louisa Pratt, his wife, convey to Charles C. McColgan, for $45,000, roughly twenty-seven numbered lots 'lately a part of Baltimore County' — the ground on BOTH sides of Oxford Street (now 27th) at the York Turnpike, plus Barclay Street frontage. The lots are numbered on 'the plat of Oxford,' filed in the case of PARKHURST vs. FRISBY in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County — the plat that still governed deed descriptions here in 2001. Lots 72-74 with 114-115 run north from Oxford Street 150 feet along the east side of the Turnpike, 400 feet deep to FRISBY STREET: the ground under 2701-2719 Greenmount, which McColgan would lease to builder William L. Dail in 1898. Lots 75-82 (part) with 107-113 run 375 feet SOUTH from Oxford 'to the lot conveyed by said Enoch Pratt and wife to EDWARD J. COLL' — with 'the use benefit and advantage of a reservation of TWENTY FEET of the Easternmost portion of the lot conveyed as aforesaid to Coll to be used for the purpose of a Street to be opened fifty feet wide.' That clause is the birth certificate of BOONE STREET, the paper street that haunts 2601's deeds into the 1960s. Recital: Pratt himself took the tract from Horatio L. Whitridge and Robert Dobbin, Trustees, December 18, 1868 — the philanthropist held this edge of Waverly for 24 years. Test Jno. T. Maddox, J.P.; per Jas Bond, Clerk.

summary: Lease dated and recorded May 24, 1898, 1:15 P.M. (Liber RO 1734, folio 497): Charles C. McColgan leases to WILLIAM L. DAIL ten lots — the entire future row 2701-2719 Greenmount, each 15 x 90 feet on the east side of the York Turnpike Road running north from the northeast corner of Oxford Avenue — for 99 years renewable forever at NINETY DOLLARS a year ground rent on each lot severally, with a 6% capitalization clause. This is the row's birth instrument: Dail was the BUILDER (his same-run indemnity mortgage pledges the corner lot against $1,200 owed Jacob Klein for building materials), and the ten $90 ground rents created here are the ones traced through the row's deeds for the next century. Recitals: Enoch Pratt and wife to McColgan, August 1, 1892 (JB 1404/446); James T. Lowe to McColgan, surrender, August 17, 1894 (JB 1526/714). Test George McCaffray; Robt Ogle, Clerk.

summary: The August 1, 1892 Pratt-to-McColgan deed (JB 1404/446) reveals 2601's pre-history: Pratt's lots south of Oxford Street run 375 feet down the east side of the York Turnpike 'to the lot conveyed by said Enoch Pratt and wife to EDWARD J. COLL' — the big unsubdivided corner tract, which the 1940 City plat shows as 375 feet along York Road by 90 feet deep. So 2601 (and 2565 and 2567 beside it) sit in Coll's parcel, bought from Enoch Pratt before August 1892. The deed carries 'the use benefit and advantage of a reservation of TWENTY FEET of the Easternmost portion of the lot conveyed as aforesaid to Coll to be used for the purpose of a Street to be opened fifty feet wide should such a street be hereafter opened to Oxford Street' — the origin of the 20-foot BOONE STREET reservation that rides every 2601 deed through 1946 and 1961. A street promised in 1892, never opened, formalized as a utility corridor by Coll's heirs in 1940, and still a paper ghost when Edgar Phoebus signed by mark in 1961.

summary: Agreement dated May 21, 1940, recorded June 7 at 9 A.M. (Liber MLP 6043, folio 136, plat at 136a): JULIA A. COLL AND ELLA C. COLL, joint tenants — heirs of the Edward J. Coll who bought the corner tract from Enoch Pratt before 1892 — grant the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, for ONE DOLLAR, the right to lay 'sewers drains water pipes and other municipal utilities' through the family land, per Department of Public Works plat R.W. 20-32930 (drawn May 14, 1940, W.O. 1949). The recorded plat maps the tract: YORK ROAD frontage of 375 feet from 27th ('OXFORD') Street, 90 feet deep to a 10-foot alley, with a 10-foot right-of-way running through the back land — the utility corridor that tracks the never-opened BOONE STREET reservation of the 1892 Pratt deed. No buildings may ever be erected over it. Test/notary Leo C. McDonagh; approved George Cobb, Chief Engineer, and City Solicitor Charles C. G. Evans; M. Luther Pittman, Clerk. Two single women signing away a strip of an 1892 family purchase so the pipes could go in — the Colls still owned the 2601 tract in 1940, six years before the Russells sold it out of the family orbit.

summary: Fee-simple deed dated February 7, 1991, recorded March 6 at 2:00 P.M. (Liber SEB 2773, folio 131): THEODORE FRANK conveys 2565 Greenmount (east side, 425 feet south of 27th, 20 x 90, Block 4070) to DARRELL WHITE for $35,000 (MD transfer $175, documentary $192.50 confirm the price). RECITAL: Frank held under a December 1974 deed (Liber 3194/739) to 'Theodore Frank, Frances Katz and Harriett Schwartz, with full power of appointment to Theodore Frank during his life' — a life-estate-with-powers family arrangement of exactly the kind the Levys used at 2705 in 1947. THE FINANCING IS THE STORY: the same run carries White's purchase-money mortgage back to Frank, Katz and Schwartz — $17,500 at 12 PERCENT, $215 principal plus $175 interest, $390 a month for six and three-quarter years (folios 134-136). No bank money touched the deal. By May 11, 1998 the lot went to tax sale under White; Haven of Rest foreclosed his redemption rights in 2001. Test Mildred M. Frank; notary Brenda Lockhart; attorney Charles L. Williams — the same attorney-and-notary pair who papered the widow Purdie's $65,000 all-seller-financed sale of 2567 next door eleven months earlier. Two adjacent storefronts, no bank would lend, sellers carried the paper at 12-14%, and both buyers drowned.

summary: Tax-sale deed dated June 19, 2001 (Liber FMC 1580, folio 19): PEGGY J. WATSON, Director of Finance of Baltimore City, conveys 2565 Greenmount in fee to HAVEN OF REST, SANCTUARY OF PRAISE, INC. for $8,287.68. The machinery, fully recited: taxes went unpaid under DARRELL WHITE (the $35,000 buyer of 1991); the City sold the lot at tax sale May 11, 1998 and assigned its certificate to the church April 30, 1999; the Circuit Court entered a Judgment Foreclosing Rights of Redemption May 29, 2001 — Haven of Rest, Sanctuary of Praise, Inc. v. Darrell White, et al., Case No. 24-C-99-002300. THE SAME DAY the church took two more tax deeds in the same liber run (FMC 1580/17-25): 2567 Greenmount next door for $11,635.37 (prior owners Breeta White and Lauren Ryce, the widow Purdie's 1990 buyers) and 455 E. Lorraine Avenue for $1,361.77. The congregation assembled its Greenmount corner out of the wreckage of the block's seller-financed 1990s — then donated 2565 to the City in 2018, which sold it to Kelley & Bowen in 2020: the lot passed through the City twice in twenty years. Notary Helen J. Westfall; attorney A. Keith Weiner (Pettit & Weiner).

summary: In November 1843 the Rev. W. A. Hewitt was sent to the village of Huntingdon by the Rt. Rev. William Rollinson Whittingham, Bishop of Maryland, at the request of Mr. THOMAS HART, who wished to have his grandchildren baptized without the journey to the mother parish, St. Paul's, downtown. The congregation was born with those baptisms and the ideals of the OXFORD (Tractarian) MOVEMENT that Bishop Whittingham was planting in Maryland. Huntingdon was then a village of some seventeen great estates (Montebello, Clover Hill, Homewood, Guilford, Greenmount, Homestead); it was annexed to Baltimore City in 1888 and renamed Waverly after Scott's novels. On 24 November 1843 Bishop Whittingham himself preached in the congregation's temporary chapel. St. John's is the anchor of a three-parcel campus that survives today: the church and its 1.83-acre churchyard (3009½ Greenmount), the rectory (3001 Old York Road), and this 1914 parish hall (3009 Greenmount).

summary: Eleven years after its consecration, the first St. John's church was destroyed by fire. A contemporary account in The Daily Exchange (Baltimore), May 17, 1858 — 'Incendiarism. Burning of a Church in the County' — reports the fire discovered between 1 and 2 a.m. on May 16, 1858 (RESOLVING the CHAP-vs-parish-history date discrepancy in favor of May 16), destroying the church built ~1848 in 'plain Gothic style, of dark granite'; only the walls stood. Insured for just $1,700, 'far from covering the loss.' Rev. George F. Adams was pastor. 'The impression prevails that the church was first robbed of all valuables therein, and then fired' — matching the CHAP report's arson finding. The blaze lit up the sky as far as the city; most Baltimore fire companies halted at Green Mount Cemetery, too distant to help, and only the Independent Company reached the scene, too late to save the building. The Vestry's $200 reward went unclaimed; the arsonists were never caught.

summary: The cornerstone of the present church was laid on the old foundations by Bishop Whittingham on 11 September 1858; first service 22 May 1859; consecrated All Saints' Day, 1 November 1860 (Samuel Wyman gave $2,000 toward the debt). Designed by New York architect JOHN WELLER PRIEST (1825-1859) — a founding member of the American Institute of Architects and the American architect recommended by the Ecclesiological Society — it was patterned after ST. MICHAEL'S, LONG STANTON, England: pure English 'country gothick' of long nave, lancet windows, thick low medieval walls and steep roof. As first built it was only the first four nave bays with a south porch and a new tower. Scharf's 1881 history records St. John's as a MOTHER CHURCH: the mission that became St. Michael's & All Angels' 'was originally a mission of St. John's Church, Waverly.'

summary: In 1875 the church was enlarged into its cruciform shape: transepts, a baptistery (now the Lady Chapel), a sacristy, an enlarged sanctuary, and the bell tower and spire. Designed by HENRY MARTYN CONGDON (1834-1922) of New York — Priest's protege, an AIA Fellow — who also designed the reredos; builder W. H. Allen of Baltimore; Samuel Wyman paid for the new slate roof. (The 1975 National Register form dates this campaign 1878 and credits an 1849 tower plan to Frank Wills.) Interior decoration was completed in 1895; the original decoration was restored 1983-85 (Rev. R. Douglas Pitt) and from 1994 by decorative artist Janet Pope, J. Pope Studios. The stained glass makers, organ builder and bell founder remain undocumented online.

summary: St. John's ~1.83-acre churchyard (Find A Grave #2219356, ~583 memorials, earliest death 1820) holds a remarkable roster. DR. RICHARD WILMOT HALL (1785-1847) — twice DEAN of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, professor of obstetrics, a War of 1812 surgeon and author of 'Memoirs of Military Surgery' — lies here; his and his wife Eliza Taylor Hall's portraits hang in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. THOMAS ROBERT HART (1788-1850), whose request for his grandchildren's baptism founded the parish, is buried in the churchyard he created. The Maryland State Archives' Civil War Burials survey (SC6197) indexes SEVEN Civil War veterans here — six Confederate, including Lt. David Stone Briscoe of MOSBY'S RANGERS (43rd Va. Cavalry), Lt. Col. William F. Beasley, surgeon Dr. Arthur Brogden, Adjt. Robertson Taylor, Pvt. Charles W. Daniell; one Union soldier, Pvt. John H. Cooper (51st N.Y.); and Sister Margaret Hickey, a Church Home Hospital nurse who 'cared for both northern and southern troops.' Founding families (Hart, Hall, Chew, Gabler, Baldwin, Aitken, Ellicott) recur across the stones.

summary: The St. John's Rectory at 3001 Old York Road was built in 1868 (the parsonage lot had been purchased in 1854), congregation-funded in matching 'gothick' style; its architect is unknown (the CHAP report suggests a pattern book; the city assessment dates the structure 1872). It served as the parish's clergy residence and remains the parish's mailing address. One of the three surviving parcels of the St. John's campus (with the church + churchyard at 3009½ Greenmount and the 1914 parish hall at 3009 Greenmount); after the 2023 closure it remains titled to the St. John's Church Vestry, held for the Diocese of Maryland.

summary: The CHAP Landmark Report (Apr 8, 2014, p. 6) records, in one sentence: 'While most burials have a marker (and there are hundreds), there is an unmarked section in the rear of the church where the servants were buried.' That is the ONLY institutional acknowledgment of these dead — and its lone source, endnote 39, is 'Father Jesse Parker, personal communication, March 29, 2014': a single oral statement from the rector, resting on no burial register, plat, or survey. The published record is silent on everything more specific — whether the servants were enslaved or free, their race, their number, their dates, or whose households they served. What CAN be documented is the surrounding world: the cemetery's rear lot opened in 1850; Maryland held people in slavery until Nov 1, 1864, and (per the diocese's own 2007 history, Klein & Smith, 'Racism in the Anglican and Episcopal Church of Maryland') its Episcopal parishes were 'almost entirely segregated' — so a section set apart from the marked family plots is fully consistent with the pattern (enslaved people before 1864, free Black and immigrant domestics after). The parish's leading benefactor, Samuel Wyman, bought the Homewood estate in 1839; Homewood is the corridor's most-documented slavery site — but its documented enslaved history (Johns Hopkins' 'Enslaved at Homewood') is the CARROLL era through 1836, BEFORE Wyman, and Wyman-era slaveholding is not established by available sources. The poet Lizette Woodworth Reese, buried in this same churchyard, portrayed Waverly's Black domestic community in her memoir 'A Victorian Village' (1929) — 'Daddy Black and Others,' 'old black Eli... the butler' — but did not tie them to these graves. The Episcopal Diocese of Maryland's 'Trail of Souls' slavery-reckoning project (2014; a ~$1.39M reparations fund) invites every parish founded before 1864 to research its ties to slavery; St. John's qualifies (founded 1843) but has NOT participated — it is absent from the project and the diocesan history. So these servants remain, for now, real stakeholders in this ground whose story has not been told: the honest next step is the primary research St. John's has not done — burial registers, vestry minutes, and a physical survey of the rear section — that would let them be counted and, where possible, named.

summary: Robertson Taylor (1840–1924), coffee-and-sugar importer of the clipper-ship era who organized the firm Taylor & Levering and was later with the U.S. Fidelity & Guaranty Co. A native of Norfolk, Va., he came to Baltimore in 1865 just after Appomattox, having served throughout the Civil War in the Confederate Army — enlisting as a private, promoted (per the obituary) to colonel, and wounded at the Battle of the Wilderness. He helped organize and establish the Protestant Episcopal Church of St. Michael and All Angels (the parish St. John's, Waverly, had spawned), and donated the houses at Charles and Twentieth Streets that became a hospital for crippled children — later the Kernan Hospital and Industrial School. Died Oct. 15, 1924 at his summer home in Carroll County, age 84; interred in St. John's churchyard (Find A Grave #30939895). Note: his Find A Grave record lists him as Adjutant, 6th Virginia Infantry — a rank discrepancy with the obituary's 'colonel.'

summary: Oliver Perry Baldwin (d. July 17, 1878), of the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun (earlier a Richmond newspaper editor). On July 29, 1878 the Sun ran a front-page memorial tribute written — anonymously, at his own wish — by Professor George Frederick Holmes of the University of Virginia, opening with Hamlet's line for Yorick ('Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio; a fellow of infinite jest') and praising his wit, learning, and 'unstinted generosity which embraced all conditions.' Interred in St. John's churchyard, Waverly (Find A Grave #32287331).

summary: Nathaniel Chew (c.1834–1905), of the Chew family, early Huntingdon/Waverly gentry. Son of Washington P. and Mary Hall Chew of Havre de Grace (a Chew–Hall marriage tie; his mother shares the name of the Mary Hall Chew, d.1837, among the churchyard's earliest stones). Brother of James W. Chew, longtime clerk of the U.S. District Court. He lived in retirement at 1431 Madison Avenue, where he died Nov. 14, 1905 at age 71; his funeral was held from St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church, Waverly (Find A Grave #32289322).

summary: New York Times obituary (June 21, 1932): Oliver Perry Baldwin Jr., ~50 years on the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun and its managing editor during the 1904 Baltimore fire, died at his Baltimore home June 20, 1932, aged 82. Born Richmond 1850, son of Sun editor O.P. Baldwin; UVA law, Maryland legislator, late-life anti-Prohibition leader. Survived by widow Caroline Frances Sutton, daughters Anna Lee and Dorothy, and son Hanson W. Baldwin of The New York Times (later Pulitzer-winning military editor). Buried St. John's, Waverly.

summary: The Maryland General Assembly passed 'An act to divorce Elizabeth Blakeley, and her husband John Blakeley, of Baltimore county' (reported passing in the Maryland Gazette, Annapolis, Jan. 25, 1827) — a legislative divorce, decades before Maryland's courts could grant one. This John Blakeley appears to be the one buried at St. John's (1803-1860): he would have been about 24 in 1827, and his churchyard wife Maria Elizabeth Robinson (b.1820) was far too young to be the 'Elizabeth' of the act — consistent with Elizabeth being a divorced first wife and Maria a later marriage. Identification is a strong lead, not yet confirmed against the session-law text (Laws of Maryland, Dec. 1826 session) or Meyer's 'Divorces and Names Changed in Maryland by Act of the Legislature, 1634-1867'.

summary: Blum's 'The Jews of Baltimore' (1910, p. 243) publishes the biography of MOSES N. FRANK — the 'Oriole VP Moses N. Frank' who re-signed Lefty Russell (of 2825 Greenmount) on the street, beating Savannah's offer by $50/month (see linked 1908 feature). Blum documents him as president and vice-president of the Eastern League Baseball Club for seven years, b. Baltimore 1853, wholesale clothier, Second Branch City Council 1899-1901, trustee of Oheb Shalom Congregation, director of the Hebrew Benevolent Society, Phoenix Club governor for twenty years. The Jewish-Baltimore canon and the corridor ballplayer canon converge on one man.

summary: The 'Kennedy Estate' on the 1876 Hopkins plate — the east-side ground running from the modern 2400 blocks toward 25th St — was the country seat of Capt. William Kennedy (1801–1873), the clipper captain who founded St. Ann's Roman Catholic Church (Greenmount & E 22nd) in fulfillment of an 1833 storm vow off Veracruz; the Wanderer's anchor still stands by the cornerstone, and Kennedy and his wife Mary Ann Jenkins lie beneath the center aisle. Kennedy's fortune had roots in the Veracruz trade including a documented 1834 voyage selling enslaved people. He died Oct 3, 1873; after the 1894 B&O Belt Line came through above 25th St, the estate was cut into rowhouse streets (500 blocks of E 22nd/23rd built by 1896) — the fabric under the corridor's southern blocks. Bonus corridor crossover: Orioles legend John McGraw married Blanche Sindall at St. Ann's on Jan 8, 1902, with Kelley, Robinson, Keeler and Jennings in attendance.

summary: Dec 8, 2019, Baltimore Sun front-page feature ('Peanut King,' Tim Prudente): Maurice "Peanut" King returns to East Baltimore after 37 years in federal prison. The story documents the K.R.M. era at 2400 Greenmount — the grocery King, Meredith and "Joe Dancer" Ricks outfitted with a plush boardroom and a $105,000 upstairs boxing gym — the $50M/year heroin organization that employed juveniles, the 1982 bust (Sgt. Gary Childs, Lt. Joseph Newman — then Baltimore's largest), the 50-year kingpin sentence, and the 1988 forfeiture. It also records the cost, in the words of deacon Bernard Corprew of Holbrook St: 'People would stop working, lose their jobs and homes. You began to lose block by block, a few houses on a street at a time… This was one of the most beautiful communities you've ever seen. Drugs killed all of that.' King, 68, freed in 2019, proposed a reentry center with drug treatment and computer classes; the North Ave store now trades as Bernal Deli & Grocery.

summary: Charles B. Baker bought the old City school property at Greenmount Avenue & 33rd Street at public auction for $75,400, subject to an irredeemable $50 ground rent — the origin of what became the 'Baker Block.' The lot fronted 193 feet on 33rd St and 143 feet on Greenmount and held a schoolhouse of the first school district; contents (books, desks, furniture) had been removed before the sale. The city had tried the previous winter to sell the site to the American Oil Company for $48,700 for a drive-in filling station, but the City Council refused to ratify that deal after opposition (there were already filling stations at the SW and NE corners of Greenmount & 33rd). Reoffered at auction (Meyers & Meyers, auctioneers), bidding opened with New York's Morris Schapiro at $70,000, climbed past a Board of Estimates-appraised value of $47,500, and came down to a final duel between Schapiro ($75,350) and Baker, who topped him at $75,400. Other bidders included Lester L. Smith ($45,500), Thomas J. McDonald ($37,000) and William A. Harris ($50,000); American Oil's Louis Blaustein — the company's founder — had made an unsuccessful individual offer of $50,000 to the Board of Estimates before the auction. The sale proceeds were earmarked to help pay off the mortgage the city took to buy the Hoen Building (A. Hoen & Co.'s former lithography plant) as a City Hall annex under the Broening administration — directly tying the Baker Block's origin to the corridor's other marquee 19th-century name, August Hoen.

summary: By 1979 Maurice "Peanut" King — a former longshoreman who, authorities said, never finished the seventh grade — had risen from the corners to head K.R.M. (King, Clarence Meredith and Thomas "Joe Dancer" Ricks), the dominant heroin organization of East Baltimore. Its high-purity product sold in glassine bags stamped like a brand: contemporaneously "Pac-Man," "Snow," "The Whiz" and "Show Down," with seasonal issues ("Super Bowl" in January, "Valentine" in February); a 2019 retrospective recalled "Honey," "Fifth Avenue," "Gold Rush." Authorities estimated the ring at roughly $75 million a year employing "over 100 people" (a later Sun retrospective cited ~$50M/yr). Lead investigator Sgt. Gary Childs: "Peanut just had the opportunity and ability and he took off like a rocket... It was just a good business thing. If you had $70, you'd buy his dope because it was the best value." ### AND IT WAS A MARKETING CALENDAR. Police told the AP the organisation 'marketed the heroin in a special way to show consumers it was from Peanut,' stamping the glassine bags with brand names TIED TO THE SEASON: 'In February, the heroin was marketed under the name VALENTINE and in January, it was SUPER BOWL.' In March the bags were stamped PAC MAN — the biggest pop-culture phenomenon in America that year. Other stamps included 'The Whiz,' 'Snow' and 'Show Down.' And the branding carried a quality promise: 'Of all the transactions recorded by police, SUPER BOWL HAD THE HIGHEST HEROIN CONTENT — ranging between 6 percent and 6.5 percent, twice as potent as any other available.' A seasonal product calendar, a house brand, and a premium line.

summary: K.R.M.'s signature distribution innovation: a fleet of mopeds ridden by neighborhood teenagers running money and product between corners. The ring owned between 20 and 25 mopeds, each bought for about $950, and employed youngsters aged 15-18 as delivery boys paid up to $500 a week, moving heroin on the bikes down back alleys to elude police. As Sgt. Gary Childs put it: "They always used kids, that was Peanut's trick. He let them hold the dope" — to insulate the leaders, and because "if arrested, high bails are seldom set for juveniles." The exhaust-pipe burn scars the kids carried became a badge of employment; It is often said that Maryland later added moped licensing partly to give police a reason to stop the couriers — TREAT THAT AS UNVERIFIED (see the separate legislative-context entry): a contemporaneous account of a major moped-recategorisation bill shows it was pushed by dealers seeking protection against STOLEN machines, opposed by the moped industry, and voted down in committee. Columnist Michael Olesker sharpened the human cost: kids as young as 11 ran the dope; the ring grossed 'upward of $200,000 a day'; and the trap was structural — 'They turn 18; what are they gonna do, get a job for $175 a week? Give up $500 a week riding mopeds?' Lt. Joe Newman: 'These kids are ruined. Forever.' Olesker fixes the fleet precisely: King went to a Highlandtown cycle shop and bought 18 mopeds at about $950 apiece, giving them to school kids — roughly 20 children working for him, a transportation fleet costing maybe $20,000. Against a ring taking in tens of millions a year, that was, as the column put it, 'strictly small change.' AND HERE IS THE MODEL, STATED PLAINLY BY THE MAN WHO BROKE THE CASE, IN 1982: youths under 18 'with little or no police records' were paid up to $500 a week to deliver and pick up heroin on a fleet of twenty mopeds. 'The juveniles were enlisted because if arrested, THEY WOULD BE RELEASED TO THEIR PARENTS,' said Sgt. Gary Childs, who directed the investigation. 'IT WOULDN'T COST THE ORGANIZATION ANY MONEY (FOR BAIL).' Lt. Joe Newman put the rest of it in the paper the same week: kids as young as ELEVEN were running dope; the alleys were 'too narrow for police cars to tag behind'; 'You get the kids running the dope, and that takes the heat off the dealers… You know what happens when they get to juvenile court? Nothing is what happens.' And the exit that never came: 'They turn 18; what are they gonna do, get a job for $175 a week? Give up $500 a week riding mopeds…? THESE KIDS ARE RUINED. FOREVER.' ### THE PURCHASE RECORD, PUT IN EVIDENCE: James Kearney, co-owner of Baltimore Cycles Inc. in Highlandtown, testified that the organisation bought EIGHTEEN MOPEDS FROM HIS STORE BETWEEN JULY 1980 AND AUGUST 1981, on four separate occasions — and that he was PAID IN CASH EACH TIME, 'generally with bills of small denominations.' Clarence Meredith, described by witnesses as the No. 3 man in the organisation, bought seven in the summer of 1980; Kerney Lindsey, a top lieutenant, bought five in August 1981; Stanley Rogers bought one in July 1981; and five more went in June 1981 to five individuals Kearney identified from his own sales records — Kenneth Hurt, Tony Benton, Lionel Brown, Dennis Lindsey and James Reddick. The government's laundering case ran through the same bills: small denominations taken in street heroin sales were used to buy luxury goods or carried to Atlantic City casinos 'where the money would be exchanged for bills of larger denominations.' The fleet was bought with the dollars the children collected. ### BRAND CONFIRMED: the AP reported that 'the ring owned between 20 and 25 CASAL MOPEDS, each purchased for about $950, police say.' Casal was precisely the Portuguese marque that BALTIMORE CYCLES, INC. of 6020 Eastern Avenue advertised as 'America's Largest Moped' — closing the loop between the police account, the trial testimony of co-owner James Kearney, and the shop's own display advertising. (The $950 police figure still sits well above Baltimore Cycles' advertised retail of $399-$449.95; treat the unit price as unresolved.) Childs, in the same account: 'They always used kids, that was Peanut's trick. He let them hold the dope TO INSULATE THE LEADERS and because if arrested, high bails are seldom set for juveniles.'

summary: King cultivated a 'Robin Hood' reputation on the blocks he supplied — Christmas dinners and U-Haul toy giveaways at the Lafayette Courts projects, and cash handed out for school supplies, rent and gas bills. The paternalism made a heroin kingpin a neighborhood patron even as the same trade was hollowing the community out, a contradiction central to the story's meaning. That folk-hero memory persists: in Baltimore nostalgia spaces (e.g. the 'Baltimore Past and Present Photos' group's Nov 2021 'A Legend, Maurice "Peanut" King' post — the Odell's peacock-chair portrait, 400+ reactions), commenters still celebrate that he 'gave back to his community' — the same veneration the 2019 Charles Hong letter warned against (see #18849). Both halves are true at once, and the film has to hold them together.

summary: The physical seat of the enterprise, described contemporaneously: the ring ran two recently-renovated grocery stores that "stand in marked contrast to their surrounding neighborhoods." Above one was the HEADQUARTERS — "a board room, separate offices for each of the three corporation officials and a room housing a computer for records," protected by "electronic locks, bullet-proof glass and closed circuit cameras." Above the other was a "mirrored gymnasium containing weightlifting equipment, a sauna and a whirlpool bath." The 2019 Sun feature places the board room at 2400 Greenmount — the parcel titled to K.R.M., Inc. — with the gym at the North Avenue/Chester Street store (reported for $105,000). Either way, 2400 was the corporate seat: the board room where undercover officers bought heroin in the weeks before the raid. This is the physical fact that ties the King story to this exact parcel. ### THE ADDRESS, NAMED IN PRINT ON DAY ONE. The sourcing question that hung over this record is now closed. Rafael Alvarez's June 5, 1982 report — the first account of the bust, published the morning after the raids — states it plainly: 'THE RING REPORTEDLY OPERATED OUT OF TWO CITY GROCERY STORES, ONE IN THE 2400 BLOCK GREENMOUNT AVENUE, THE OTHER IN THE 2000 BLOCK EAST NORTH AVENUE.' That is this parcel, named in the contemporaneous press, on the first day, matching exactly the two properties the United States would later condemn by decree — 2400-2404 Greenmount (titled to K.R.M., Inc.) and 2049-51 E. North Ave. The deed and the newspaper now agree with each other, independently, from opposite ends of the case.

summary: The case was built by Baltimore City police narcotics: informants Otis 'Mike' Smith and Delphine Robinson, with Detective Arlene Jenkins working undercover as Smith's companion, all coordinated by Det. Sgt. Gary Childs. Per the Fourth Circuit, Smith had bought heroin from King and Meredith in 1979-80; he approached Ricks in late January 1982 (refused), and on March 16, 1982 Ricks began dealing with him directly — three transactions that month totaling more than $10,000 on 50% credit, assisted by Moffett. Videotaped undercover buys and deals in King's boardroom became the core of the case. (Sun coverage adds that Commissioner Frank Battaglia stood up the special narcotics task force under Lt. Joseph P. Newman in September 1981.) ### AMENDED 2026-07-18b (September 1983 trial coverage: Allegra Bennett, 'Nine guilty of heroin conspiracy', The Baltimore Sun; Patrick Gilbert, 'King, cohorts convicted in conspiracy' / 'Smith absent as trial ends in victory', The Evening Sun; Ann LoLordo, 'Heroin kingpin fell, as they usually do, by informant's hand', The Sun, Sunday Sept 18 1983) — THE INFORMANT'S FULL ARC. The case began in the SUMMER OF 1980 with OTIS MICHAEL SMITH and Sgt. Childs driving East Baltimore watching deals. Smith had volunteered to Childs in NOVEMBER 1981 from the MARYLAND HOUSE OF CORRECTION, where he was held on a parole violation; his release was due May 1982 but BECAUSE HE AGREED TO HELP HE WAS RELEASED IN JANUARY. Motive: he believed King, Ricks and Meredith were responsible for THE MURDER OF HIS BROTHER, HOWARD. He worked up from small buys to the top three, wearing a transmitter while Childs videotaped key encounters; Jenkins posed as his girlfriend and driver because Smith was known never to have driven. The government's dates: MARCH 17, 22 and 30, 1982 (Ricks selling directly); APRIL 23 (King telling Smith he could adjust the price); APRIL 26 (King taking the money, then delivering 100 glassine bags). Childs: "Mike was probably the best informant I've worked with... Without Mike, we would have never gotten King and Ricks." AND THE CLOSING IMAGE: when prosecutors and detectives shook hands after the verdict, Smith was absent — HE WAS SET TO LEAVE FOR ANOTHER STATE TO BEGIN LIFE UNDER ANOTHER NAME.

summary: On June 4, 1982 police launched daybreak raids across the city and Towson and announced the indictment of 11 people — 'the largest heroin bust in the city's history' (front page, The Baltimore Sun & Evening Sun, June 5, 1982, by Rafael Alvarez). They described a 40-to-50-member organization that ran heroin out of two East Baltimore grocery stores and 'employed more than 100 people — including children,' paying juveniles up to $500/week to ferry bags on mopeds, and blamed it for four deaths. Seized: 4½ lbs of 'about 70 to 90 percent pure' heroin (~$6.7M street value), $172,650 in cash, firearms, jewelry and furs. King, 28 (of the 5800 block Clover Road), surrendered June 7, 1982 and was held without bail by Judge Edgar Silver pending a state trial (State's Attorney William Swisher; prosecutor Mark S. Cohen). The AP's inventory of the raids was more precise still: 4½ pounds of high-quality heroin valued at $6.5 million; $302,650 in cash; seven handguns; four rifles including an M-15; six fur coats; and an assortment of jewellery. City prosecutor William A. Swisher put the organisation at as many as 100 people; police themselves dubbed it 'THE PEANUT KING ORGANIZATION.' Three were held on $250,000 bail, including lieutenants Gary Mackey, 20, and Harold Kendricks, 44, and Alexander Mannigault, 19. Assistant State's Attorney Mark S. Cohen traced the whole thing back to its origin: the ring had begun selling heroin about two years earlier 'over the counters of two snow-cone stands,' and with the profits 'acquired two supermarkets in the inner city.' ### CORRECTION (2026-07-18, read off the page itself): the contemporaneous front pages of BOTH The Baltimore Sun and The Evening Sun for June 5, 1982 read "5800 block Clover road" and "about 70 to 90 percent pure" heroin. This entry previously carried 5400 and 70-80 percent. The Sun front page also puts the ring as having "grossed between $50 million and $70 million annually" - a figure that PREDATES the AP wire's $75 million estimate by three weeks, and should be recorded alongside it rather than replaced by it.

summary:
In the first federal trial (which the Fourth Circuit later noted 'took five weeks to try'), King, Ricks and Meredith were convicted of a continuing criminal enterprise (21 U.S.C. Sec. 848) plus §846 conspiracy and substantive distribution counts; the verdict made the front page of The Baltimore Sun on Sept 20, 1983. King, about 29, drew a reported 50-year federal term without parole plus a consecutive 10-year state handgun sentence (per the Sun's later retrospective — the published appellate opinions do NOT state any defendant's sentence). At sentencing the court told him he had been 'dealing in human misery.' A contemporaneous AP wire on the 1985 reversal put the sentences on the record: King drew 50 years, and Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks 45 years, for the continuing criminal enterprise (co-defendants Carter, Moffatt, Lindsey, Rodgers and Roberts were convicted on possession/distribution counts). Clarence Meredith would also draw 45 years at the 1987 retrial. The full first-trial slate: King 50 years, Ricks 45, Marcel 'Black Barney' Moffatt 15, and James A. Carter — a bail bondsman who owned the Dixon Bail Bonding agency on North Fulton Avenue and served as the ring's financial adviser — seven years and a $10,000 fine. NOTE these are the FIRST-trial (1983) terms; after the 1987 retrial the court resentenced everyone — see the June 19, 1987 resentencing entry, where Ricks and Carter both drew enhanced sentences. ### AMENDED 2026-07-18 (writers-room research round, read off the source pages) — DATE CONFLICT, UNRESOLVED. This entry dates the first federal conviction to the Baltimore Sun front page of SEPT 20, 1983. But the Evening Sun of NOV 11, 1985 states plainly that "King and eight others were convicted in federal court in JANUARY 1983", and the record separately cites a Michael Olesker column of JAN 16, 1983 discussing the outcome. The likeliest reconciliation is that the JURY RETURNED IN JANUARY and the COURT SENTENCED IN SEPTEMBER — which would mean "the first verdict" and "the first sentencing" are two different dates currently run together here. Settle against the Sept 20 1983 front page before either date is asserted. ### AMENDED 2026-07-18b (September 1983 trial coverage: Allegra Bennett, 'Nine guilty of heroin conspiracy', The Baltimore Sun; Patrick Gilbert, 'King, cohorts convicted in conspiracy' / 'Smith absent as trial ends in victory', The Evening Sun; Ann LoLordo, 'Heroin kingpin fell, as they usually do, by informant's hand', The Sun, Sunday Sept 18 1983) — DATE — SEE THE RETRACTION BELOW. The Nov 11 1985 Evening Sun recap saying "January 1983" is simply WRONG. The Sun of SUNDAY, SEPT 18, 1983 already carries LoLordo's full retrospective on the fall, illustrated with the seized $175,000 Silver Spring house — so the verdict landed days earlier; both papers' news accounts say the jury convicted "yesterday". Mid-September 1983 is firm; the exact day is not yet pinned, and "Sept 19-20" should not be asserted.
THE TRIAL: EIGHTEEN DAYS, EIGHT HOURS of deliberation, verdict at 2:25 P.M. NINE defendants convicted of conspiracy; King and Ricks additionally of CONTINUING CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE and of interstate travel to violate narcotics laws (King two counts possession w/intent, Ricks three). MORE THAN 400 EXHIBITS, 38 GOVERNMENT WITNESSES, eight defence witnesses.
PROSECUTED BY U.S. ATTORNEY J. FREDERICK MOTZ HIMSELF — "in his first trial since taking over that job" — with AUSA JAMES P. ULWICK. The same Motz who signed the Oct 1982 notice of lien on 2400 Greenmount and later went to the federal bench. Motz afterwards: "It was one of the best, most thorough investigations I've seen of a street drug organization."
THE NINE AND THEIR ROLES: King and Ricks at the top; JAMES A. CARTER financial adviser (a West Baltimore bail bondsman, coin-laundry owner and part-time contractor; acquitted on one cocaine count; counsel Ransom Davis); MARCEL MOFFATT and KERNEY LINDSEY top lieutenants; KENNETH L. HURT and CLIFTON L. FRISBY lower-level operatives — HURT CONTROLLED FEDERAL AND NOLBROOK STREETS (a corner not previously in this record); STANLEY ROGERS courier; BEATRICE ROBERTS, Ricks's girlfriend.
THE DEFENCES: King's (attorney Kenneth M. Robinson) was that the money came from GAMBLING AND COUNTERFEITING, and — held open rather than pressed — that his LOOK-ALIKE BROTHER BRYAN KING was the man investigators saw. Ricks's (Howard Cardin) was that Smith pressured him. Against both, criminal investigator EUGENE P. TWARDOWICZ of the U.S. Attorney's office detailed MORE THAN $1.3 MILLION in expenditures.
A PRESS ERROR TO IGNORE: the Sun's verdict story places the stores "in the 2000 block East North avenue and at the intersection of Greenmount and East North avenues." The second is wrong — the deed, the June 5 1982 first-day report and the 1988 decree all give 2400-2404 Greenmount.
THE PAPER PEGGED A SERIES TO IT: the Sun ran a multi-part "WAR ON DRUGS" package across the same days — LoLordo's retrospective and "Squad seeks to contain problem" (Sun, Sept 18), "While addicts wait for help, crime goes on" and "Police hope facts sway young" (Tue, Sept 20), and a closing preventive-education instalment in which Det. CHARLIE SMITH of the Narcotics Task Force addresses HERRING RUN JUNIOR HIGH — students "about the same age as the youngsters who rode mopeds and ferried drugs for Maurice D. (Peanut) King" — telling them "There are a lot of holes in the cemetery that are waiting for someone who is stupid enough to do drugs." ### RETRACTION 2026-07-18c — THE CONVICTION WAS JANUARY 1983. An amendment earlier the same day asserted September 1983 and was WRONG. The court's own forfeiture notice (Amended Exhibit B, Public Notice of Intent to Forfeit, U.S. District Court, District of Maryland, CIVIL NO. H-83-148) states: "On JANUARY 5, 1983, a verdict adjudging forfeited certain properties of Maurice David King and Thomas Calvin Ricks was returned in Criminal No. H-82-00401." Claims deadline in the same notice: FEBRUARY 17, 1983. So the conviction verdict came days before Jan 5, and the Nov 11 1985 Evening Sun recap saying "January 1983" was CORRECT — as was the Olesker column of Jan 16 1983 (#18846), which sits days after the verdict rather than months before it.
HOW THE ERROR HAPPENED, recorded so it is not repeated: Ann LoLordo's "Heroin kingpin fell, as they usually do, by informant's hand" (The Sun, SUNDAY SEPT 18 1983) was read as verdict-day coverage. It is a RETROSPECTIVE — part of the Sun's multi-part "WAR ON DRUGS" package that ran Sept 18-20 1983, eight months after the trial, and pegged to the case. The Bennett and Gilbert verdict stories belong to JANUARY 1983. Check the dateline on the clipping itself, never the date of a clipping sent beside it.
The trial detail added in that amendment — 18 days, 8 hours' deliberation, verdict 2:25 p.m., nine convicted, 400+ exhibits, 38 government witnesses, Motz trying it personally with Ulwick, the nine roles, Hurt at Federal and Nolbrook, the Bryan King look-alike defence, Twardowicz's $1.3M — all stands. Only the MONTH was wrong.

summary:
The convictions did not hold on the first pass. On Oct 10, 1985 the Fourth Circuit reversed and ordered a new trial over the effective denial of peremptory jury challenges (United States v. Ricks, 776 F.2d 455), affirmed in banc Oct 2, 1986 (802 F.2d 731; cert. denied). King, Ricks, Meredith and Moffett were retried and reconvicted, sentenced June 19, 1987 before Chief Judge Alexander Harvey II (AUSA Charles P. Scheeler). The second convictions were affirmed Aug 18, 1989 (882 F.2d 885). The opinions fix the enterprise — King/Ricks/Meredith as heads, Moffett a corner lieutenant, 'more than twenty-four individuals' — but state no sentences. The Fourth Circuit's 1989 affirmance was blunt: in a 20-page opinion the judges summarily rejected every argument, holding that while Chief Judge Alexander Harvey 2nd 'may have committed some minor errors during the trial, plenty of evidence existed to convict the three,' and that there was 'AN ABUNDANCE' of evidence linking King to drug trafficking and weapons offences despite his contention that he made his living as a gambler. Moffatt was by then serving 15 years for heroin distribution. King had already pleaded guilty in MAY 1989 to the separate federal conspiracy tied to the $750,000, five-kilogram Boston deal his associates attempted while he ran the network from his penitentiary cell by telephone and mail. ### AMENDED 2026-07-18 (writers-room research round, read off the source pages) — the Fourth Circuit reversal, from the AP wire report ("Re-trials ordered; jury pool cited", Richmond, Oct 1986).
THE VOTE WAS 7-3. The holding: jury lists given to counsel should contain only the approximate number of veniremen needed to empanel after peremptories; a longer list, without clear instruction where the judge would begin choosing, diluted the right. The majority called peremptory challenges "an essential part of the right to trial by jury."
THE DISSENT WAS JUDGE J. HARVIE WILKINSON III: the majority "substitutes appellate fiat for trial flexibility in an area where district judges perform the daily duties of administration", and "Defendants do not have the right to determine the composition of their jury."
SEVEN DEFENDANTS WENT BACK, NOT THREE. Besides King (50 yrs) and Ricks (45), the reversal reached JAMES A. CARTER, MARCELL "BLACK BARNEY" MOFFATT, KERNEY WILLIAM "WILCO" LINDSEY, STANLEY RODGERS and BEATRICE ROBERTS — convicted on possession and distribution counts. This is where Roberts, described in the appellate record only as "the girlfriend of Ricks who allowed her apartment to be used", gets a first name.
U.S. Attorney BRECKINRIDGE L. WILLCOX, before he had even read the opinion: "since the cases were remanded for new trials, we absolutely will try them again. We will be ready to proceed as soon as the judge sets them in." ### APPELLATE DOCKET RECORD (2026-07-18d, from CourtListener's index of the reported opinions). Trial court: CRIMINAL NO. H-82-00401; forfeiture: CIVIL NO. H-83-148, U.S. District Court, District of Maryland. Fourth Circuit: NOS. 83-5060(L), 83-5061 THROUGH 83-5066, AND 83-5081 — appeal numbers DOCKETED IN 1983, independently consistent with a January 1983 verdict.
FOUR REPORTED DECISIONS, not three: 776 F.2d 455 (panel, decided OCT 10 1985; reversed; EIGHT appellants — Ricks, James A. Carter, Marcell Moffatt, Stanley Rodgers, Kerney William Lindsey a/k/a Wilco, CLIFTON LEO FRISBY, Beatrice Roberts, Maurice David King); 784 F.2d 544 (decided FEB 13 1986) — A THIRD OPINION IN THE SEQUENCE NOT PREVIOUSLY IN THIS RECORD, sitting between the panel decision and the rehearing; 802 F.2d 731 (IN BANC, decided OCT 2 1986; SEVEN appellants — FRISBY IS NO LONGER IN THE CAPTION); and 882 F.2d 885 (Nos. 87-5096(L), 87-5097, 87-5098, decided AUG 18 1989; affirmed; three appellants — Ricks, Moffett, King).
THIS RECONCILES THE WIRE COPY: the AP reported new trials for "seven narcotics defendants", which sat oddly against a panel caption naming eight. Frisby is in the 1985 caption and out of the 1986 in banc caption; the AP was reporting the IN BANC decision accurately.
WILKINSON DISSENTED TWICE: at the panel stage (776 F.2d 455, 468) and again in banc — against this outcome from first decision through rehearing.
AVAILABILITY: only 882 F.2d 885 is freely readable in full (law.resource.org). The 1985 and 1986 opinions are indexed on CourtListener with full captions and dates but their text sits behind paywalls or blocks (casemine/Justia/openjurist 403, casetext 410) — budget a PACER or law-library pull before quoting them.
NOT THE PLACE TO LOOK: Maryland Judiciary Case Search indexes MARYLAND STATE courts only, with coverage generally beginning late 1980s-1990s. It will not hold this federal case. King's STATE matters (the 10-year handgun sentence; the 1982 proceedings before Judge Edgar Silver; the murder-conspiracy trial before Judge Mary Arabian) are Baltimore City Circuit Court paper — clerk's Records Section or the Maryland State Archives, not the online portal. ### FULL OPINION READ 2026-07-18e — United States v. Ricks, 882 F.2d 885 (4th Cir. 1989), read end to end from the reporter text (9 pp). Argued MAY 11 1989, decided AUG 18 1989. Panel: ERVIN, C.J., with WINTER and CHAPMAN; opinion by HARRISON L. WINTER. For defendants: PAUL MICHAEL WEISS and WARREN GARY KOHLMAN (Kohlman & Fitch). For the government: CHARLES PRESTON SCHEELER, AUSA, with U.S. Attorney BRECKINRIDGE L. WILLCOX on the brief. Cert had been denied on the first appeal at 479 U.S. 1009 (1986).
*** ELLSWORTH AND BOND IS NOW SOURCED. *** This record previously carried "Ellsworth and Bond" as a corner with NO citation, flagged as needing one. The Fourth Circuit supplies it: informant Otis "Mike" Smith "began making small purchases of heroin from individuals at THE ORGANIZATION'S ELLSWORTH AND BOND STREETS LOCATION" and represented that he was reselling "in the county" where he could double his money — which is how he plausibly financed ever-larger buys. It is not merely a real corner; it is the corner THE CASE WAS BUILT THROUGH.
THE APRIL 1 1982 SCENE AT TAILSPIN LANE, in the court's own words. Ricks was arrested outside his apartment on a HOMICIDE charge unrelated to the drug case and stayed in custody for the rest of the investigation. Childs saw the arrest being watched from the window by BEATRICE ROBERTS, Ricks's girlfriend AND ROOMMATE. At the door officers HEARD THE SHOWER RUNNING AND THE TOILET FLUSHING. Roberts opened it saying she had been in the shower — "however, the officers observed that SHE WAS NOT WET and her shoes were COVERED WITH WHITE POWDER." With no warrant yet issued and fearing destruction of narcotics, Childs entered: sink and shower STILL RUNNING, room COVERED WITH WHITE POWDER. He checked a closet, unloaded a revolver, and waited. The subsequent search found MANNITE (used to cut heroin), paraphernalia, a second loaded weapon, and A BULLETPROOF VEST.
A THREAD NOBODY HAS PULLED — ALICIA ELEY. The search-warrant affidavit rested partly on a confidential informant, ALICIA ELEY, whose identity was NOT originally disclosed and was given up ONLY BECAUSE THE ISSUING JUDGE REFUSED TO SIGN OTHERWISE. In APRIL 1983, about a year after the search, ELEY EXECUTED AN AFFIDAVIT SPECIFICALLY DENYING THE ALLEGATIONS ATTRIBUTED TO HER. The court disposed of the Franks v. Delaware challenge on the ground that her statements were merely corroborative, expressly declining to "speculate as to the reasons the presiding judge insisted on the disclosure of her identity or as to the consequences of her disavowal." The court is on the record leaving a question alone.
ADDRESS CONFLICT: the forfeiture notice gives 9802 TAILSPIN LANE, APARTMENT I; this opinion gives Ricks's apartment as 9801 TAILSPIN LANE. One digit apart — two units, or a typo in one document. Unresolved.
THE DEFENCE KING WAS NOT ALLOWED TO RUN: at the retrial he sought to prove MEREDITH ran a substantially similar business from June 1982 (when King and Ricks were arrested) until Meredith's capture in late 1985, to show MEREDITH ALONE HEADED THE RING. Excluded under F.R.E. 403 — properly presenting it "essentially would have required a retrial of the other multi-week case." Affirmed. A jury never heard it.
ON WARD, the court's own footnote: "OFFICER WARD WAS MURDERED BY ANOTHER DRUG DEALER AFTER THE FIRST TRIAL." *Another* — a third independent source placing his death outside this organisation. His direct testimony came in under F.R.E. 804(b)(1)/(5); the appellate fight was over how much of the CROSS-examination came with it, because King wanted excluded the parts about his own prior COUNTERFEITING and MARIJUANA arrests (evidence the government admits it could not have introduced independently under F.R.E. 404). King lost; prejudice held "de minimis". NOTE the court spells him "Marcellius"; the newspapers and his own department spell it MARCELLUS.
OTHER DETAIL: Ricks ran an ENTRAPMENT defence (overcome by Smith's persistence; a mere middleman), and testified he supported himself after release from prison in EARLY 1981 by gambling and working in a grocery store. The 1979 stop — car carrying Ricks, DRIVEN BY KING — produced thirty glassine bags thrown from the window; Ricks was convicted of a handgun violation and ACQUITTED of the drug charges in STATE court, and the collateral-estoppel challenge to using it failed on DUAL SOVEREIGNTY. King and Moffett moved to sever from Ricks and were denied; notably Ricks's testimony CORROBORATED King's gambling account and never linked King to the transactions. CCE affirmed: "more than twenty-four individuals"; a defendant cannot "insulate himself from CCE liability by carefully pyramiding authority so as to maintain fewer than five direct subordinates."

MEREDITH, 824 F.2d 1418 (4 Cir. 1987) for a co-conspirator-statement proposition, and a footnote refers to "a separate trial of Meredith and others on unrelated conspiracy charges." Whether that reported case is OUR Clarence Meredith is NOT established — check before relying on it.

summary: King ran a heroin network from inside the Maryland Penitentiary — federal authorities said he had 'continued to deal in drugs from his cell since 1982.' The thread began in custody: King met a Pakistani man IN PRISON in Baltimore in 1982 and asked him to arrange heroin deliveries to his organisation. The man pleaded guilty and was deported — but BEFORE HE LEFT THE PRISON, KING GAVE HIM A TELEPHONE NUMBER AND A POSTAL ADDRESS and told him to maintain contact with the organisation. In 1984 and 1986 a King associate met him IN PAKISTAN and others phoned repeatedly; those deals collapsed because no down payment ever came. In 1987 the Pakistani returned to the United States as a government cooperator. In January 1988 King called him from the penitentiary AND wrote him a letter, directing him to a gang member; King supplied a BEEPER NUMBER for 'No. 66' — Roland Hines, who also used 'Don.' The Pakistani and '66' negotiated a five-kilogram, $750,000 heroin deal at LOGAN INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT on Jan. 23, but it stalled for months: the informant wanted cash, King's people wanted to sample first (Stephen Chenault met him in Boston in March as 'Mike' to buy a sample). It finally closed Oct. 11, 1988 under DEA surveillance in a Boston hotel room — recorded and VIDEOTAPED. Stanley Ananda 'Spuddy' Rodgers, 30, using the name 'Tammy,' was arrested in the room; Kevin J. Scott, 25, was arrested carrying a suitcase holding $250,000 as he stepped out to wait for the heroin. Chenault, 24, was taken in Baltimore two days later; Hines could not be found. A 12-count indictment followed on Nov. 9, 1988 (heroin conspiracy, money laundering, interstate travel in aid of racketeering), alleging eight contacts across 1981, 1984, 1986 and 1988 and at least four calls between Jan. 17 and Sept. 18, 1988. THE TELLING DETAIL: Rodgers, Hines and Chenault were all on parole from King-connected convictions of the early 1980s — Rodgers 'one of numerous drug dealers convicted during King's fall from power.' The 1988 crew was assembled from his own 1982 alumni. Scott presented as an entertainment promoter (Street & Street Promotions-Second Generation Inc., 2500 block St. Paul St.) who also owned beauty salons. Task-force chief Harvey E. Eisenberg on King, not yet charged: 'if we find we have enough evidence to prosecute him, you bet we will.' THE INFORMANT IS NAMED: TAUQIR ISLAM, whom King met at the Baltimore City Jail in 1982 while Islam was there on drug charges. Knowing Islam would be deported, the two 'talked of establishing a network, with Islam sending heroin to Peanut's people in Baltimore.' In 1984 King sent a courier to Pakistan; by 1987 the DEA had turned Islam, who returned to the United States 'leaving word where he could be reached.' The terms: five kilograms at $150,000 a kilo — worth roughly $7 million on the street. King worked it from a tapped penitentiary phone he never suspected, using what he believed was clever code — 'I like the quality of the pictures,' he kept saying, of the heroin samples. Hines, Rodgers and Chenault, each a prior co-defendant of King's who had already done time, simply visited him in the pen's visitors' room to iron out purity and down payment: 'such are conditions at the pen that visitors may come and go, regardless of their backgrounds.' In the Boston hotel room neither man noticed the closed-circuit camera recording everything; Scott left to fetch the down payment and returned in 45 minutes with $248,000, apologising that he had misplaced the other $2,000. Then the room filled with police. King, in his cell, learned it was over by reading the newspaper. Charges against Melvin Fowlkes were later dismissed for insufficient evidence; Hines, Rogers, Scott (also money laundering) and Stephen Chenault (a half-kilo count; King introduced him to Islam by phone, and he flew to Boston in March 1988 with a $5,000 'good-faith payment') all pleaded guilty. Stephen 'Mike' Chenault, 25, was sentenced by Judge Joseph C. Howard to five years and ten months without parole plus three years' supervised release; his lawyers, Robert B. Schulman and A. Dwight Pettit, argued he was never a member of King's gang and played only a minor role.

summary: The roots, per the AP feature and the Fourth Circuit. King was the fourth of five children, raised in a small two-story East Baltimore rowhouse after his father left when he was five; first arrested at 12 (assault) and, authorities said, at least 24 times since (from driving on a revoked license to shoplifting to homicide). His start, the assistant state's attorney Mark Cohen said, came when he and Clarence Meredith opened a snow-cone stand on an East Baltimore corner that sold heroin over the counter alongside the crushed ice — supplied by one of the city's major dealers who was later killed in a still-unsolved murder; investigators believed King inherited that heroin connection. His first heroin charge came in 1979: he was acquitted but found in violation of probation and fined $100. The Fourth Circuit's record aligns — informant Otis 'Mike' Smith 'had purchased heroin from King and Meredith in 1979 and 1980,' and in early 1979 an officer watched a car 'driven by King,' carrying Ricks, who threw out 'thirty glassine bags' of heroin. A related Maryland state matter ended in an acquittal for Ricks that (dual-sovereignty) did not bar the later federal case.

summary:
King's prison years were not quiet. In early 1987 a State Police internal-affairs unit and Maryland Penitentiary officials opened a probe into a drug-trafficking network King was alleged to be running inside the prison while serving his 10-year state handgun sentence. The trigger: on Feb. 28, 1987 King was found with a probationary female correctional officer in a locked fourth-floor restroom — normally used by women, with access to the roof — in a hospital section off limits to inmates. A second officer, who had authorized King's admission to the hospital that weekend (which other officers testified was 'highly unusual'), also faced charges. IMPORTANTLY, the allegations against the officer were never proven: at the Department of Personnel hearing NO EVIDENCE OF ANY SEXUAL ACT WAS OFFERED, the officers' testimony was described as 'highly contradictory' (a supervisor said he searched for her more than ten minutes and heard 'scuffling'; another officer testified both were already out of the restroom by then), and a union representative noted she had been rated satisfactory with no prior discipline and that there was 'no evidence she was involved in anything illicit.' She admitted being alone with King and conceded she never radioed for help or triggered her body alarm — she said she was shocked to find him there and was trying to work out whether she had been set up: 'I could have used a bit more better judgment.' Management sought her dismissal for poor performance. Warden Howard N. Lyles confirmed the trafficking probe but said no drugs were found on Feb. 28; King, who did not attend the hearing, was held in punitive segregation afterward. The episode sat inside a broader institutional tragedy: the previous October an inmate informer had hanged himself, leaving a note saying he was in love with a female officer — the same officer later found with King — and a pregnant officer alleged to have had sex with an inmate had been dismissed. A Sun editorial drew the structural point: the penitentiary sits in the very neighbourhood the ring served, and many of its guards came from those same blocks, 'making them vulnerable to pressure to do favors for friends and relatives doing time.' ### AMENDED 2026-07-18 (writers-room research round, read off the source pages) — the Feb 28 1987 penitentiary episode, from the fuller AP and Evening Sun accounts (AP, "Prison drug network probed"; Michael Wentzel, "Drug ring inside Pen is probed / Female officer found with 'Peanut' King", The Evening Sun).
THE OFFICER'S OWN ACCOUNT GOES FURTHER THAN "NO EVIDENCE WAS OFFERED". She testified that AN INFORMANT AND ANOTHER GUARD HAD TOLD HER KING WOULD TRY TO USE HER to bring drugs into the prison, and that SHE HAD ALREADY PASSED THAT WARNING TO THE WARDEN HERSELF. She said she was "SET UP" to deflect suspicion away from AT LEAST ONE OTHER CORRECTIONAL OFFICER who may have been helping King.
The second officer — a male, in charge of the hospital that day — AUTHORISED KING'S ADMISSION on a weekend, which officers testified was "highly unusual". He faced charges too. Warden Howard N. Lyles confirmed the trafficking probe but said NO DRUGS WERE FOUND on Feb 28; King was held in "punitive segregation" afterwards.
She should not be named in any published treatment: probationary, satisfactory rating, no prior discipline, and nothing proven.

summary: The supply chain, upstream — now confirmed contemporaneously. Federal authorities charged Ronald 'Ronnie Bump' Bassett, 33, of Queens, N.Y. — who used the aliases Ronald Bump, Zachary Jackson and Harry VanDyke behind a used-car and towing business — as the man who supplied the heroin that fueled the multimillion-dollar empires of Maurice 'Peanut' King and other top Baltimore dealers. Bassett was charged with conspiring with King, William 'Little Will' Franklin and others to distribute heroin beginning January 1982; he later supplied Clarence Meredith's revived ring, taking in $1.3 million over a nine-week stretch in the fall of 1985. Arrested Dec. 9, 1985 leaving a Baltimore County apartment, he was held without bail and faced a continuing-criminal-enterprise charge (life). Separately, the Baltimore Mobtown history blog states Meredith was sentenced to 45 years in 1987. He was sentenced to 25 years — a 20-year, no-parole term for operating a continuing criminal enterprise plus five years consecutive for heroin possession — by Judge Frederic N. Smalkin, after pleading guilty in exchange for the government dropping 39 other charges from a 1986 indictment. Prosecutor Thomas F. O'Neil 3rd told the court Bassett had become a heroin addict at 14 and went on to victimize others. His lawyer called him 'a kind, decent, respected man' who had supported '30 to 40 families' in New York with a massive numbers racket — and turned to heroin only when the state lottery destroyed his gambling business. Smalkin: 'People who engage in drug activities are the enemies of this country.' A second New York supplier, Theresa 'Sally Brown' Tucker, was charged alongside him, and he also supplied the West Baltimore ring of William 'Little Will' Franklin. Before sentencing he pleaded guilty to operating a continuing criminal enterprise and possession with intent to distribute heroin; task-force chief Harvey E. Eisenberg said prosecutors would recommend 35 years, 20 of them without parole — in the event he drew 25. And while awaiting trial he tried to buy his way out of a small problem: charged in Caroline County with attempting to bribe a jail guard who found two bags of marijuana and cigarette papers in a shopping bag a visitor had brought him. Bassett offered the officer $500, then $1,000 not to report it, then $1,500 to flush the marijuana, then $2,000 to simply hand it over. The guard refused every offer — a quiet counterpoint to the corrupted staff at the Maryland Penitentiary. Federal agents said Bassett — also described as an alleged numbers kingpin in Queens — had supplied massive amounts of narcotics to Baltimore rings since at least 1979. His business manager and confidante, Theresa 'Sally Brown' Tucker, 36, of Queens, pleaded guilty before Judge Smalkin to conspiracy to distribute heroin; she faced up to 15 years, with prosecutors recommending five.
