summary: The dominance had enemies. As Peanut King's operation grew, a rival Baltimore faction being 'forced out' — Kenneth Jackson, Walter Ingram, Melvin Stanford, Norman Ellett, Ronald Johnson and Shelley Jones — 'began to gather an army together so they could wage war on Peanut King,' prosecutor Steven Wyman said, leading to two shootouts with King and his men at the Lafayette Court projects in July 1981 (King was wounded). Acting on a July 21, 1981 tip from admitted dealer/addict/stickup man Anthony Hollie, police raided an apartment in the 1500 block of Pennsylvania Ave and seized four handguns, a rifle and nine glassine bags of heroin; the six were charged with conspiracy to murder King. But on March 15, 1982, City Criminal Court Judge Mary Arabian granted acquittal, ruling Hollie a police informant whose testimony could not independently establish the conspiracy. Hollie entered the Federal Witness Protection Program. A coda: one of the acquitted six, Walter Louis Ingram, was later profiled by Baltimore Sun reporter DAVID SIMON ('State spends time in effort to make Walter Ingram do time') as a two-decade career defendant — charged twice in major narcotics conspiracies, twice with drug-related slayings, once for biting a city detective in the groin during a courthouse melee — who had served only brief sentences. Police and prosecutors identified him as an enforcer allied with several of the city's larger narcotics distributors.

summary: The partner who ran. Clarence Meredith fled after the September 1982 K.R.M. indictment and stayed a fugitive for three years — during which, federal officials said, he built his OWN heroin organization; an informant described roughly 2,000 bags a day moving through the Preston and Washington streets area (Meredith allegedly supplied 400 bags twice a week at $45 a bag). On Oct. 30, 1985, agents hiding in construction trucks and vans took him in a stakeout at an apartment complex at Sinclair Lane and Radecke Avenue in Northeast Baltimore, arresting Meredith, 30, and 15 others on drug-conspiracy charges; raids at eleven locations netted roughly $69,000 in cash, handguns, jewelry and cars (a 1985 BMW, two 280Z Datsuns, a 1980 Mercury). The case was built by Sgt. Gary Childs and Sgt. Anthony Cannavale — Childs the same detective who had cracked K.R.M. — and the arrest came just weeks after the Fourth Circuit overturned the 1983 K.R.M. convictions. The 1985 case turned on informant James R. Wiggins ('007'); a co-defendant, Rubin Parker, was accused of threatening that if Wiggins 'weren't dead in a month, his mother would be,' while another, Marvin Gentry, cooperated with the grand jury. It was in part a family operation — the federal grand jury charged Meredith along with his brothers Melvin and Robert and his sister Diane. He pleaded guilty before Judge Frederic N. Smalkin to operating a continuing criminal enterprise AND income tax evasion, admitting he had revived King's East Baltimore heroin operation in early 1983 while a fugitive — re-establishing contact with the ring's New York supplier, Ronald 'Ronnie Bump' Bassett, expanding it, and moving what prosecutors called 'unprecedented' quantities from 1983 to 1985. The arithmetic of the revived ring: by the summer and fall of 1985 it was putting 4,000 bags of heroin on the street every seven to ten days at a profit of about $15 a bag, and Meredith paid Bassett $1.23 million for heroin in a single nine-week stretch. His sentencing was set for July 10, with prosecutors recommending it run concurrent to — and no greater than — whatever he received in the King case. Sentencing came on July 10, 1987 and ran in two parts: Chief Judge Alexander Harvey II gave Meredith 45 years without parole for the original King ring, telling him he had 'profited greatly' by taking money 'out of the pockets of poor blacks in East Baltimore' — prosecutors had urged LIFE without parole, saying only prison would protect society from his 'evil genius,' but Harvey declined to exceed King's own 50-year term. An hour later Judge Frederic N. Smalkin added a CONCURRENT 40 years for the second ring plus a CONSECUTIVE five years for income tax evasion (failing to file while collecting 'huge quantities of currency'). At its height the rebuilt network bought up to $100,000 of wholesale heroin a week, cut it to street purity and resold it. In all 19 members of Meredith's operation were indicted — including four of his brothers, Andrew, Lawrence, Melvin and Robert — and 18 pleaded guilty or were convicted; the remaining member, James 'Scottie' Wiggins, cooperated with the government.

summary:
A cost borne in a stairwell. Detective Marcellius Ward — who had testified against King at the first (1983) federal trial — was murdered while working undercover on the drug ring that included King, Meredith and others. Ward had gone to an apartment over a candy store on Frederick Avenue to complete a narcotics buy, wearing a body wire; when the suspect, Simmons, heard back-up officers enter the store below, he shot Ward before Ward could draw, then fired down the stairway at the incoming officers before surrendering. Ward's own wire recorded the shots and his dying. Simmons was sentenced to life. Because Ward was dead, his recorded prior testimony was read into King's 1987 retrial (United States v. Ricks, 882 F.2d 885). Prosecutor Ty Cobb called it 'no small irony' that he left Ward's killer's sentencing to attend a bail hearing for Meredith and 20 others in the ring Ward had helped build the case against. ### AMENDED 2026-07-18 (writers-room research round, read off the source pages) — the Ward killing, corrected and filled in from the trial coverage (Peter Ruehl, "Ward slaying evidence startling" / "Evidence is startling in slaying of Ward", and Dan Rodricks, "Stark horror spills out on a tape recording", The Evening Sun, Mar 15 1985; Ruehl, "Officer's killer is given life term", Nov 5 1985).
SPELLING: the contemporaneous copy reads MARCELLUS "MARTY" WARD, not Marcellius.
THE RING WAS NOT K.R.M. Ward was "a city police officer working in cooperation with federal narcotics agents investigating a SOUTHWEST BALTIMORE drug ring." He testified against King at the 1983 trial and was killed FOURTEEN MONTHS LATER on a different case. Do not present his death as a K.R.M. reprisal.
THE PLACE, EXACTLY: a third-floor room above the KANDY KITCHEN at 1829 FREDERICK AVE ("candy store" in the prior summary was a business name misread). Ward, wearing a body tap and playing a big-time dealer, waited with Simmons for MARK BYRON WALKER, from whom he was to buy heroin. A police setup.
WHAT THE PRIOR SUMMARY GOT WRONG: it has Simmons shooting "before Ward could draw" and then firing down the stairway. The trial reporting says Ward NEVER FIRED HIS SERVICE REVOLVER AT ALL, was shot four times, and that Simmons was panicked and confused about whether the men outside were police. AUSA Ty Cobb told the jury Simmons jammed the gun into Ward's chest and "BLEW OFF THE TOP OF HIS HEART."
CHILDS WAS WARD'S LONGTIME PARTNER — the single most important connection in this file. The detective who ran the K.R.M. investigation, gave the precut-fence testimony and the tennis-shoes line was the man shouting from the hallway, and SIMMONS SURRENDERED ONLY AFTER CHILDS THREW HIS BADGE INTO THE ROOM. Childs sat at the prosecution table and turned his eyes away when Ward's bloodied clothing was brought out.
WHAT IS UNDER THE KILLING ON THE TAPE: a television was on. The body tap carries the canned laughter and theme from THE JEFFERSONS, then the theme from BARNEY MILLER, and Ron Glass as Det. Harris mourning "I haven't been able to write a thing since 'Blood On The Badge.'" More canned laughter, then the deal, then the shots.
THE INVENTED MAN: to draw Simmons and Walker out about past murders, WARD AND CHILDS FABRICATED A CHARACTER — "MICHAEL GREEN" — whom Ward said he wanted killed. It never went further because Ward died first.
DISPOSITION: killer LASCELL W. SIMMONS, 26, of the 3800 block Park Heights Ave — federal conviction Mar 19 1985; city Circuit Court conviction (second-degree murder) Oct 19 1985; LIFE imposed Nov 5 1985 by U.S. District Judge JAMES R. MILLER JR., who called the mandatory term "appropriate even if it were not mandatory." Ward carried federal-officer status, the only reason a federal murder charge existed.
ALSO IN THE ROOM: Sgt. JAY LANDSMAN ran the murder scene and testified to collecting Ward's clothing; ARA CROWE, assistant city state's attorney, was sworn in as a special U.S. attorney to try it federally; COURTLAND TOWNSEND was Simmons' court-appointed counsel. ### AMENDED 2026-07-18b (September 1983 trial coverage: Allegra Bennett, 'Nine guilty of heroin conspiracy', The Baltimore Sun; Patrick Gilbert, 'King, cohorts convicted in conspiracy' / 'Smith absent as trial ends in victory', The Evening Sun; Ann LoLordo, 'Heroin kingpin fell, as they usually do, by informant's hand', The Sun, Sunday Sept 18 1983) — WARD WAS ON THE K.R.M. SQUAD, NOT MERELY A WITNESS. The 1983 trial coverage names the team Sgt. Gary Childs assembled in the SUMMER OF 1980: narcotics detectives MARK GERMAN and MARCELLUS WARD, and undercover officer ARLENE JENKINS. Ward helped BUILD this case. Both this record and earlier drafts had him only as someone who happened to testify. He was murdered fourteen months after the verdict on a DIFFERENT (southwest Baltimore) investigation, and his prior testimony was then read back into King's 1987 retrial because he was dead. Childs lost a squad-mate and a partner; it is one sequence, not two unrelated ones.

summary: The second verdict, and the inventory of an empire. After a monthlong retrial before U.S. District Judge Alexander Harvey II, a federal jury convicted Maurice 'Peanut' King, 33, and his partners Clarence 'Yo' Meredith, 30, and Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks, 33, of operating a continuing criminal enterprise — maximum life without parole — plus heroin and cocaine conspiracy, along with James A. Carter and Marcel 'Black Barney' Moffatt. (King and Ricks were each acquitted of a racketeering count; Moffatt of possession with intent.) The jury deliberated four hours, returned at 11:30 a.m., and was then sent back to decide forfeiture. Several hours later it stripped the enterprise bare: a 1981 DeLorean, a 1982 Mazda, two 1981 Datsun 280Zs, a 1981 Honda Accord, a 1981 Datsun 200SX, a 1981 GMC van and a 1981 Datsun Maxima; THE TWO GROCERY STORES; two rental properties; the $175,000 Silver Spring home prosecutors said King bought for his mother; and more than $300,000 in cash. Harvey set sentencing for June 19 (King, Ricks, Moffatt, Carter) and July 10 for Meredith.

summary: Inside the store, on the record. At the retrial, undercover agent Arlene K. Jenkins — who posed as informant Michael Smith's girlfriend for four months in early 1982 — testified she once handed Smith $6,000 and watched him give it to King inside an East Baltimore grocery store 'that prosecutors claim was a front for drug distribution.' summary: How it actually ran, per the prosecution. AUSA Charles P. Scheeler told the retrial jury the ring poured thousands of dollars of heroin a day onto East Baltimore streets from 1979 to 1982, operating on two street corners through 'a sophisticated network of street lieutenants with walkie-talkies and runners who used mopeds' — many of them teenagers; Meredith bought the mopeds for seven of the couriers. The profits were laundered through the two grocery stores the three men owned and through Atlantic City casinos. And they spent: more than $1 million in an eighteen-month stretch on clothing, jewellery and sports cars, with King outfitting his lieutenants at Bernard Hill, an exclusive downtown clothier. King's lawyer Gary Coleman countered that the money came from gambling, not drugs — that King had become 'a big-time gambler' who invested with his childhood friends Ricks and Meredith. The three were not business partners who met in the trade; they grew up together. At the 1987 resentencing, prosecutor Charles P. Scheeler put a figure on a single corner: the King-Ricks-Meredith organisation sold more than $2.5 MILLION in heroin alone from the corner it controlled at Federal and Holbrook streets, while the three men spent more than $1.5 million on cars, clothes, furniture and investments in little more than a year. Scheeler called James Carter 'the financial mastermind of the conspiracy,' the man who guided drug money into stock and property investments and taught the partners to launder it through Atlantic City casinos; Michael Middleton called Ricks 'the strong arm' of the network.

summary: The decade-long thread that finally caught him. King met a Pakistani man in Baltimore in 1982 — while in custody — and asked him to arrange heroin deliveries to members of his organisation. The man pleaded guilty to narcotics charges and was deported to Pakistan. In 1984 and again in 1986, King contacted him THERE, from the penitentiary, and King's people negotiated for heroin. The Pakistani then became an informant for the federal Drug Enforcement Administration and returned to the United States. In January 1988 King contacted him again about buying heroin — setting in motion a chain of meetings (a Jan. 23 negotiation with Roland Hines; a March meeting in Boston where 'Mike' — Stephen Chenault — paid $5,000 for a sample; an Oct. 7 approach by 'Tammy' offering $250,000 up front) that ended in the Boston hotel arrests of Oct. 11, 1988. A relationship formed in a Baltimore jail in 1982 reached across six years and two continents to close the case.

summary: The deal that made 2019 possible. Facing the prison-ring indictment, King — 34, and by then moved out of the penitentiary to Maryland's new super-maximum security prison on East Madison Street — agreed to plead guilty to the federal drug-conspiracy count and to DROP his appeal of his continuing-criminal-enterprise conviction. Under the sentencing guidelines he faced 30 years of CONSECUTIVE imprisonment without parole as a career offender, a term that, in the Evening Sun's words, 'would all but guarantee that King would die in prison.' Instead, prosecutors agreed to recommend that all but 96 months — eight years — of the new sentence run CONCURRENTLY with what he was already serving. He pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Joseph C. Howard, with sentencing set for Sept. 12. If Howard accepted the recommendation and King earned good time, reporters noted, 'the drug kingpin has a chance of getting out of prison when he is about 70 years old.' He walked out in June 2019, at 68. This bargain — not the original 50-year term — is the hinge on which the third act turns. The prosecutor's own forecast is the perfect button on the act. Asked what the deal meant, Assistant U.S. Attorney Katharine J. Armentrout said: 'He could get out when he's 70 years old. That is, if he's an absolute model prisoner between now and then, with no infractions. I'M NOT SURE I'D BET ON THAT HAPPENING.' He walked out in June 2019, at 68. DEFINITIVE: Judge Howard imposed THIRTY YEARS for the Boston conspiracy, ruled that TWENTY-TWO of them would run concurrently with what King was already serving, and ordered that he serve EIGHT YEARS of the new sentence AFTER completing his current terms — eight years of consecutive, no-parole time stacked on the 50. (At the time he was serving a 12-year state sentence and the 50-year federal term.)

summary: A byline worth noting, and the supply line laid bare. On Feb. 11, 1987 The Baltimore Sun ran 'Properties linked to alleged drug czar seized' — bylined DAVID SIMON, then the paper's police reporter, later the author of 'Homicide' and the creator of 'The Wire' and 'We Own This City' (the latter starring Jon Bernthal, who would interview King on camera 35 years afterward). Simon reported that federal investigators seized a $300,000 Long Island home in Westbury and a Queens commercial property housing a crafts business — about $700,000 in real estate — from Ronald B. 'Bump' Bassett, supplier to both King and Clarence 'Yo' Meredith. Per task-force coordinator Harvey E. Eisenberg and cooperating defendants: in one nine-week stretch from August to October 1985, Meredith paid Bassett $1.2 million for New York-to-Baltimore shipments, buying three to five kilograms of heroin a month; a kilo wholesaled at $70,000-$100,000 and retailed for two to three times that. Twenty-six others were charged in the case and twenty convicted or pleaded guilty. Simon noted the significance: Bassett's arrest 'marks one of the few times that a Baltimore-based drug investigation has succeeded in tracing the supply of heroin back to a New York distributor.'

summary: The definitive sentence slate. On June 19, 1987, after the retrial, Chief Judge Alexander Harvey II resentenced Maurice 'Peanut' King, 33, and Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks, 33, each to 50 YEARS in federal prison without parole — plus 20 years of probation to follow — for running what prosecutors called one of the largest heroin and cocaine operations in Baltimore history. Ricks' term was ENHANCED from the 45 years he drew after the 1983 trial, at the request of prosecutors Charles P. Scheeler and Michael B. Middleton. Harvey sentenced lieutenant Marcell 'Black Barney' Moffatt to 15 years plus 10 years probation, and bail bondsman James C. Carter — the man who laundered the profits — to eight years and a $15,000 fine (up from seven years and $10,000). Harvey accused them of 'dealing in human misery' and noted that two juries, in 1983 and 1987, had found the evidence against them 'overwhelming.' Both Ricks and Carter had taken the stand to deny involvement; Ricks claimed his money came from gambling. 'The jury didn't believe you and neither did I,' Harvey told him.

summary: A defendant names the pattern, in open court. At his 1987 resentencing Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks — who, the Evening Sun noted, 'like the other defendants is black' — told Chief Judge Alexander Harvey II that since returning to Baltimore for the retrial, 'it seems to me all the white guys [sentenced in federal court] get between 10 and 20 years' on continuing-criminal-enterprise convictions, 'but blacks get far longer sentences for the same offense.' Harvey IGNORED the remark, and instead chastised Ricks for lying at the second trial. Ricks then drew 50 years without parole. Whatever one makes of the speaker, the observation sits in the public record of this case — a defendant identifying federal sentencing disparity in 1987, years before it became a national reckoning, and being met with silence from the bench.

summary: What replaced them. When Ronald Conquest, leader of a ten-man crew called 'The New York Boys,' pleaded guilty to federal heroin charges, a Drug Enforcement Administration spokesman said plainly that the gang 'set up shop in Baltimore to fill a void left by the federal prosecutions of such local drug kingpins as Clarence "Yo" Meredith and Maurice D. "Peanut" King.' The crew moved at least a kilogram of heroin into Baltimore every month or two — some of it 91.1 percent pure — funding a $35,000 BMW, a $4,500 fur coat and custom shoes at $300 to $1,200 a pair, and armed itself with Magnum pistols fitted with laser sights and hollow-point rounds. The kingpin prosecutions removed the men; they did not remove the market. Everything the corridor lost to heroin after 1987 happened on a corner someone else had already claimed.

summary: ODELL'S ITSELF WAS DRUG MONEY — and it was taken. On Dec. 3, 1987 at 7 p.m., about 50 federal agents from the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force forced open the metal roll-down door of Odell's, the cavernous East North Avenue nightclub — two dance floors, room for 1,000, the flashiest discotheque in Baltimore — broke a dead-bolt and raided it, seizing business records and a pistol-grip shotgun. The club was padlocked as proceeds of an illegal enterprise. Its owner, Phillip A. 'Phil Boy' Murray, had bought Odell's in 1984 while working — for eighteen years — as a cable inspector in the city's Bureau of Highways. Intelligence from the 1985 Clarence 'Magic' Meredith investigation revealed Murray was the source of supply not only for William E. 'Little Will' Franklin's West Baltimore organisation but for THE EAST-SIDE RING HEADED BY MEREDITH AND MAURICE 'PEANUT' KING. Casino records showed Murray and Franklin gambled at least $1.6 million in Atlantic City while Murray drew a city salary of at most $20,000; he was separately indicted for bribery and stealing $4,651.40 in city wages. Both pleaded guilty (Murray by Alford plea); the government recommended six years for Murray, eleven for Franklin. Reported by DAVID SIMON — his third byline in this story.

summary: The detective who broke the case, on the children he could not reach. Years later, Gary Childs — by then a city homicide detective, but working CID narcotics during the King case — told Michael Olesker about delivering a morality pitch to King's fourteen-year-old couriers and getting absolutely nowhere. 'You tell a kid, "Listen, this is no good for you. Go back to school and learn a trade,"' Childs said. 'And one kid says, "You gotta be kidding, right?" And another says, "What else should I do, man?"' He explained why the children could not see it: 'They don't think they're hurting anybody. It's just a delivery service they're running. They don't see the addict shaking and his nose running. All they see is the brown bag they're carrying, and the house they carry it to.' And why the dealers loved it: 'If the kid gets caught, they know he won't talk. He's got allegiance to the money and the moped.' Then the detail that holds the whole tragedy: 'One of the kids working for Peanut had a father who was a bus driver. The kid had more tennis shoes than the father had neckties.' 'How do you reach a kid like that?' Childs said. 'I don't know. The dealers get to more people than we do.'

summary: The claim that makes this a national story, not a local one. Writing after an EIGHT-YEAR-OLD boy was arrested in Southwest Baltimore for stashing cocaine, Michael Olesker traced the practice to one man: 'This is a legacy of Peanut. He is the godfather of child labor in the narcotics field.' A city policeman who worked the King case agreed: 'Peanut hired all these kids, and other drug dealers around town saw it. In fact, HE MIGHT HAVE BEEN THE FIRST ONE IN THE COUNTRY WITH THE IDEA. I guess that's his claim to fame.' And then the mechanism of inheritance, which is the darkest thing in this entire record: 'Some of those kids were 12 and 13 years old back then. They're still on the street, only they're about 20 years old now. In other words, old enough to hustle dope and hire some 8-year-old kid to stand in a back yard and stash the stuff, and look real innocent when the cops come around.' The city logged 14,000 drug arrests that year, nearly 1,400 of them juveniles. 'When Peanut King got his brainstorm to hire children, he set off ripples that are still reaching shore.' Olesker set all of it against Reagan's State of the Union boast of 'an untold American success story' in the drug war. ### MAJOR CORRECTION — 'FIRST IN THE COUNTRY' IS WRONG, AND WE CAN NOW PROVE IT. The officer's claim that King 'might have been the first one in the country with the idea' is contradicted by contemporaneous evidence, including in the Sun's own pages. New York had been using children as pushers since the early 1970s, and reporting at the time attributed it directly to policy: 'The use of children as dope pushers reportedly has been GROWING SINCE THE STATE MANDATED TOUGH PRISON TERMS FOR CONVICTED ADULT PUSHERS. Children under 16 are not subject to such penalties, under rules of the family courts where their cases are processed.' Most decisively, THE BALTIMORE SUN ITSELF PUBLISHED A FULL ACCOUNT OF THE MODEL ON SEPT. 21, 1980 — Jill Nelson's 'The kids who serve crime,' on Harlem's 115th Street (see the separate entry) — while King's own moped fleet was still being assembled (purchases ran July 1980 to August 1981). The honest and stronger claim is therefore NOT that King invented the juvenile-courier model, but that he IMPORTED AND INDUSTRIALISED IT IN BALTIMORE, and that his genuine innovation was the DELIVERY SYSTEM: a moped fleet and precut escape fences, which Harlem's block-bound crews did not have. Olesker's 'godfather of child labour' stands as a Baltimore-local judgement about legacy, not a claim of national priority.

summary: The sharpest contemporaneous critique of the veneration itself — and it came from a Black Baltimorean. In a Sun op-ed titled "Where the one-eyed man rules" (illustrated with a crowned figure by Carfagno), Margaret D. Pagan took the Greek proverb "in the land of the blind the one-eyed man is king" and applied it to her own city: "We nod our heads in confused amazement when we see men like Maurice "Peanut" King, "Little Melvin" Williams and, in past years, Little Willie Adams venerated as kings. These men earned a fortune and built a power base on criminal activity. But the land of ignorance, degradation and poverty to which black Americans have historically been assigned has become and still remains the land of the blind." On the Robin Hood myth specifically: "it should not be surprising that drug dealers are the kings of the ghetto. For they alone among the masses have overcome the odds and acquired the trappings of royalty: money, power and prestige. IN RETURN FOR CRIPPLING THE LIVES OF THEIR SUBJECTS, THEY TOSS OUT ALMS HERE AND THERE TO RELIEVE THE SUFFERING OF A FEW." And the cost of the veneration: "because we venerate these one-eyed kings, we are further blinded to what can be achieved with full vision. Black ghetto-dwellers need the help of those who live fully in the light. But they also need to remove the scales from their own eyes and take a good look at the destruction their blindness has allowed."

summary: A judge names the aftermath from the bench. Circuit Judge John Prevas — a city prosecutor for fifteen years before taking the robes — told Michael Olesker that everything about narcotics distribution had changed. In the early 1970s the big shots were men like John 'Liddie' Jones, who 'employed scores of people in an operation with tentacles throughout the community… a great Superfly model, full of swagger.' Then: 'THE LAST GUY WHO CONTROLLED ANY TYPE OF SERIOUS ORGANIZATION AROUND HERE WAS MAURICE "PEANUT" KING, who's now ensconced at the state penitentiary. He's out of street circulation, BUT HE LEFT A KIND OF LEGACY. With King, a lot of his employees were kids.' What replaced the organisations was not order but fragmentation: 'Everything is splintered. It's hard for the cops to know where to turn first, when there are independent, fly-by-night people hustling dope in every direction, instead of large organizations on which they can focus.' And the human arithmetic of the legacy: 'Today, if a dealer reaches 20 years old, he's either dead or in prison. That's how young they're starting, and how quickly they burn themselves out. We've got kids who are superstars at 11, and they're in for 20 years when they're 19.' In the same column a city officer pointed out a boy 'about waist high' — 'He's 8 or 9, and he sells dope' — while in Prevas's courtroom the defendant was Florence Blue, 55, in a wheelchair with oxygen tubes in her nostrils. 'Juries are a little shocked. They expect Superfly to be the defendant. But the truth is, a lot of your drug dealers are the halt, the lame, children, grandparents.'

summary: The detail the film cannot honestly omit. WHILE he was running the Boston heroin deal from his cell, King sent word out of the penitentiary that he might be available for interviews. Michael Olesker: 'Peanut wanted to talk about his life behind bars. He wanted to say he was rehabilitating himself. HE WANTED TO SAY HE WAS URGING KIDS TO STAY AWAY FROM DRUGS. It would be a double joke on society: dealing while in captivity, and lying about his dealing. But the interview was laughed off.' Olesker's diagnosis of why a man doing fifty years kept dealing at all: 'Peanut's problem was this: HE BOUGHT INTO HIS OWN LEGEND. He was about to get 50 years in prison for heroin dealing and he still wanted to pull strings from behind bars. He needed to show the law he couldn't be stopped. EGO WAS ALL.' Any account of King's 2019 return has to reckon with the fact that he had run the rehabilitation-and-saving-the-kids pitch once before — in 1988, as cover, while brokering five kilos of heroin.

summary: Where heroin money actually went: into Baltimore's entertainment economy. In a statement of facts before Judge Joseph C. Howard, prosecutors said Kevin J. 'Abdul' Scott — King's 'money man,' known for promoting jazz concerts and boxing matches — had invested hundreds of thousands of dollars in businesses since 1985 while reporting only a few thousand dollars of income. The itemised list: $90,000 into the MARYLAND JAZZ FESTIVAL at Oregon Ridge; $75,000 into the MIKE TYSON-LEON SPINKS FIGHT of June 1988; $70,000 into a WAYNE NEWTON CONCERT SERIES; $25,000 into four rental properties that were eventually foreclosed on; and stakes in two beauty shops — Alta's Nail and Hair Care in the Ashburton Woods apartments, and La Mirage in the 2300 block of Druid Hill Drive. The festival, fight and concert investments were made in partnership with ELZIE STREET, a local bail bondsman and entertainment promoter (the second bail bondsman to surface in this story, after James Carter). Scott lost money or made none on nearly all of it. An IRS investigation found his spending exceeded his income by nearly $800,000 over four years.

summary: Another body in the orbit — and a child in the back seat. Sherman J. Chenault, 26, of the 700 block of North Patterson Park Avenue, was shot to death at 12:30 a.m. as he sat in a parked car in the 6600 block of Waning Moon Way, in the Owen Brown village of Columbia. He died of multiple gunshot wounds to the head. His companion, Sharrell Y. Hudson, 25, of Essex, was shot in the face and rushed to Shock Trauma in serious condition. THE COUPLE'S FOUR-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER WAS LEFT UNHARMED IN THE CAR. Police had neither suspects nor motive; no drugs or weapons were in the vehicle, and detectives ruled out robbery and murder-suicide. Sherman was a state parolee and the older brother of Stephen Chenault, indicted with King. He had been linked to King in the fall 1988 investigation, and as late as that November was incarcerated at the Maryland Penitentiary WITH King — where federal agents raided Sherman's prison cell looking for documents relating to the conspiracy. They never charged him. Reported by DAVID SIMON — his fourth byline in this story. CORRECTED AND COMPLETED: the shooting was shortly after midnight on Aug. 12, 1989. Sharrell Hudson — shot in the head, later in satisfactory condition — recognised the gunman; a second man waited in another car and the two drove off together. Howard County police charged Kent Daniel Tillman, 25, of the 900 block of Belnord Avenue, and Michael Butler, 27, of the 4600 block of Manordene Road, with first-degree murder, assault with intent to murder and conspiracy; both were still being sought weeks later. And the cruellest turn: Sherman Chenault had been convicted in 1986 of assault with intent to murder (alongside his brother Stephen's obstruction-of-justice conviction), an appellate court had OVERTURNED that conviction and ordered a new trial — and he was killed before he could be retried.

summary: THE SENTENCE THE WHOLE STORY TURNS ON. On Oct. 10, 1989 — seven years into King's fifty-year sentence — the Evening Sun published 'A New Breed,' on conditions at the Charles H. Hickey Jr. School, Maryland's juvenile facility. Cynthia Swann, a youth supervisor there for seven years, described what had changed: when she started, 'we had kids here for auto thefts, a little possession of drugs, mostly runaways… It was a training school.' Now, she said, 'we have rapists, armed robbers, drug dealers and users, and murderers.' Then the line: 'RIGHT NOW WE'RE PREPARING THEM FOR JAIL. A LOT OF THEM WILL TELL YOU THAT THEIR GOAL IS TO SELL DRUGS, BE LIKE "PEANUT" KING, AND GO TO JAIL.' The paper glossed him for readers: 'Maurice "Peanut" King was an East Baltimore heroin dealer known for his high style of living. He is now serving a 50-year, no-parole federal narcotics sentence.' Between March and July 1989, drug distribution was the second-largest offence category at Hickey, at 30.3 percent. Swann — herself the mother of an eight-year-old daughter and twin three-year-old boys — said the work had taken everything: 'I used to love to go to work. I really thought I was helping. Not anymore… I've had enough.'

summary: HOW THE COUNTRY RECEIVED IT — and the answer is: it could not decide. Martin Steinberg's AP feature ran coast to coast in late June 1982. The wire copy itself foregrounded the children: the lede put heroin 'on sale at snow cone stands, ghetto storefronts and FROM TEEN-AGERS ON MOPEDS,' and one edition pulled exactly that clause as its display quote. But the headlines splintered ten ways. THREE led with the children — The Miami Herald: 'Teenagers on mopeds made him drug king'; the Anderson (S.C.) Independent-Mail: 'Suspected Heroin Pusher Profited With Kids' Help'; and a Baltimore-area edition, ''Peanut' gang busted,' which chose the moped clause as its callout. THREE led with the money — 'Dismantling $75 million heroin ring' (Stevens Point, Wis.), ''Peanut' King built $75 million heroin business,' 'Police agencies dismantle $75 million heroin ring.' TWO led with the police — 'Baltimore police break heroin distribution ring' (Winchester, Ky.), 'Peanut King's Heroin Ring Is Dismantled' (Jackson County Floridan). ONE led with the origin: 'More than snow cones sold at small stands.' And one, the Wisconsin State Journal, made a joke of it: 'POLICE: "PEANUT" KING'S RING HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH NUTS' — a pun, printed directly above that day's death-notice index, over a story containing four murders and a teenage mother shot holding her child. An eleventh masthead, The Madison Courier of Madison, Indiana, ran it as 'Dismantling a $75 million heroin ring' — money again. The reception is the finding: within a week the story was already being consumed as novelty as readily as atrocity, and the child-labour model competed for attention with a DeLorean. The making of a legend and the missing of a warning happened simultaneously, in public, in 1982.

summary: The premature victory, on the record. Lt. Joseph Newman of the police narcotics squad told the Associated Press that 'the effects [of the busts] on the drug traffic have been dramatic,' and then made the claim the next forty years would answer: 'IT'S THE FIRST TIME WE WERE ABLE TO TAKE OUT AN ENTIRE ORGANIZATION AND HAVE AN EFFECT ON THE SUPPLY OF HEROIN.' Set it against what this same record documents happening next. Within three years Clarence Meredith had rebuilt the ring while a fugitive and was moving 4,000 bags every seven to ten days. Within six, a DEA spokesman was explaining that a New York crew 'set up shop in Baltimore to fill a void left by the federal prosecutions' of King and Meredith. summary: CONTEXT THAT REFRAMES THE INVENTION: King did not invent a technology. He found an application for the hottest consumer product in Baltimore. In the late 1970s the city was in the middle of a moped boom, and the classified pages sold it as a gold rush. 'MOPED DEALER — Get in on the ground floor for the spring of 1980. Modest investment gets you started. BALTIMORE'S HOTTEST MOPED. Area's still open.' — Casal Motors, 6020 Eastern Ave. 'Get into the exciting latest world of THE FASTEST MOVING ITEM, the MO-PEDS Motorized Bikes… a new line of European imports with an exclusive franchise of being the only distributor in the United States.' — AHC, 5130 McFaul Rd. Dealers advertised Garelli mopeds at Eastpoint Kawasaki, 7418 Eastern Ave, and Wheel World on Baltimore National Pike sold Motobecanes — 'THE WORLD LARGEST' — new at $329. CRUCIALLY: the AP reported King bought his fleet from 'a HIGHLANDTOWN cycle shop,' and Eastern Avenue through Highlandtown and Eastpoint was the city's moped row — Casal Motors at 6020 Eastern and Eastpoint Kawasaki at 7418 Eastern are the leading candidates for the shop that sold him the fleet. What he bought was not contraband. It was the season's must-have consumer good, sold on an ordinary commercial strip by ordinary dealers chasing a franchise — and he turned twenty of them into juvenile logistics infrastructure. ### RESOLVED: THE SHOP HAS A NAME. Trial testimony identifies it — JAMES KEARNEY, co-owner of BALTIMORE CYCLES INC., a Highlandtown cycle shop, took the stand in U.S. District Court and testified to selling the organisation eighteen mopeds between July 1980 and August 1981. Neither Casal Motors nor Eastpoint Kawasaki — the candidates inferred from the classified ads — was the supplier. The ads remain valuable as context for the moped boom King exploited; they are not the source of his fleet. ### THE SHOP'S OWN CHARTER RECORD: BALTIMORE CYCLES INC. filed its ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION on APRIL 29, 1977 (Maryland SDAT, Film F2386, Folio 3507, five pages) — incorporating precisely into the moped boom the classifieds were advertising. Its charter was FORFEITED BY PROCLAMATION OF THE GOVERNOR on OCTOBER 17, 1984. A seven-year corporate life that brackets the whole episode: incorporated at the height of the fad; selling eighteen mopeds to the King organisation for cash in small bills across 1980-81; its co-owner James Kearney on the witness stand in federal court in 1983; and the company gone from the register sixteen months later. Whether it died because the national moped fad collapsed, because of the notoriety, or because its owners simply moved on, the record does not say. ### THE SHOP, FULLY IDENTIFIED — AND AN EARLIER CORRECTION PARTLY REVERSED. Display advertising establishes BALTIMORE CYCLES, INC. at 6020 EASTERN AVENUE, Baltimore 21224, telephone [phone redacted], styling itself 'BALTIMORE'S LARGEST MOPED DEALER.' That is the SAME address and the SAME telephone number as the 'Casal Motors, 6020 Eastern Ave, 633-4620' franchise classified. CASAL was not a rival dealer: it was the Portuguese moped marque Baltimore Cycles sold — advertised as 'AMERICA'S LARGEST MOPED,' two speeds, a two-gallon tank, 125-150 mpg — and that classified was Baltimore Cycles recruiting sub-dealers for the Casal line. The shop also sold Ski-Doo snowmobiles, Ideal Motocross bicycles at $139 and Bell helmets. (Eastpoint Kawasaki at 7418 Eastern Ave remains an unrelated business.) ### A PRICE PROBLEM WORTH RESOLVING: Baltimore Cycles advertised Casal mopeds at $399 INCLUDING TAX, with the larger models 'starting at $449.95.' Police and press put King's cost at about $950 per unit and the fleet at 'maybe $20,000.' At the shop's own advertised retail, eighteen mopeds come to roughly $7,200-$8,100 — well under half the reported figure. The $950/unit number should be treated as unverified: it may reflect a higher-spec model, accessories and registration, later price inflation, or simply a police estimate.

summary: A CHECK ON A TIDY CAUSAL CLAIM. Joe Gardiner's 'Wheeling' column reports a Maryland General Assembly fight over the moped section of the vehicle code. A bill proposed 'major surgery': removing the moped from the BICYCLE category so it could be 'legally registered like a motorcycle,' deleting the pedal requirement, moving the drive wheel front to rear, adding footrests, capping speed at 35 mph. And the rationale its proponents gave the House Judiciary Committee had nothing to do with narcotics: registration, they argued, 'would protect them against dealing in STOLEN MACHINES. More than one dealer found he had a "hot" moped on his hands, one that he had sold unused to a regular customer.' The opposition — the Moped Association of America's vice president and 'numerous moped dealers' — 'overwhelmed these dealers in both numbers and reasoning,' and Jay Goldberry of Spokes 'n Paddles in northeast Baltimore urged the industry 'to be vigilant toward any reshaping of the moped concept away from what it was intended to be.' THE BILL RECEIVED AN UNFAVORABLE COMMITTEE VOTE. The companion bills that session, from Delegate Anne Perkins (D-Baltimore), concerned flashing yellow lights (HB1539) and legalising bicycle racing (HB1540). In this instance, Maryland's moped-registration politics were driven by the industry, bicycle safety and theft — not by juvenile drug couriers.

summary: THE DETAIL THAT PROVES IT WAS ENGINEERED, NOT IMPROVISED. Testifying at the federal trial, Sgt. Gary Childs described conducting preinvestigation observations of the King organisation through the summer of 1981 and watching mopeds drop heroin at the locations where it was sold. The mopeds were used, he said, because they could go places police vehicles could not manoeuvre. Then he described one pursuit: he had seen a narcotics transaction in the vicinity of BOND AND OLIVER STREETS, and in an unmarked car he CHASED A MOPED DOWN SEVERAL ALLEYS — until the moped went through a FENCE near railroad tracks. THE FENCE HAD BEEN PRECUT. That is the whole thesis in one image. This was not a gang that happened to own motorbikes. It had surveyed the alleys of East Baltimore, identified the chokepoints, and CUT THE FENCES IN ADVANCE so that a child on a moped could complete a route no police car could follow. The organisation modified the physical fabric of the city to fit the couriers it had chosen — and the couriers it had chosen were chosen because they were children.

summary: THE ECONOMICS UNDERNEATH THE FLEET — and they are not what anyone would guess. On THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 12, 1981 at 1:00 p.m., Jonathan Melnick Auctioneers (Larry Makowski, auctioneer, 1100 E. 25th Street) held a CREDITOR'S SALE of '41 REPOSSESSED MOPEDS & MINI-BIKES' at 1734 Edison Highway (rear) — BY ORDER OF BALTIMORE CYCLES, INC. The catalogue is overwhelmingly 1979 Casals, listed by serial number and odometer, and the mileages tell the story: 12 miles, 4 miles, 2 miles, 'Miles-None,' 140 miles, 388 miles — machines barely ridden before they were taken back — alongside others at 1,091, 1,204 and 1,171 miles. TERMS: 'Cash or guaranteed funds only. All items sold AS-IS.' Read that against the timeline. Baltimore Cycles sold Clarence Meredith seven mopeds in the summer of 1980. Five months later it was liquidating forty-one repossessions. Then in June 1981 it sold five more to King associates, and in August 1981 five more to Kerney Lindsey. The consumer moped boom was already collapsing into defaults and repossessions — ordinary Baltimoreans failing on instalment payments for machines they had barely ridden — at precisely the moment the King organisation became the shop's most dependable customer, arriving four separate times and paying cash, in small bills, every time. The legitimate market was going bust while the illegitimate one paid up front.

summary: THE SUPPLY SHOCK THAT MADE THE EMPIRE POSSIBLE — and it is the missing explanation for why 1979-82. The American heroin market moved in documented waves: the French Connection was disrupted in mid-1972 and heroin stayed scarce until about mid-1974, when MEXICAN BROWN HEROIN filled the void; in 1976 the Mexican government's opium-poppy eradication programme, run with U.S. anti-smuggling efforts, sharply cut that supply; and by 1977 federal officials were reporting an abating epidemic — addiction down roughly 100,000 in two years, heroin deaths down about fifty percent from 1976, to around 950. THEN IT REVERSED. 'Since 1979, southwest Asia has become the major source of heroin smuggled into this country, AND THE ASIAN HEROIN IS FIVE TIMES MORE POTENT THAN THE MEXICAN HEROIN that had been the major source before that time' (Judith Samkoff and Susan P. Baker, Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, American Journal of Public Health, Nov 1982). Federal authorities noted the same shift specifically in Baltimore — away from the brown Mexican heroin 'which had been prevalent in Baltimore during the '70s, back to the purer Mideast variety.' The Hopkins team warned that upheaval in Iran and Afghanistan 'may presage an increase in heroin-related mortality in the early 1980s,' and pointed to Washington, D.C., where heroin deaths soared FROM SEVEN IN 1978 TO 115 IN 1981. King's organisation rose, peaked and fell inside that window. His product's reputation — Childs: 'If you had $70, you'd buy his dope because it was the best value' — was not only salesmanship. He was riding the largest potency upgrade in the American heroin supply since the French Connection.

summary: WHY THE CHILDREN SAID YES — the same answer, from a different city, in an official's mouth. As heroin surged again in the early 1980s, Lawrence Forberg, commander of the Chicago police department's narcotics division, refused the word epidemic and gave an economic diagnosis instead: 'We're not in store for an epidemic. We're in the process already… IT'S ECONOMICS. MORE PEOPLE ARE BECOMING DRUG DEALERS BECAUSE IT'S THE ONLY TYPE OF EMPLOYMENT THEY CAN HAVE RIGHT NOW.' That is the structural version of what Baltimore's own detectives were hearing on the corner — Lt. Newman's 'they turn 18; what are they gonna do, get a job for $175 a week?' and the boy who asked Sgt. Childs, 'What else should I do, man?' TWO FURTHER THREADS FROM THE SAME REPORTING. First, the burden was never evenly borne: the Hopkins mortality study found opiate death rates 'highest among non-white males,' at roughly TWICE the rate of white males. Second, the international pattern behind King's own downfall was already visible — the DEA reported in the early 1980s that 'Pakistani heroin was not a problem until eight months ago. The Pakistanis are controlling it and shipping directly to Pakistanis in the United States.' When King met Tauqir Islam in the Baltimore City Jail in 1982 and handed him a phone number on his way to deportation, he was not improvising an exotic connection. He was reaching for the supply line that was then reshaping the entire American market.

summary: THE CONTROL GROUP — and it may be the most important comparison in this entire file. In January 1987 the Sun ran David Simon's five-part investigation of MELVIN 'LITTLE MELVIN' WILLIAMS, mapping a West Baltimore organisation that operated 1980-84 — overlapping King's years, in the same city, at comparable scale. Detectives identified MORE THAN 200 STREET DEALERS supplied through its lieutenants. The published org chart runs Williams at the top over lieutenants Glen Hawkins (20 years), Louis Savage (30), Lamont Farmer (7), Elwood Farmer and Kenny Jackson, with James Ricks (30), Franklin Tolson (20) and NATHAN BARKSDALE (15) beneath Savage, and enforcers Victor Smith, Marando Warthen and Roland Bell under Barksdale. The parallels to King are uncanny: Williams was a dues-paying member of the International Longshoremen's Association (King, 'a former longshoreman'); he laundered through cash businesses — an Edmondson Avenue pool hall that became The Underground nightclub, a towing firm, eleven west-side properties held by his Scrapp Investment company (King: two grocery stores); and when the money had to be explained, he reported $80,000 in 'CHANCE WINNINGS' as a gambler (King: the $53,000 for his stores 'was from gambling winnings'). Lt. Joseph Newman, who ran the King task force, was by now a Major directing the city narcotics squad and pursuing Williams: 'It's not hard to be a good businessman when your business runs on drug money.' AND HERE IS THE POINT. Williams' couriers were adults: 'The couriers — mules — are WELL-PAID VETERANS unlikely to deal with authorities if arrested.' Same city. Same years. Same scale. Adults. King's use of eleven-to-fifteen-year-olds was therefore NOT an inevitability of the trade, not something the market forced on anyone — it was a CHOICE, and a rival organisation of equal size demonstrably made the opposite one. ### CHART READ AT FULL RESOLUTION — one correction and two additions. CORRECTION: NATHAN BARKSDALE (serving 15 years) reports to LAMONT FARMER, not to Louis Savage as I first recorded; beneath Barksdale sit Victor Smith, Marando Warthen and Roland Bell, labelled 'enforcers and street dealers under Barksdale.' Under Louis Savage sit James Ricks (30 years) and Franklin Tolson (20 years). Elwood Farmer and Kenny Jackson carry an asterisk: 'not indicted but named in court affidavits.' ### CAUTION — TWO DIFFERENT RICKSES: the JAMES RICKS in the Williams organisation is NOT Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks of K.R.M. Two unrelated men named Ricks, in two rival Baltimore organisations, in the same years. Do not conflate them. ### THE ASSETS, PHOTOGRAPHED: the Sun ran a four-picture spread — a Miami-based sailboat traced to Lamont Farmer, 'believed to have invested in the craft as a means of importing Latin American cocaine'; the Scrapp Investment-owned UNDERGROUND nightclub on Edmondson Avenue, its name spelled out in oversized letters across the facade; Williams' stately Reservoir Hill home; and Williams' $52,000 Maserati sedan, bought by the Scrapp firm, Maryland tag JZF 562 — photographed PARKED AT CITY POLICE HEADQUARTERS, where it had been seized and, per the reporting, reserved for the occasional use of Police Commissioner Bishop L. Robinson.

summary: AN EXTRAORDINARY DOCUMENT: THE ENTIRE CREATIVE GENOME OF 'THE WIRE', ON ONE 1987 NEWSPAPER PAGE. David Simon's byline sits atop the series. Quoted within it as investigators are DETECTIVE EDWARD BURNS — who would co-create The Wire with Simon — and DETECTIVE HARRY EDGERTON, the homicide detective Simon would follow for his book 'Homicide' and who became the basis for Frank Pembleton. The subject, MELVIN WILLIAMS, would later be cast in The Wire himself, as The Deacon. In the org chart published alongside sits NATHAN BARKSDALE, whose surname and elements of whose story the series would draw on. And the tradecraft described is, precisely, the plot of the show's first season: Lamont 'Chin' Farmer, a thirty-three-year-old business-college student whom Burns called 'the coming thing,' had built 'an elaborate system of PAY PHONES, CONTACT BEEPERS and organizational CODES to avoid court-ordered wiretaps and keep federal agents at bay' — photographed by detectives on Oct. 12, 1984 waiting for a call at a Guilford Avenue phone booth while they watched from East North Avenue. Simon's own framing of Williams opens the piece: 'Any good gambler understands this mathematical certainty: no matter how high you stack the odds in your favor… if you play long enough — letting your money ride — you will eventually lose.' Police were startled, late in the investigation, to hear senior ring members call Williams 'DAD'; one lieutenant's lawyer told a court his client saw Williams as 'the only real father-figure he ever knew.' ### FURTHER CONFIRMATIONS FROM PART 3 (Jan 13, 1987): the series names NATHAN 'BODIE' BARKSDALE — so The Wire drew BOTH the surname 'Barksdale' AND the name 'Bodie' from this one man. 'PROPOSITION JOE' JOHNSON, 48 — the Pennsylvania Avenue hustler who had once tutored the young Melvin Williams — is shot dead working as a doorman at the Club Chandelier in April 1984. summary: THE VENERATION CAME FIRST — a full generation before King monetised it. In Part 1 of Simon's series, Baltimore police sergeant EDWARD COLBERT describes the young Melvin Williams on Pennsylvania Avenue in the 1950s and '60s: 'HE WAS LIKE THE PIED PIPER. He had money and style AND THE KIDS LOOKED UP TO HIM. It was always, "Did you hear what Little Melvin did today?"' A policeman, reaching unprompted for the Pied Piper — the man who leads a town's children away. That is the mechanism, named by the law, about the kingpin of the PREVIOUS generation. And the city itself supplied the validation: the same file that records Williams allegedly waving a machine gun in a Mount Street bar also records that, only days earlier, he had been 'hailed as Little Melvin the Citizen, speaking AT THE REQUEST OF NATIONAL GUARD OFFICIALS during the 1968 riots, urging a restless crowd to go home.' The state asked the gangster to pacify the uprising. Simon states the resulting duality with total clarity — ask police and you hear the man who 'revolutionized Baltimore's drug culture'; 'but speak of Little Melvin to the man's friends and supporters… and you will hear the story of A SELF-MADE SURVIVOR, A SHREWD GAMBLER AND BUSINESSMAN WHO CREATED POWER AND MONEY IN A GHETTO WHERE NEITHER EXISTED.' The headline over it: 'IMPRISONED LITTLE MELVIN REMAINS A GHETTO LEGEND.' THE IMPLICATION FOR THIS FILM: Baltimore had been turning drug kingpins into heroes to its children for twenty years before Maurice King worked out how to put those children on the payroll. The veneration was not a consequence of King's model — it was the precondition for it.

summary: THE WORLD KING'S MODEL ENTERED — the numbers, and the lineage. Simon's Part 1 puts Baltimore's trade in 1987 at MORE THAN $1 MILLION A DAY IN HEROIN SALES ALONE, 'thought to be responsible for 25 percent to 30 percent of the city's homicides,' in a city carrying an estimated 25,000 HEROIN ADDICTS and perhaps three times that many cocaine users. The lineage behind it: prosecutors claimed Williams was the first local dealer to establish direct ties to Frank 'Pee Wee' Matthews, New York's largest heroin importer, 'whose flash and style were said to inspire the 1972 film Superfly'; DEA agents contended Williams was THE FIRST BLACK NARCOTICS DEALER TO ESTABLISH TIES TO OVERSEAS HEROIN SOURCES INDEPENDENT OF NEW YORK'S COSA NOSTRA FAMILIES; and police believed his money-laundering education came through Julius 'The Lord' Salsbury, a protege of Meyer Lansky who held the Baltimore rackets. Simon built the series from court records, police reports, financial statements and documents running from the late 1950s to 1987, plus NEARLY 100 INTERVIEWS. Two more names from the Pennsylvania Avenue pool halls that trained Williams: 'Cherry Red' Franklin and 'PROPOSITION JOE' JOHNSON, 'a consummate gambler who once tutored Little Melvin' — and who was killed by gunfire. The Wire would borrow that name too.

summary: THE OTHER HALF OF WHY THE CORRIDOR FELL — and it is not a Baltimore story at all. Roger Twigg reported that New York City dealers were 'flooding Baltimore with heroin of better quality and about a third cheaper than local heroin' — and gave the reason: POOR SALES IN NEW YORK BROUGHT ON BY FEAR OF AIDS. New York addicts who had been sharing 'community needles' were abandoning injection for crack, so the New York heroin market collapsed and its dealers dumped the supply southward. The economics were brutal: local dealers were selling at $30 to $40 a bag while the New Yorkers arrived at $10 A BAG, at 4 percent purity — 'about twice the local quality.' Police spokesman Dennis S. Hill: 'New York heroin dealers are undercutting the local dealers and saturating the market with high-grade heroin at a much cheaper price.' They cut out middlemen and delivered personally: 'They can come in here with several thousand bags of heroin and sell them in a single day. That means they can go home with $35,000 TO $40,000 FOR A SINGLE DAY'S WORK.' They travelled by car and train, worked specific territories, and used BROWN GLASSINE BAGS AS THEIR TRADEMARK — the branding logic of King's stamped bags, inherited by his replacements. Eight New Yorkers were taken in a house in the 5200 block of Frankford Avenue with more than 2,000 bags of heroin — about a kilogram, a single day's sale — and $13,000 in cash, destined for West Baltimore. Hill on the friction with local dealers: 'They're creating tension. But as long as there is a large enough market for both of them to operate in, I don't suppose that tension will turn to violence.' READ WITH #18871: the DEA said New York crews came to fill the void left by the federal prosecutions of King and Meredith. That was the PULL. This is the PUSH — an epidemic in another city destroying its heroin demand and flushing the surplus into Baltimore at a third the price and twice the strength. The corridor did not simply lose its organisations. It became the dumping ground.

summary: THE SAME OFFICER, THE SAME NEWSPAPER, FIVE YEARS APART — the cleanest before-and-after in this entire record. JUNE 1982, Lt. Joseph Newman on the King bust: 'It's the first time we were able to take out an entire organization and have an effect on the supply of heroin.' JANUARY 1987, now MAJOR Joseph Newman, in Simon's conclusion: 'But enforcement is only part of the answer. WE'RE VERY GOOD AT TAKING DEALERS OFF THE STREET, BUT THAT ONLY LEADS TO OTHER DEALERS FILLING THE VACUUM.' He did not need anyone to tell him. He worked it out himself, in public, in the same paper that had printed his victory lap. And Simon set that reversal inside a much longer history: in APRIL 1950 Baltimore police 'proudly announced' the arrest of Levi 'Crips' Acion, a 50-year-old poolroom operator called 'the No. 1 dope peddler on the East Coast,' and declared the city's heroin trade 'in disarray'; the following year the chief federal narcotics agent in Baltimore told city officials that a squad of two or three detectives and an appropriation of no more than $10,000 could 'WIPE OUT' the city's drug trade. Simon's verdict: 'NO ONE TALKS LIKE THAT ANYMORE.' By 1987 officials no longer named a No. 1 dealer at all, because the market had fragmented among independents. Thomas O'Grady, lately head of the DEA office in Baltimore: 'We can't stop the distribution of drugs. The best that enforcement can do is keep the lid on it.' The FBI's Bill Colombell: 'It's a war without an end, but I don't see any alternative to fighting it.' And law enforcement itself came to describe the removal of Melvin Williams as 'NOTHING MORE THAN A CHANGING OF THE GUARD.' Simon also states the King lineage outright: Clarence 'Yo' Meredith went underground after his 1983 indictment and 'returned to Baltimore to rebuild the multimillion-dollar drug ring THAT ONCE BELONGED TO MAURICE "PEANUT" KING.'

summary: THE MODEL DID NOT JUST SURVIVE — IT INFLATED. King paid children up to $500 a week to run heroin on mopeds in 1980-82. By January 1987, STOP squad Detective William Matthews: 'WE'VE ARRESTED KIDS, 16 YEARS OLD, WHO ARE MAKING A THOUSAND DOLLARS A WEEK. They sit there with thousands of dollars in jewelry on them. HOW DO YOU DEAL WITH THAT?' The wage had doubled in five years. Police Commissioner Bishop L. Robinson framed the task as persuasion and admitted its difficulty: 'There's so much money in drugs. We've got to convince these kids that there's more to it than that. That there's no future in dealing drugs, getting the money quick and living the Hollywood life.' Simon notes that 'the endless supply of willing participants in the drug trade — FROM THE 17-YEAR-OLD ENFORCERS to the middle-aged wholesalers — is a reality that even the most optimistic law enforcement officer accepts.' AND THEN HE ENDS THE SERIES ON THE CHILDREN. Community leaders and police both stress that most residents of drug-deluged neighbourhoods hold 'little respect or awe' for dealers and are more often their victims. 'BUT FOR OTHERS THE MYTH ENDURES. Police officers saw it firsthand, when Williams would glide through west side streets in that black Maserati Quadraporte, a $52,000 apparition against a landscape of boarded-up row houses and battered housing projects.' The last words of the five-part anatomy belong to Detective Matthews, shaking his head: 'When he rode around in that car, everyone knew who it was. You'd hear them yelling, "Hey, it's Little Melvin. Hey, Melvin." ... EVEN THE YOUNGER KIDS KNEW IT.' ### CORRECTION, ON BETTER EVIDENCE: an earlier version of this entry said the courier wage 'doubled' between King's era and 1987. That overstated it. Simon's own survey in the same series is precise: 'CHILDREN MAKING $200 A WEEK AS LOOKOUTS, OR $500 A WEEK AS RUNNERS.' The RUNNER wage in West Baltimore in 1987 was still $500 — exactly what King paid in 1980-82 — with lookouts, a younger and lower rung, at $200. Detective Matthews' '16-year-olds making a thousand dollars a week' describes teenagers who had moved up to DEALING, not runners. So the accurate finding is not inflation but ENTRENCHMENT: five years on, the same rate, the same ages, now city-wide and with a rung added below it for even younger children.

summary: THE MECHANISM BY WHICH THE CORRIDOR'S LEGITIMATE COMMERCE DIED — stated plainly by the officer who ran the King case. Major Joseph Newman, on drug money inside ordinary businesses: 'THE DEEPER PROBLEM FOR THE COMMUNITY IS THAT A LEGITIMATE BUSINESSMAN CAN'T COMPETE WITH A BUSINESS THAT IS SUPPORTED BY NARCOTICS MONEY. With all that money being funneled through his business, A DRUG TRAFFICKER DOESN'T HAVE TO WORRY ABOUT WHETHER HE'S MAKING A PROFIT.' Simon reports that narcotics investigations had by then linked drug money to 'city nightclubs and taverns, office buildings, shopping centers, GROCERIES, towing companies, rental properties and restaurants' across Baltimore, and that traffickers were increasingly hiding assets behind front companies and falsified liens — one Franklin associate allegedly paid a realty manager to fake a lien on a renovated home to block federal seizure, and Franklin himself allegedly concealed his financial interest in ODELL'S, 'a popular nightspot on North Avenue.' Newman on the diminishing returns of forfeiture: 'When we first got that law, we were catching people with all kinds of money. But over time, the dealers have become more adept at hiding assets and we're no longer getting as much.' PUT THIS BESIDE THE FEBRUARY 1981 CREDITOR'S SALE (#18888): forty-one mopeds repossessed from Baltimoreans who defaulted after riding them a dozen miles, while the organisation that bought eighteen more paid cash in small bills. That is the corridor's commercial death in one sentence — you cannot compete with a competitor who does not need to make a profit.

summary: THE PIPELINE, WITH NAMES AND AGES — Olesker's generational argument, documented. Simon's third part opens on the contrast: 'From the top it seems so clean, so professional… They are businessmen, with accountants and corporate titles… The heroin and cocaine they market could just as well be pork futures, or machine parts, or widgets. BUT AT BOTTOM, IT IS WAR. Nineteen-year-olds killing 20-year-olds for a fraction of a kilo. CHILDREN MAKING $200 A WEEK AS LOOKOUTS, OR $500 A WEEK AS RUNNERS.' And then the mechanism, stated plainly: NATHAN 'BODIE' BARKSDALE and his childhood friend MARANDO WARTHEN 'were TUTORED AS LOOKOUTS AND RUNNERS BY OLDER DRUG TRAFFICKERS' — the children of the courier system, grown. Barksdale was crippled at 11 (a truck backed him against a wall; the leg was amputated to the knee in 1983), a drug user at 13, carried a dozen juvenile arrests 'for which probation was the inevitable penalty,' and was running a corner at 17. Warthen, a year older, was THE SON OF A FORMER BALTIMORE POLICE OFFICER, living with his mother on North Ellamont Street — 'tall, but slight of frame, with a boyish face and soft voice… shy and detached.' The tutoring was enforced: Barksdale's own mentor, trafficker Frank Harper, once punished him for holding back profits by locking the boy in a rowhouse basement with an angry German shepherd. In July 1982 Barksdale was charged with Harper's murder, and acquitted. The next rung down was already filled: VICTOR SMITH was an enforcer selling cocaine in the Murphy Homes at 16, and had first come to homicide detectives' attention at 15. Years later a prosecutor asked Smith in open court whether he would kill someone who identified him as a dealer. 'I PROBABLY WOULD,' the teenager replied — then agreed he would hold a gun to a person's head and fire. Detective William Matthews of the STOP squad: 'The kids running drugs are getting YOUNGER AND YOUNGER. They will kill you for a $5 debt, or just for looking at them the wrong way. They just don't care.' And Police Commissioner Bishop L. Robinson — himself a narcotics detective in the 1960s when Melvin Williams was coming up — on whether that era could even repeat: 'IF MELVIN WERE COMING UP TODAY, HE WOULDN'T LIVE TO BE 21.' The terminal point of the escalation is on the record and does not need retailing here: a three-year run by Barksdale's group that police tied to five homicides and four attempted murders, including a prolonged torture in an 11th-floor Murphy Homes apartment that a prosecutor compared to Mengele. Warthen drew 103 years for a double murder at an after-hours club; Barksdale's plea bought him 15. Homicide Detective Ed Burns, on the tally: 'And that is just what we know about.'

summary: THE DRESS REHEARSAL FOR THIS DOCUMENTARY'S RECEPTION — and it should be read before a frame is shot. Simon's five-part series began in the Sunday Sun and ended ON MARTIN LUTHER KING'S BIRTHDAY, during the week-long celebration of it. About SEVENTY DEMONSTRATORS picketed the Baltimore Sun, chanting 'SHAME ON THE SUN!' and then 'We Shall Overcome,' carrying placards including 'WE WILL NOT BE TREATED LIKE CRIMINALS.' The march was organised by CITY COUNCILMAN NATHANIEL McFADDEN (D-2nd) and the REV. WALTER S. THOMAS, pastor of New Psalmist Baptist Church, who appears in the Sun's own photograph with a bullhorn; McFadden also called for a one-day BOYCOTT of the paper and demanded an apology. Crucially, McFadden said he did NOT take issue with the substance of the reporting — he objected to running 'an exhaustive series on a notorious black drug dealer' during a celebration of Dr. King: 'LITTLE MELVIN IS NOT PART OF DR. KING'S DREAM.' Demonstrator Lawrence Monroe: 'The fact that they ran it on Martin Luther King's birthday says something about the paper's philosophy.' Elsewhere McFadden put the charge in the word this project has been circling for days: 'WHY DO WE HAVE TO HAVE A SERIES GLAMORIZING A SUPERFLY DRUG DEALER WHO SELLS DEATH TO BLACK PEOPLE?' — and 'Why not a five-part series on Thurgood Marshall? Clarence Du Burns? Or Parren Mitchell?' Sun managing editor JAMES I. HOUCK replied that the paper had hoped to show 'the devastating impact one person has had on this community,' and conceded: 'I understand why people would be upset. It was inadvertent and regrettable because we inadvertently allowed the timing to become a side issue that overshadowed a fine piece of journalism.' The Enoch Pratt Free Library scheduled a public forum on the press and the black community for Jan. 24.

summary: THE MOST USEFUL CRITICISM IN THE ENTIRE RECORD — because it is precise about what actually went wrong. Columnist WILEY A. HALL 3rd, writing as the protests unfolded, refused the easy arguments on both sides. On timing: 'The insensitivity has nothing to do with The Sun's decision to run the series during the week of King's birthday. That's nonsense. TIMING IS IRRELEVANT.' On substance: it has 'nothing to do with the substance of the ENGROSSING, EXCELLENT anatomy of a convicted drug dealer's empire by Sun reporter David Simon.' Then the diagnosis: 'The paper was insensitive ONLY IN THAT ITS WRITERS AND EDITORS FAILED TO PERCEIVE THE SERIES THE WAY ITS BLACK AUDIENCE PERCEIVED IT.' And he located the failure in a single line of type — THE HEADLINE: 'Behind Bars, Melvin Williams still a ghetto legend' was 'PERCEIVED AS A BROAD BRUSH THAT PAINTS BLACK PEOPLE LOOKING UP TO, RESPECTING, A CONVICTED HEROIN DEALER.' Hall's corrective is the sentence this film should keep on the wall: 'MOST BLACKS DO NOT USE OR SELL DRUGS. Most black teen-agers do not carry weapons and carry on as if they were in Dodge City. Most black families struggle to stay together… IT IS A SLOW, AGONIZING LESSON FOR THE MEDIA TO LEARN: THAT THE UNDERSIDE OF BLACK LIFE IS NOT THE ONLY SIDE THERE IS.' And note what he asked for instead — not 'positive, mushy portraits,' but hard reporting on: why the black-white WEALTH gap 'defined as PROPERTY, savings, etc.' keeps widening while the salary gap narrows; why 'black business people have so much trouble getting BONDING AND LOANS'; why discrimination suits against state agencies persist a decade after consent decrees. In 1987 a black columnist told the Baltimore Sun that the story it should be chasing was PROPERTY, CAPITAL ACCESS AND THE WEALTH GAP. That is, precisely, the corridor project's subject.

summary: A CONVERGENCE WORTH NOTICING. Reporting his own beat alongside the series, David Simon covered a STOP-squad raid on THE UNDERGROUND at 2114 Edmondson Ave — the nightclub owned by Scrapp Investment Corp., which until recently listed Melvin Williams as a corporate officer and whose records then listed his wife and father-in-law. Detectives battered the door at 4:15 p.m. on a Sunday during a dance party and made 21 arrests, recovering 106 caps and 13 paper bags of cocaine, 35 glassine bags of suspected heroin, marijuana, two hypodermic needles — and FIVE HANDGUNS, despite a working metal detector at the entrance. Nineteen of those arrested were 'in their late teens and early 20s,' a younger crowd not suspected of belonging to any large organisation. Williams' nephew Barry Henderson, 24, a manager of the club, and his 19-year-old brother were charged. Police discussed applying the city's new PADLOCK LAW to the club, appraised after renovation at more than $100,000. AND THEN THE LAST LINE OF SIMON'S STORY: the Underground 'last year was the scene of a DEBATE BETWEEN CANDIDATES FOR THE 7TH DISTRICT CONGRESSIONAL SEAT — who later claimed ignorance of the nightclub's connection to Melvin Williams.' Set that beside incident #18861: in the summer of 1986 a candidate for THAT SAME 7TH DISTRICT SEAT, St. George I.B. Crosse III, staged a campaign event standing on Greenmount Avenue in front of the former headquarters of Peanut King, calling for the execution of drug dealers. One congressional race, two kingpins' properties — one used as a debate hall, the other as a backdrop for demanding executions.

summary: THE POLICY THAT INVENTED THE CHILD COURIER — and it was not invented in Baltimore. New York's 1973 drug law, conceived by Governor NELSON ROCKEFELLER, raised penalties for heroin sale and mandated 15-years-to-life for high-level adult dealers. The trade adapted within a year by moving its retail workforce below the age of criminal liability: an AP report noted that 'the use of children as dope pushers reportedly has been GROWING SINCE THE STATE MANDATED TOUGH PRISON TERMS FOR CONVICTED ADULT PUSHERS. Children under 16 are not subject to such penalties, under rules of the family courts where their cases are processed' — in a case where an 18-year-old was accused of using an ELEVEN-YEAR-OLD as a front for a heroin operation. And on SEPT. 21, 1980 — before King's moped fleet was even complete — THE BALTIMORE SUN PUBLISHED JILL NELSON'S 'THE KIDS WHO SERVE CRIME,' a full anatomy of the model on Harlem's 115th Street: '13-, 14- and 15-year-old blacks sell heroin almost as fast as McDonald's sells hamburgers,' $400 of heroin a minute, $96,000 a day on one block. 'Most of those selling dope on 115th street are under 16, PRIMARILY BECAUSE OF NEW YORK'S 1973 DRUG LAW.' The crews were organised exactly as Baltimore's would be — four to six boys, several posted at each end of the block as LOOKOUTS warning of 'ness' (from Eliot Ness), one taking money, a third handing out product stashed in a nearby building. Officer John Lluvera: 'They get minors to do the transactions. We pick up the youth… Family Court usually gives them a slap on the wrist and they're back on the street.' Daryl, 15, out of school since ninth grade, earning more than $800 a week: 'Hey, would you go to school if you could make two, three hundred dollars a day?' Officer Gerald Robbins: 'After tasting $500 a week, why's he going to go stack shelves in some grocery?' And the actuarial forecast from Officer Lluvera: of every five boys selling on that block, in five years one would be dead of a drug-related gunshot, one would get a regular job, one would become an addict, and two would be living by crime. Daryl's answer: 'Who's thinking about five years away? Anyway, that would probably happen even if I weren't selling dope, so I got nothin' to lose.'

summary: WHO THE CHILDREN WERE SERVING — and the answer runs straight through this corridor. Scott Shane's Sun series 'Shooting Up in the Suburbs' (Mar 18, 1985) followed white suburban addicts from Towson, Pikesville and Owings Mills into East Baltimore to buy. 'Addicts, drug treatment workers, police and prosecutors agree that the retail heroin trade remains essentially an inner-city phenomenon. THE CITY KINGPINS HAVE A STRANGLEHOLD ON THE HEROIN TRADE,' said Baltimore County prosecutor Anthony R. Gallagher. 'So white, suburban heroin users inevitably learn the cross-cultural skill of buying in tough, black neighborhoods.' Melanie, 30, of Towson, named the market precisely: 'You drive down to 22d and Kennedy, or BARCLAY AND NORTH AVENUE, or really ALL ALONG BARCLAY STREET.' Barclay runs one block WEST of Greenmount — this is the corridor, named as a retail counter for the suburbs. And the counter staff were children: David Lonsdale, an ex-addict from Towson, 'Usually, you're dealing with a runner — KIDS 13, 14, 15, KIDS ON 10-SPEEDS. As soon as they'd see a white boy, they'd know why you were there.' Charlotte, 32, of Towson, recalled driving down in 1982 and 1983 'in a Grand Prix, wearing a wool suit and a gold necklace,' completing a deal and heading to her job running a suburban nursing home. Debbie and Alfred Dalcin ran $1,000 of heroin a day out of an Owings Mills apartment for six months to about fifty acquaintances — 'All the customers were white, of ages ranging from 23 to 50. More than half were women… A lot came from wealthy families. A lot of them had businesses.' The economics of the corridor's destruction are therefore not internal to it: THE MONEY CAME FROM WEALTHY WHITE SUBURBS, THE PRODUCT CAME FROM NEW YORK, AND THE CHILDREN OF EAST BALTIMORE STOOD AT THE POINT OF SALE ABSORBING THE RISK. ### CORRECTION (2026-07-18): this entry previously stated that Barclay runs one block EAST of Greenmount. summary: THE CITY CAME TO THE CORRIDOR WITH WHISTLES. Mayor WILLIAM DONALD SCHAEFER, Police Commissioner BISHOP ROBINSON, State's Attorney KURT SCHMOKE, Circuit Judge Joseph H. H. Kaplan and about eighty bureaucrats, police brass and reporters left City Hall aboard two of the city's trolley-style Inner Harbor shuttle buses, escorted by four motorcycle officers, to tour 'three of the city's most notorious street-corner drug marts.' THE FIRST STOP WAS BARCLAY AND 22ND STREETS — 'an intersection police identified as one of the centers of cocaine and heroin traffic,' two blocks from 2400 Greenmount. Schaefer to onlookers: 'You do not have to tolerate drugs in your neighborhood… You don't deserve to have a drug dealer standing on your corner trying to hurt your kids.' Schmoke: 'We didn't come all the way here in 1985, through a great struggle, through a civil rights movement, trying to get people employed, only to see our young people cut down on the streets of the city.' The residents split. John Jenkins, of the first block of Barclay St: 'Drugs are going to be here. If they're not here, they'll be somewhere else.' Mary Clay, whose mother lived a block from the dealing: 'There's a lot of us scared to be out of our houses… They're like taking over.' At the second stop a man in his early 20s holding a baby, whom Schaefer had pointed to as the reason for the campaign, said afterwards he had been falsely accused of selling marijuana and that the city should spend its money on REHABILITATION rather than crackdowns. A neighbour there, Bill Taylor: 'This corner is crazy. All this cocaine and heroin, ALL THESE KIDS 5 TO 10 YEARS OLD. You can buy anything you want.' Then Schaefer stood at the front of the bus and blew a red-and-white plastic whistle with the drug hot line number embossed on it — one of hundreds handed out to encourage people to 'blow the whistle' on dealers — and the bus rolled on 'amid what seemed like deafening noise.' Calls to the hot line went from about 12 in a day to 112.

summary: THE CYCLE, PROVED — because the same officer describes it TWICE, seven years apart, about two different generations. In a Michael Olesker column published BEFORE King's rise was broken (c.1980-81), Lt. JOE NEWMAN, head of CID Narcotics, describes a Baltimore that had ALREADY been through this: 'You don't have the big organizations here that you had in the EARLY SEVENTIES. A guy like Big Head Brother could put 10 or 15 kilos on the table at one time… I don't know if there's anybody in Baltimore today who's capable of controlling a large organization of people… But today, you've got LOTS AND LOTS OF RELATIVELY SMALL BULK DEALERS. In a sense, IT MAKES ENFORCEMENT TOUGHER FOR US.' Olesker: 'A decade ago in Baltimore, you could pinpoint the major dealers. They wore high profiles and carried memorable names: BIG HEAD BROTHER and LITTLE MELVIN, JUNIOR BUNK and PROPOSITION JOE, GHOST AND TOAST and BIG LUCILLE… Today, they are not so easy to pinpoint. The big names are in prisons, AND IN THEIR PLACE YOU HAVE DOZENS OF SMALLER PIRANHAS FEEDING OFF EACH OTHER.' So the sequence runs: early-1970s organisations dismantled → splintering (described 1980) → KING CONSOLIDATES → dismantled 1982 → splintering again (described by the SAME MAN in 1987, as a Major) → New York crews fill the vacuum. The kingpin strategy does not end markets; it runs a loop, and Newman narrated two full turns of it. ALSO IN THIS COLUMN: a narcotics cop, quoted from roughly 1972-73 — a DECADE BEFORE KING — pounding a restaurant table: 'FORGET MORALITY. YOU GOT 18-YEAR-OLD KIDS OUT THERE RUNNING DOPE AND MAKING $1,000 A DAY. What am I gonna do, say to the kid, "Look, this ain't good for you. Settle down and get a job?" You gotta be crazy.' Further evidence that the youth-labour model long predates King. And Newman on the coming supply shock — U.S. Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti had just announced that six American cities INCLUDING BALTIMORE were targeted for a major influx of heroin from Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan: 'They're calling this OPERATION CERBERUS… Those governments cooperated with us. They killed the poppies… But you think Iran is gonna spray anything for us? Politically speaking, they're happy about it.' Newman: 'This thing's scary. We haven't seen any of this influx yet, but if it happens, WE'RE BACK IN THE SIXTIES AGAIN.' Olesker's forecast closed the column: 'Heroin street purity will go up… There will be MORE KIDS OVERDOSING.' He was right on every count.
