summary: THE INITIATION, IN HIS MOTHER'S WORDS — and the fullest specification of the headquarters. Court papers quoted by the AP record that King told a state investigator in 1980 that 'EVERYBODY HE GREW UP WITH HAS BEEN IN CONFLICT WITH THE LAW.' The investigator quoted his mother agreeing, and describing the neighbourhood's rite of passage: 'THE TEST WAS TO GO TO SEARS DEPARTMENT STORE ON NORTH AVENUE AND STEAL SOMETHING.' His record: first arrested at 12 on an assault charge; at least 24 arrests since, from driving on a revoked licence to shoplifting, drug possession, deadly weapons and homicide (the homicide charge was dropped); found guilty eight times. First charged with heroin possession in 1979 — acquitted, but found in violation of probation and fined $100. THE HEADQUARTERS, fully specified: King formed TWO LEGAL CORPORATIONS with two other men 'ostensibly to operate two small supermarkets,' the recently renovated stores standing 'in marked contrast to their surrounding neighborhoods.' Above one was the ring's headquarters — a BOARD ROOM, separate offices for each of the three corporation officials, and a room housing a COMPUTER for records, protected by ELECTRONIC LOCKS, BULLET-PROOF GLASS and CLOSED-CIRCUIT CAMERAS. Above the other, a MIRRORED GYMNASIUM with stainless-steel universal equipment, a HEAVY BAG, a SAUNA and a JACUZZI — and 'a CLIMATIC ROOM WITH 12 COMPUTERIZED SETTINGS.' AND ONE MERCY, newly recorded: the innocent teenage mother killed in the hail of shots from a passing car was 'carrying her 2-year-old daughter' — and 'THE LITTLE GIRL ESCAPED INJURY.'

summary: THE MIRROR — and it is the hardest juxtaposition in this file. While Black children in East Baltimore were being recruited to SELL heroin, white children in the northern suburbs were using it, and disappearing from every count that mattered. Scott Shane's 'Shooting Up in the Suburbs' opens on DAVID LONSDALE, 29, 'his blue blazer, button-down shirt and club tie the uniform of suburban American affluence,' a successful businessman who used heroin for ten years. He took his first shot at 16, a tenth grader at DULANEY SENIOR HIGH — 'one of the most affluent public high schools in Maryland' — and 'he and other Dulaney students used to SHOOT HEROIN BETWEEN CLASSES IN THE CEMETERY ACROSS FROM THE SCHOOL.' John, 28, first used in a bedroom of his grandparents' $200,000 house on Dulaney Valley Road. Vince, 32, watched his 17-year-old brother inject in the parking lot of LOCH RAVEN ELEMENTARY SCHOOL when he was 13 — 'Here's my big brother doing it with his big teen-age friends. I WAS IMPRESSED' — and three years later joined the teenagers gathering off Oakleigh Road near Towson: 'Towson High School, Calvert Hall… At first, maybe 25 percent were shooting dope. After a couple of years [about 1971], 80 PERCENT WERE SHOOTING DOPE.' Terry Fishler of the Sheppard-Pratt methadone programme estimated 30 to 40 percent of its 185 addicts came from middle-class or wealthier families. AND HERE IS THE ASYMMETRY, stated by the paper itself: 'THE WELL-TO-DO OFTEN DON'T HAVE TO RESORT TO CRIME TO PAY FOR THEIR HABITS, SO THEY DON'T ALWAYS SHOW UP IN POLICE RECORDS. And middle-class addicts can afford — or have health insurance to cover — costly private counseling or out-of-state hospitalization. So they don't have to turn to the state treatment programs WHERE THEY CAN BE COUNTED.' Same drug, same metropolitan area, same years: the white children were users who became invisible; the Black children were workers who became statistics, arrests and obituaries. A decade earlier the pattern was already set — in June 1977 a recovering addict speaking under the pseudonym 'Larry Hop' told students at Joppatowne High that he had begun at 13 on codeine cough syrup and had driven 'in a packed car to NORTH AND GAY in Baltimore… to cop heroin,' arrested nearly thirty times, six years in jails. He used a false name for one reason: 'I don't want my oldest son to be confronted in his school by kids whose parents read the papers.' A white suburban addict could ask a newspaper to protect his child's name. The children on Barclay Street were photographed.

summary: THE VICTORY LAP WAS REFUTED WITHIN WEEKS — IN THE SAME NEWSPAPER, BY THE SAME REPORTER. Rafael Alvarez had written the June 5, 1982 front page announcing the largest heroin bust in Baltimore's history. Weeks later he reported the aftermath under the headline 'HEROIN AVAILABLE DESPITE BUST.' Methadone clinics recorded no surge at all: 'NOBODY'S COMING IN WITH WITHDRAWAL,' one counsellor said, and the Baltimore City Health Department's Drug Abuse Directorate concluded 'there was not an increase in treatment demand based on the drug bust.' A 33-year-old East Baltimorean, an addict since 1968, agreed the bust 'put a dent' in east-side operations — and then described the replacement mechanism precisely: the traffic had simply MOVED ABOUT THREE BLOCKS from Hoffman and Holbrook, where police estimated $20,000 in heroin was dealt daily. 'There was somewhat of a panic for a little while, but ONCE ONE DEALER GOES DOWN, A COUPLE OF MORE POP UP. It really didn't go dry, and there's still a fair amount available.' Jurgen Swermer of University Hospital's clinic: 'EVEN A GOOD-SIZED BUST HAS A LIMITED EFFECT, BECAUSE NO ONE GROUP HAS A MONOPOLY. The money involved is just so enormous.' Dr. James Hawthorne of City Hospitals: 'Major busts of this kind don't necessarily result in a great influx' into treatment. The city's addict population was estimated as high as 15,000, and every government-financed treatment programme was full with a long waiting list — as counsellor Leslie Abramowitz put it, 'THE GRIPE NOW IS NOT HOW HARD IT IS TO GET THE STUFF ON THE STREET, BUT HOW HARD IT IS TO GET INTO A PROGRAM.' The trade also adapted tactically within weeks: Lt. Newman noted a move away from hand-to-hand sales — 'NOW DEALERS WANT THEIR MONEY FIRST AND THEN THEY'LL TELL YOU WHERE THE DOPE IS.'

summary: THE LAW THAT WOULD TAKE THE BUILDING ARRIVED THE SAME SEASON AS THE BUST. In the aftermath reporting, Lt. Joseph Newman argued that seizure — not arrests — was the only real weapon: he 'sees the elimination of profits as the one real method of eradicating the heroin trade,' and pointed to the recent signing of SENATE BILL 83 by Governor Harry Hughes as 'a welcome tool in crippling the dealers.' The bill, the Evening Sun noted, 'goes into effect Thursday' and 'ALLOWS POLICE TO CONFISCATE ALL MONEY AND PROPERTY PURCHASED WITH FUNDS TRACEABLE TO DRUG DEALS.' Maryland's asset-forfeiture machinery, in other words, took effect within weeks of the June 1982 raids on the K.R.M. organisation — and the federal government would go on to record a notice of lien against 2400 Greenmount that October and condemn the building by decree in 1988. Newman had the analysis right, and it is the reason this parcel's chain of title reads the way it does. Note the irony the record now supports: seizing the profits was the strategy the police themselves believed in, and by 1987 Major Newman was conceding that dealers 'have become more adept at hiding assets and we're no longer getting as much.'

summary: THE ECOLOGY KING ENTERED — and it included a woman-led family dynasty. Baltimore's heroin trade in the decade before K.R.M. was already large, organised and diverse. In one case, ANNA M. JONES, 46, headed a CITYWIDE operation that testimony valued at $6 MILLION A YEAR AND USED 300 TO 400 DRUG PEDDLERS — an organisation 'that involved HER GRANDMOTHER AND DAUGHTER.' She had taken it over in 1975 after her son, William Cooper, 32, was hospitalised, and Judge Mary Arabian sentenced her to 40 years; a second woman, Phyllis Poore, 31, drew 15 years for stashing Mexican brown heroin brought down from New York for cutting with milk sugar and bagging. Detectives first learned of the operation by HIDING A MICROPHONE IN THE HOSPITAL ROOM of a suspect; twenty-six people were arrested. Separately, in August 1978, PHILLIP B. KANE — known as 'GHOST' — was sentenced to ten years in federal prison on heroin and weapons charges, the weapons count alleging he had acquired a gun to kill ELIJAH 'DITTY WO' DAVIS, a reputed narcotics dealer shot dead on a West Baltimore street. Both men recur in the later record: Olesker listed 'GHOST AND TOAST' among the vivid early-1970s kingpin names, Simon's 1987 series reports Kane sentenced again to THIRTY YEARS and 'close to tears' in federal court, and Elijah Davis appears among the execution-style victims in the Sun's old photo file. King did not arrive in an empty market. He arrived in a mature one — with its own dynasties, its own dead, and its own generations.

summary: THE WORD, AND THE ADMISSION — both on day one. THE WORD: the Sun's first-day account gives the Baltimore street term and the reasoning behind it in a single sentence. 'JUVENILES KNOWN AS "HOPPERS," SOME AS YOUNG AS 11 YEARS OLD, ARE USED BY AREA DRUG DEALERS BECAUSE ONCE ARRESTED, THE YOUTHS ARE USUALLY RELEASED TO THE CUSTODY OF THEIR PARENTS, ELIMINATING THE NEED FOR BAIL MONEY.' Note that this is stated not as a King peculiarity but as general practice among 'area drug dealers' — more evidence the model was ambient rather than invented here — and note that 'hoppers' is the vocabulary The Wire would carry to the world twenty years later. State's Attorney William Swisher added the transport rationale: the organisation used mopeds 'because police cruisers have difficulty following them through alleys.' THE ADMISSION: in the very press conference announcing the largest drug bust in the city's history, POLICE COMMISSIONER FRANK J. BATTAGLIA 'acknowledged that OTHER ORGANIZATIONS WERE ALREADY JOCKEYING TO FILL THE HEROIN VOID LEFT BY THE RAIDS,' even as he warned dealers, 'We know who you are… and our detectives are poised to grab you.' So the vacuum thesis was not a later revision by critics. It was conceded by the Police Commissioner, on the record, in the same article in which Lt. Newman called it 'the first time we were able to take out an entire organization and have an effect on the supply of heroin.' The claim and its refutation ran in the same story.

summary: 'IT'S ELECTION TIME' — AND HE WAS NOT WRONG ABOUT THAT. From the Baltimore City Jail in June 1982, King told the AP: 'I think I was set up. IT'S ELECTION TIME. They're just trying to put it on somebody.' It has been easy to read that as a defendant's deflection. It was also a description of fact. The Sun's own first-day coverage reports that State's Attorney WILLIAM SWISHER 'has come under fire from KURT SCHMOKE, a Baltimore lawyer who is CHALLENGING HIM IN THE DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY, for what Mr. Schmoke contends is A LACK OF AGGRESSIVE INVESTIGATION AND PROSECUTION OF NARCOTICS CASES' — Schmoke arguing there should be a unit in the state's attorney's office devoted SOLELY to narcotics. Swisher's spokesman Richard D. Byrd insisted 'our special investigative unit IS our narcotics unit,' while the assistant state's attorney who actually headed that unit, JOHN N. PREVAS, said narcotics made up only about 50 to 75 percent of its caseload. So the largest drug bust in Baltimore history was announced by an incumbent prosecutor in the middle of a primary campaign whose central issue was whether he prosecuted drugs aggressively enough. NONE OF THIS MAKES KING INNOCENT — two juries convicted him, and the evidence was called 'an abundance.' It does mean his complaint had a real referent, and it belongs in an honest telling. The afterlives compound it: Schmoke won, became State's Attorney and then Mayor — and in 2019 sat down with Maurice King to discuss his reentry plans. Prevas went to the bench, and years later told a columnist that King was 'the last guy who controlled any type of serious organization around here.'

summary:
THE CUSTODIAL SYSTEM AROUND KING LEAKED AT EVERY LEVEL — and it is a run of prosecutions, not an inference. This matters because KING MET TAUQIR ISLAM AT THE BALTIMORE CITY JAIL IN 1982 and handed him a telephone number on his way to deportation (#18836); the institution where that introduction happened was, on the government's own account, one in which inmates, guards and other employees were under investigation together.
JUNE 1985: a City Jail guard named PRANGLE BROWN was charged with POSSESSION OF HEROIN WITH INTENT TO DISTRIBUTE — maximum 15 years and a $125,000 fine — and scheduled for arraignment in U.S. District Court. The charge was announced by TY COBB of the U.S. Attorney's Office, who said the information leading to the arrest "RESULTED FROM AN ONGOING INVESTIGATION ON USE AND DISTRIBUTION OF NARCOTICS BY INMATES, GUARDS AND OTHER EMPLOYEES OF THE CITY JAIL," conducted jointly by Baltimore Police Department detectives and federal DEA special agents. Cobb would not say how long the investigation had run or whether more charges were expected.
THE PATTERN AROUND IT: another City Jail guard had been arrested and suspended without pay for marijuana possession the previous September, discovered during a SURPRISE DRUG SHAKEDOWN OF JAIL PERSONNEL. And in NOVEMBER 1983, SIX CITY JAIL GUARDS — INCLUDING A LIEUTENANT AND A SERGEANT — were arrested and charged with possession of cocaine and marijuana; narcotics officers took them as they sat in a van parked in front of the jail.
SET THIS BESIDE THE PENITENTIARY (#18847 and #18860): the Maryland Penitentiary sat in the neighbourhood the ring served and drew guards from those same blocks, and a Sun editorial drew the structural point that this made them "vulnerable to pressure to do favors for friends and relatives doing time." The City Jail record shows the same problem one institution over, prosecuted repeatedly across at least three years.
NOTE ALSO: this is a THIRD independent citation placing TY COBB as an assistant U.S. attorney in Baltimore on exactly these matters — with the Ward prosecution and the Meredith indictment, it removes any doubt about the identification (see #18859).

THE EARLIEST KNOWN IMAGE OF THIS GROUND — a Baltimore Streetcar Museum photograph captioned in a clerk's hand "YORK RD. NEAR 24TH ST, 2-27-09", plate numbered 58, credited Baltimore Streetcar Museum via DIGITAL MARYLAND.
WHAT IT SHOWS. The street is YORK ROAD, not yet renamed Greenmount — unpaved and rutted, with TWO SETS OF STREETCAR TRACKS up the middle and a forest of utility poles carrying perhaps a dozen crossarms each. On the near left, filling the frame, a long timber shed painted with its own address: "GEO. J. STORCK & SON — 2406-2408 — LUMBER & MILLWORK." That is the SAME BLOCK FACE as this parcel, two doors north — Block 3825, the next lot up (#18794). Opposite, on the east side, three-storey rowhouses and a corner commercial block. A SMALL GIRL IN A PALE DRESS stands on the pavement at the left edge, looking at the camera. A single early automobile is parked far up on the right.
WHY IT MATTERS. In 1909 this was A LUMBER AND MILLWORK YARD ON A DIRT TURNPIKE WITH STREETCARS — a working industrial edge, not a residential corner and not yet a retail one. The grocery that becomes a boardroom in 1981 is not built into a slum; it is built into a yard that made window sashes and door frames for the houses going up around it. Any account of "what was lost" on this block has to start earlier than deacon Bernard Corprew's memory of McMillion's grocery and Arundel's ice-cream parlor (#18837).

summary: During a two-week civil-rights campaign to desegregate white-only Greenmount Ave bars, police closed the Blue Front Lounge (owners Richard & Mrs. McFarland) after a 40-minute standoff with ~40 Black demonstrators inside and ~100 more across the street. The Liquor Board then ruled that any bar practicing racial discrimination would have its license revoked; the Blue Front, Mickey Griffin's (roughly across Greenmount from it), the Lewis Inn a block north, and Harvey's Oriole Tavern all served Black patrons for the first time that week.
data: {"url":"https://www.newspapers.com/image/jeff-blue-front-desegregation-1967","excerpt":"For the fourth consecutive night, groups of Negroes sought — and were denied — service last night at the Blue Front Lounge, in the 2400 block Greenmount avenue. Police ordered the white-only tavern closed at 10.40 P.M. after a 40-minute siege... The Liquor Board ruled yesterday that any bar which practices racial discrimination will have its license revoked, effective immediately... Negroes went later yesterday evening to the Blue Front Lounge and Mickey Griffin's, both in the 2400 block Greenmount avenue, to the Lewis Inn, in the 2500 block of Greenmount, and to Harvey's Oriole Tavern, in the 2700 block of Greenmount avenue. The Negroes were served quietly in all of the taverns in which they stopped.","headline":"Blue Front Lounge (2405 Greenmount Ave) desegregates under Liquor Board ruling","image_id":"jeff-blue-front-desegregation-1967","clipped_by":"jeff516","confidence":"documented"}

summary: Samuel Grier, 24, and Lonnie Grier, 29 — using each other's names as aliases — were sentenced to 20 years each for a masked armed robbery of the Blue Front Lounge, 2405 Greenmount Ave. Lynn McFarland, the owner's daughter and bartender, let Lonnie in as a known customer; he produced a sawed-off rifle from a shopping bag and, with Samuel holding the door, robbed 8 customers and the register of $456. Owner Richard McFarland shot at the fleeing robbers, wounding Samuel. Date is approximate — sentencing judge Robert L. Karwacki, prosecutor L. Douglas Jefferson.
data: {"url":"https://www.newspapers.com/image/jeff-grier-robbery-blue-front","excerpt":"Evidence disclosed that Lynn McFarland, 26, the bartender at her father's tavern in the 2400 block Greenmount avenue, opened the electrically-controlled door about 9:40 p.m. June 17 to admit the younger Grier, a known customer. The gunman ordered the eight customers to lie on the floor and demanded money from Ms. McFarland, who handed $456 to the unmasked Grier... data: {"lot":"002A","block":"3855","criteria":["A","B","C"],"district":"Waverly Main Street Historic District","listed_on":"2013-12-31","relevance":"Resource record for 2920 Greenmount Avenue in the Waverly Main Street Historic District.","clipped_by":"nrhp","confidence":"documented","description":"This building is a streamlined one story structure of red brick with a US bond course that is comprised of alternating bond and running bricks. summary: The lots that became 3413 and 3415 Greenmount originate in an 1886 TRUSTEE'S SALE out of the Baltimore County equity partition DAMES vs. DAMES. Court-appointed trustees ROBERT R. BOARMAN and C. BOHN SLINGLUFF sold to JACOB H. AULL a parcel on the east side of the York turnpike — the southwest corner of lot No. 1 on the plat filed in the case, 50 by 252 feet — for $2,075 (deed dated Feb 1, 1886; Balt. County JWS 150/406 for the 3415 side; the adjoining 3413 lot came from C. Baker Slingluff et al, Trustee, JWS 160/406). A companion deed, Wm. Dames and wife → Jacob H. Aull (lot No. 1, NW corner, 80.5 x 49.33 ft, $1,750), passed the balance of the partition. C. Bohn Slingluff was a Towsontown attorney (Slingluff & Slingluff; German-language advocate 'Dutscher Advocat,' opposite the Towson courthouse) who with R. R. Boarman was regularly appointed to sell under Circuit Court decree. Jacob H. Aull — the Waverly family whose son wrote 'Old Land Marks of Baltimore' — was himself an active 1880s real-estate developer/subdivider, not only the shoemaker-chronicler. This is the deepest documented anchor for both parcels.

summary: Immediately after acquiring the Dames-partition ground, JACOB H. AULL and wife conveyed lots Nos. 1 and 2 (on the Dames vs. Dames plat) to WM. H. BRUNE, JR. for $8,333.33; Brune then re-conveyed to Aull the whole as ten subdivided lots (Nos. 1-10) on the east side of the York turnpike and west side of old York road, creating GROUND RENTS of $60 each on the first five and $40 each on the last five. Brune sold several of the ten off the same period (to Wm. and Rachel Ann Waggner, Bernard N. Baker, Geo. B. Baker, Olivia C. Starring). This Brune ground-rent subdivision is the mechanism that turned the Aull parcel into the leasehold lots of the 3400 block — and is why WM. H. BRUNE, JR. is the lessor of the 1887 ground lease on 3415 (the next instrument in this chain). 3413/3415 descend from this subdivision; the exact lot-number mapping is not pinned to the newspaper's 19-ft lots.

summary: Near midnight on April 27, 1921, a fire of undetermined origin destroyed the 2 1/2-story frame pattern shop in the corner of the George J. Storck & Son lumber yard (2406-2418 Greenmount Ave), at 24th & Buchanan Sts. The flames spread into the second floor of the adjoining home of Hezekiah Williams, a Black neighbor at 406 E. 24th St; Black families along 24th St and the rear on Buchanan St readied to evacuate before a second alarm and Fire Chief Emrich brought it under control within a half hour. Firm head George J. Storck Sr. reached the scene 'near collapse' at the smoldering embers; damage was estimated at about $10,000, covered by insurance. The firm advertised two days later that its main plant was undamaged. The firm rebuilt the plant: the national trade journal Manufacturers Record (May 12, 1921) reported "George J. Storck & Sons, 2418 Greenmount Ave., will rebuild plant (lately noted burned at loss of $12,000)."

The Baltimore Housing Authority sponsored it; the U.S. Housing Authority and HOLC supplied technical services.

summary: The FHLBB published *Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation* (1940), prepared by economist Arthur Goodwillie under HOLC Deputy General Manager Donald H. McNeal, making the Waverly neighborhood the federal government's national demonstration project for 'neighborhood conservation' — the preventive alternative to slum demolition and a direct ancestor of postwar urban renewal. The 107-page book was offered 'for the inspiration and guidance of other urban communities... throughout the United States.' Waverly was chosen as the 'almost ideal' setting for 'an experimental study in scientific neighborhood conservation.'

summary: The 1940 study defined 'Waverly' as the white residential area north of 33rd Street; it described the district to its south — which includes the Oriole Park (V) ground at 29th–30th & Greenmount — as 'a fully developed... slum district' where 'occupancy is being gradually relinquished to an economically needy and racially mixed residential type,' and which was 'definitely threatening the Area — by its contiguity and by actual infiltration.' The two were separated only by 'a wedge-shaped tract, improved with modern homes... narrow at the west and continuously widening toward the east,' and 'the slum's pressure to cross this sharply defined barrier... [had] been successfully resisted hitherto only by means of the high neighborhood standards.'

summary: To make the conservation program permanent, the study established the Waverly Conservation League, incorporated June 13, 1940, with organizing personnel supplied by HOLC: an Advisory Committee of 25 (including the executive heads of the four local improvement associations), an Operating Committee with a chairman from each of the Area's six districts, and 'block captains' for each block. It prescribed 'beneficial restrictions' — deed covenants limiting land to single-family residential use, which it framed as 'effective protection against undesirable infiltration' — and proposed a municipal Department of Conservation to run 'clean-up, paint-up, fix-up' campaigns and enforce restrictions.

summary: The study's Appendix C proposed model legislation drawn from the Waverly experiment — a 'Neighborhood Improvement Act' and an 'Urban Redevelopment Corporations Act' — as templates for other jurisdictions, and the FHLBB explicitly offered the whole formula for 'the treatment of similarly threatened small-home neighborhoods everywhere... increasingly great urban districts throughout the United States.' The Waverly Test thus fed the legal and administrative machinery that became postwar urban renewal.

summary: When Terrapin Park opened, the city met it with force: 75 officers under Capt. Moxley at the park, 50 more at Oriole Park across the corner, a uniformed man 'at practically every corner' out the York Road, and a mounted squad. Traffic was scripted — 'all vehicles must enter Twenty-ninth street from the York road and go on through to Guilford avenue.' From day one the wedge was a place the police surrounded, choreographed, and controlled.

summary: For 1937 booking agent Douglass O. Smith secured Oriole Park for the Elite Giants' night games, opening a park 'shut to colored teams for years.' Then it closed again: owner Tom Wilson wanted the park but balked at Smith's fee, and white residents complained to park officials about 'the noise and fanfare' of the night games. For 1938 the Elites were pushed to Bugle Field. The line was undone not by a rule but by a fee and a neighborhood's noise complaint — the same pretext used to evict the Elites for good in 1942.

summary: The 1939 Elite Giants — with championship-series games played on this ground during the season — clinched the Negro National League title over the Homestead Grays. In the deciding game at Yankee Stadium, Sept 24, 1939, Jonas 'Lefty' Gaines shut out the Grays for seven innings and Baltimore won 2–0, taking the NNL championship and the Ruppert Cup — the best season in the franchise's Baltimore run, by a club shut out of the white ballpark's gate.

summary: When Black world featherweight champion Chalky Wright defended his title at the park (stopping Baltimore's Harry Jeffra by TKO, Jun 19, 1942, before ~6,000), he carried a lineage: his grandfather, Caleb Baines Martin, was a runaway from a Natchez plantation who became a Buffalo Soldier and the first African-American ranch owner in southwest Arizona. The site's clearest world-championship night ran a bloodline from bondage to a title belt onto this ground.

summary: Eighty-six years before the ballpark burned, another fire took the same corner. St. John's Episcopal — standing 'at the first toll-gate on the York road,' the exact spot where home plate would sit — was deliberately torched at 2 a.m.; the sacramental vessels stolen, the building gone before the companies arrived. 'The walls are of stone, and they are still good' — and the stone church survives today. Two fires, 86 years apart, on one tollgate corner (1858 arson; the July 4, 1944 ballpark blaze).

summary: At Shiloh AME on E. 28th St., Richard L. Steiner of the Baltimore Redevelopment Commission told ~100 families they'd get 'a good price' for homes the city had claimed. The Waverly site — 17 acres bounded by Greenmount Ave., Reese St., 27th and 30th (taking in the ballpark parcel's own blocks) — was one of Baltimore's first two blighted-area clearance projects. Residents formed the interracial Waverly Area Association to protect themselves. The graded corridor 'cleared' acre by acre — the through-line from the 1937 map to the bulldozer.

summary:
The full published obituary (supplied by Jeff, 2026-08-05) confirms and greatly expands the Find A Grave excerpt. Doris Cynthia Morton was born Nov 3, 1927 in Live Oak, Florida; as a teenager in Daytona Beach she attended Campbell Street High School and was crowned "Miss Campbell Street." She later lived in New York City, fellowshipping at Faith Temple under Bishop Dr. Alvin A. Childs Sr., before relocating to Baltimore in the early 1970s, where she married Bishop Miller Elbin Morton, founder of Eden Light Baptist Church, and became its Head Deaconess. She served as a long-time Board Member of the Eastside Democratic Organization (EDO), focused on minority representation and Black political empowerment in Baltimore City.

CRITICAL CROSS-LINK: the obituary states Doris and Miller "owned and operated two tire businesses, one on Huntington Avenue and the other on Harford Road," later combined into one Harford Road location, "Glide N Ride" (now "Quick Tire Ride") — run by the couple for nearly 40 years. This independently confirms and explains the 1983-84 white-paper finding that the Mortons' 2616 Greenmount mortgages tied the property to "Dot Tire Company" and to holdings on Huntingdon Avenue and Harford Road: Dot Tire Company was the Mortons' own tire business, the direct predecessor of Glide N Ride / Quick Tire Ride. After Miller's death in 2012, Doris ran the tire shop alone for another decade, working daily until age 94 and earning the nickname "The Tire Lady"; in her final years her son-in-law Harry M. Smith assisted.

She was predeceased by her parents, Lorenzo Washington and Stella McCray, and her youngest daughter Linda D. Cruse. She is survived by daughters Fleeter M. Reed and Deborah C. Cruse (m. Harry); sons Claude "Champ" Reed and Everett "Chubby" Cruse; step-son Romeko Morton; grandson Maurice (Belinda) Smith; granddaughter Unissa Cruse-Ferguson; great-grandson Kyle Smith; nephew Corey White; niece "Rosemary"; and several godchildren.

The 1953 Sanborn sheet (LOC item sanborn03573_044, sheet 732 -- a republication of the 1928 base plate with paste-on corrections, not an independent resurvey) depicts 2616 Greenmount as a pink-shaded (brick), 2-story ("2B") dwelling ("D"), one of a uniform unbroken row from 2614-2654 on the south side of Greenmount Ave between Boone St and the block interior -- no occupant name or commercial signage. The 1928 edition (item sanborn03573_018, same sheet 732) shows the identical footprint and story count. This is in tension with a real-estate ad (Evening Sun, Oct. 13 1922) and repeated 1978-82 tax notices describing the house as "three-story, eight-room." Possible explanations include a Sanborn surveyor undercount, a rear addition not reflected in the story label, or a genuine discrepancy between the fire-insurance survey and the real-estate description -- left as an open question rather than resolved.

summary: MD Business Express confirms LANDBANK EQUITY CORPORATION OF MARYLAND, INC. (Dept. ID D01560093) is status Forfeited, and Garrison Holding Corp. (D00462200) is also Forfeited (note: two similarly-named active MD entities, "Garrison Holding, LLC" and "Garrison Holdings, LLC," are NOT related to the 1983 mortgagee). Research into the Virginia Beach parent, Landbank Equity Corporation, found that it collapsed into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 1985 -- roughly 18 months after issuing the $50,000 deed of trust against 2616 Greenmount and 501 E 22nd St -- converting to Chapter 7 liquidation (In re Landbank Equity Corp., 83 B.R. 362 and 77 B.R. 44, E.D. Va. 1987, trustee Laurence H. Levy). Owners William R. Runnells Jr. and Marika Runnells ran a mortgage-fraud scheme -- falsifying loan documents, placing loans in employees'/relatives' names, and selling them to FNMA and savings & loans as bona fide -- and were later criminally convicted and sentenced to 30+ years combined plus $500,000 fines each (Washington Post, Jan. 29 1991, "Landbank Equity Owners Sentenced to Prison Terms"). This almost certainly explains why the white paper's supplied record set found no conventional release of the SEB 202/367-370 deed of trust: the lender ceased to exist as a going concern within about 18 months of making the loan, and any release would have had to come through a bankruptcy trustee rather than the original company -- not a data omission, but a real historical dead end in the lien's paper trail. This directly addresses the white paper's own "Medium-High" risk flag on the missing Landbank release.

summary: The R.L. Polk Baltimore city directories place two businesses at old 1129 York Road (= modern 3313 Greenmount, per the Sanborn 1915 dual-numbering): the LANVALE CYCLE CO (listed 1901 and 1905) and the ZEPP PHOTO SUPPLY CO (1905). The 1905 personal-name section names the proprietor outright: 'Zepp Simon J (Zepp Photo Supply Co), 1129 York rd'. A third 1905 entry, 'Green Wm H, 1129 York rd', appears in the bicycle trade classification. This confirms and NAMES the cycle-shop-to-photo-supply lineage that the parcel's earlier 'verify'-grade incident could only infer, and it pins the proprietor: Simon J. Zepp.

summary: Every Polk directory from 1914 through 1923 lists 3315 and 3317 Greenmount Avenue as DWELLINGS occupied by skilled tradesmen and city workers — not as shops. 3315: Robt F Crafton, bricklayer (1914, 1915, 1921); Oliver Inderrieden, bricklayer (1915); Jas O Inderrieden, bricklayer (1918); Wm B Inderrieden, plumber (1921); Wm Brew, plumber, wife Charlotta (1923). 3317: Wm H Bull, motorman (1915); Otto Gliewe, streetcar conductor (1918); Bernard A Murphy, policeman, wife Sadie (1920, 1921, 1922); Geo L, machinist (1923). No commercial listing appears at these numbers in any year. This establishes the parcel's pre-commercial condition and reframes the 1922–23 assemblage: George Esselman did not build on vacant ground — he bought and cleared an occupied residential row of bricklayers, streetcar men and a policeman to put up his garage.

summary: The buyer of the 1922 assemblage was not an abstract investor. The 1923 Polk directory lists 'Esselman Motor Co, Geo Esselman pres, Frank T Richards v-pres-sec, GREENMT AV COR 33D N' — that is this parcel, the northeast corner of Greenmount and 33rd. The 1922 directory adds 'Esselman Geo Co (Geo Esselman) LUMBER, 3225 Greenmt av', a second Esselman business four blocks south on the same avenue, and lists him personally as 'Esselman Geo (Margt V; Esselman Motor Co) h 3007 n Calvert' (in 1923, wife Virginia). Earlier books show him purely as a lumber dealer ('Esselmann Geo E lumber 208 e 31st n', 1918; 'Esselman Geo lumber 3007 n Calvert', 1921). So the man who bought 3313–3327 in June 1922 and applied to build a two-story brick garage there in October 1923 was a Greenmount Avenue lumberman moving into the automobile trade, and the garage he built was his OWN dealership. Deed-owner and operator are the same person.

summary: The Sun's restaurant column announces the end of the Greenmount Uncle Lee's: the owners are retiring, their children will not take the business, and the restaurant is for sale. It also fixes the restaurant's historical claim — that Uncle Lee's introduced Baltimore to Szechuan cooking about two decades earlier, i.e. c. 1977–79 — and separates the Greenmount house from the Inner Harbor one at 44 South Street, which it says had different owners and would not be affected by the sale. This is the closing bracket on the parcel's restaurant era, and it lands one year before Sunho Corp's charter was allowed to forfeit (6 Oct 1998).

summary: Maryland SDAT's charter record for the corporation that held this building for 38 years. Principal office: 3313-19 GREENMOUNT AVE. Resident agent: AN PAN LEE, 44 SOUTH STREET, Baltimore 21202 — the address of the second Uncle Lee's Szechuan at the Inner Harbor, which the Sun in 1997 described as having different owners; the shared agent address makes a family connection likely but not proven. Charter lifecycle: incorporated 9 July 1979 (film F2449 folio 859, 6pp) — three months after Henry Y.C. Lee bought the property on 18 April 1979 and four months before he deeded it into the corporation on 26 November 1979; FORFEITED 7 October 1987; revived 30 March 1993 (film F3500 folio 310); FORFEITED AGAIN 6 October 1998 — one year after the restaurant went up for sale; then dormant for eighteen years until ARTICLES OF REVIVAL (STOCK) were filed 3 January 2017, five months before the 29 June 2017 sale, evidently to make the corporation capable of signing the deed; ARTICLES OF DISSOLUTION filed 21 August 2019, winding it up two years after the sale. The corporate registry independently corroborates the restaurant's rise, its 1998 collapse and the 2017 exit.

summary: On 30 April 2012 Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke introduced legislation for Baltimore City to condemn, purchase and then resell 3313 Greenmount Avenue, the vacant former Uncle Lee's. Her stated reason was that the owner had no interest in improving the building's deteriorated state — and, pointedly, that the decay was threatening the Great Wall of Waverly mural on its flank. Clarke: 'When you start messing with murals on Greenmount Avenue you've gone too far.' The city never acquired the building; it stayed in Sunho Corp's hands another five years. This is the moment the parcel's public value was argued in the Council chamber on the strength of the artwork attached to it rather than the building itself.

summary: A local history feature assembling the parcel's late-20th-century story. It dates Uncle Lee's opening to 1979 and describes what it replaced: a deteriorating grocery store — matching the July 1977 liquidation auction of Eddie's Supermarket's fixtures. It records that the operation opened as HALF RESTAURANT, HALF CHINESE MARKET, selling jasmine teas and gyoza wrappers, so the building's supermarket back-of-house was carried straight over into an immigrant food-retail use. On the Memorial Stadium trade it quotes assistant manager PO CHANG from a 1993 Baltimore Sun piece: 'The stadium used to bring a lot of people, mostly tourists, from different areas like D.C., Virginia and Pennsylvania.' On the mural it credits TOM CHALKLEY and GREG GANNON, completed August 2010 at Greenmount and E 33rd, depicting neighborhood faces, street signs, the playground and the farmers market — and notes that water damage from the Uncle Lee's building was already threatening it, three months before Clarke's condemnation bill.

summary: The Baltimore City Council adopted the Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan as Ordinance 79-1029 (1979), the statutory instrument governing the Greenmount Avenue commercial corridor's 1976-1983 revitalization program. The URP, not a merchant-taxing district, was Baltimore's late-1970s corridor tool: it carried acquisition authority and binding design standards for storefront appearance. The ordinance remains recited in later amending legislation (Ord. 11-470; Ord. 12-71). Waverly was never designated a Retail Business District under the 1982 RBD ordinance, and was not among the 1977 Shopsteading areas (Jonestown, Union Square, Washington Hill) -- the three DHCD programs are distinct and are frequently conflated.

summary: A handwritten 'Waverly Business Area -- Summary of Design Standards' sheet, clipped over the typed rehabilitation-standards pages of the urban renewal plan, set a minimum visual operating standard for the whole commercial district. Rules covered show windows (not filled, boarded, or covered by signs; within 13 feet of grade), broken or painted glass, frames and trim, security grilles (inconspicuous, in repair, removable during business hours), soft retractable awnings only, and wall repair. A materials blacklist prohibited new Formstone, aluminum siding, wood shakes, and pebble-faced plywood. Strikethroughs and margin revisions on the sheet show the policy being negotiated line by line. Box 10, folder 17.

summary: The Waverly Logo folder preserves dozens of hand-drawn studies for a WAVERLY district wordmark: pencil perspective constructions, marker color comps, tracing-paper overlays, photocopied stencils, and a resolved horizontal master with registration ticks. Deputy City Archivist Jeni Spamer, examining the originals on 13 Aug 2026, confirmed that the terminal Y was modeled on Memorial Stadium. Read west to east, the most developed studies appear to encode the district's geography in order: a domed tower in the W (Johns Hopkins' Gilman Hall), an arched form over the centre letters (the Boulevard Theatre's 1948 marquee at 3302 Greenmount, at the 33rd Street crossing), the stadium as the Y, a row of street trees for the 33rd Street promenade, and Greenmount Avenue cutting through on the diagonal. Attribution of the design remains unresolved. Box 10B, folder 38.

summary: Freestanding 'WAVERLY PARKING' pylon studies on tracing-paper overlays, taped over a lined-pad layout, with human figures for scale and reviewer markup recorded in situ (one variant marked 'NOT OK'; another initialled and dated '5/8'). The pylons would have carried the district wordmark at architectural scale, functioning simultaneously as parking identification, wayfinding, district gateway, and branding. No evidence has been found that any pylon was ever fabricated or installed; they are absent from the 2013 National Register description of the district. Box 10, folders 19 and 26.

summary: The July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter, signed by president George Bluso and carrying the new WAVERLY wordmark as its masthead, announced the Commercial Revitalization Project as a merchant-city partnership and published the capital schedule: fall 1978 curb and sidewalk replacement on Greenmount from 29th to 35th; brick sidewalk paving, benches and landscaping at the 33rd Street median between Barclay and Old York Road; spring 1979 reconstruction and widening of sidewalks on 31st and 32nd from Brentwood to Greenmount with brick paving, benches, tree plantings and special lighting; and resurfacing, striping, landscaping and lighting of the Waverly Shop & Park Lot. The issue included a map of the project area.

summary: The city did not expect merchants to rescue the corridor alone. The DHCD folder sequence tracks a capital program from concept to execution: Public Improvement Miscellaneous (1977), Public Improvement (1978-79), Public Improvements with the consulting firm Hurst-Roche (1978-79), Drawing and Specification Information (1979), Parking Lot Construction (1980-81), Parking Lot Expenditures (1980), 33rd Street median (1977-80), and Tree Grates (1983). Interventions comprised curb replacement, sidewalk and brick paving, landscaping, benches, tree planting and special lighting. The theory of change was physical and economic: improve the pedestrian environment, create a coherent identity, make parking legible, strengthen individual storefronts, organise merchants, and thereby make the district competitive.

summary: A 1978-1979 folder titled 'Waverly Public Improvements (Hurst-Roche)' records the engagement of Hurst-Rosche Engineers, Inc. on the corridor's streetscape work, alongside a separate Consultants-Waverly folder (1978-79). Hurst-Rosche was an Illinois firm (founded 1937, Hillsboro) that opened a Baltimore-area office by January 1970 at 5202 Baltimore National Pike, Catonsville, later Timonium (1983) and Cockeysville (1995), operating in Maryland into the early 2000s. Its entire documented Maryland portfolio is state-highway and traffic engineering; this DHCD folder is the only known trace of any Baltimore City work by the firm, and no published record connects it to graphic or urban design. Whether the firm or a subconsultant produced the district identity is unresolved.

summary: On 19 August 1983, Herman Katkow, Director of the Mayor's Advisory Committee on Small Business, wrote to 'Dear Waverly Merchant' on City of Baltimore letterhead. The letter opens with men's-room graffiti he had seen -- 'APATHY REIGNS!' answered by 'SO WHO CARES?' -- and argues that apathy reigns in Waverly, that no insurer will write a policy against declining sales, that districts which promote collectively provide their own sales insurance, and that the city 'can't afford wheel spinning with unorganized and uninterested areas.' A reply form was attached; the letter closes 'IT'S UP TO YOU!' More than seventy merchants were trading in Waverly that year, so the failing asset was not the merchant base but the organisation. Katkow was himself a Pennsylvania Avenue merchant (the Beverly Shop, 1721-23 Penn Ave, destroyed c.1977 by a gas fire during Metro construction), founder of PALMA in 1953, and small-business director under seven mayors. Filed under 'Waverly / 29th and Greenmount.'

summary: The Waverly Merchants Association, the business body that signed the 1978 revitalization newsletter, appears in no IRS exempt-organization record: it was an unincorporated voluntary association with no charter, no standing, and no assets to outlive its volunteers, and it is functionally absent from the record after 1983. Its residents' counterpart, the Waverly Improvement Association, was IRS-recognised in April 1978 (EIN 52-1099887) and survives. The merchants' functional successor, Waverly Main Street, was not founded until 2000, leaving a seventeen-year gap in which the corridor held a residents' association and a capital program's worth of physical improvements but no merchant institution to steward them. Stanley Adler, of Adler's House of Fashion at 3220/3240 Greenmount, had served as association president in May 1974.

summary: The Baltimore Afro-American devoted its editorial page of 16 February 1946 to two integrated gatherings held in segregated Baltimore theatres. During Boy Scout Week, a thousand scouts attended a jamboree sponsored by a downtown store at the Boulevard Theatre, and 'here again members of both races were admitted without discrimination.' The paper paired this with a Jehovah's Witnesses convention at the Lyric, whose 300-odd Black members 'were seated indiscriminately throughout the Lyric, which, in the past, has discouraged interracial gatherings or refused to admit colored citizens.' It then recorded the managements' response and its own verdict: 'While the management of both the Lyric and Boulevard Theatres were quick to point out that there has been no change in their policy, these two incidents are proof enough for us that their jim-crow practices are silly.' The Boulevard, at 3302 Greenmount, therefore excluded Black patrons as stated policy in 1946, admitting them only when a scout jamboree made the rule inconvenient.

summary: The Boulevard Theatre opened 8 October 1921 at 3302 Greenmount Avenue, at the 33rd Street crossing, designed by E. G. Blanke of the firm Blanke & Zink and operated as a Durkee first-run house. Its signature street presence during the revitalization years was the projecting semicircular marquee added in 1948, which is the plausible referent for the arched element at the centre of the WAVERLY wordmark; no facade arch is documented. The house was twinned in the early 1980s and closed in 1989. It should not be confused with the earlier Waverly Theatre at 3211 Greenmount (1909-1969), one block south.

summary: A city-produced storefront drawing for the Golden Star, a Cantonese restaurant at 3326-3330 Greenmount Avenue, survives in the 1982 facade folder, dimensioned off the building face. The Golden Star was a Lin-family late-night house open by about 1970 (twenty-one years in business as of January 1991) and familiar enough locally to appear on screen in John Waters's Polyester in 1981. Its closing date is unresolved between 1991 and the arrival of a successor buffet. The drawing is evidence that the revitalization program's technical assistance reached immigrant-owned businesses on the corridor, not only long-established ones.

summary: The 1982 folder 'Waverly Harry's Facade and Logo' contains a full facade rendering for Harry's Liquors at 3113 Greenmount Avenue -- restored cornice, repaired brick, a coherent fascia sign -- plus a lettered sign-band study. A 'While You Were Out' telephone message slip preserved with the drawings records the delivery machinery: a contractor's list requested, a cost estimate from Bob Quilter, a storefront referenced. Design assistance, contractor brokering and cost estimating were a single workflow. A Harry's Liquors trades at the address today on an active licence, in a building whose retail lineage runs from Knoblock Brothers' grocery in the 1920s through leather goods by 1937 to liquor thereafter; the documentary chain for the trade name itself is continuous only from 2013, and the original Harry is unidentified. Box 10, folder 28.

summary: The revitalization program resurfaced, striped, landscaped and lit the Waverly Shop & Park Lot at 3201 Barclay Street (Block 3881A, Lot 001), with design work in 1979-80 and construction in 1980-81, plus a dedicated expenditures file in 1980. The lot has a merchants' prehistory: a June 1958 'Park Free While You Shop' co-operative announcement listed some thirty-five participating stores and a new 32nd Street parking lot. The ground itself carries a buried history, having been the site of segregated Public School No. 115, in operation from 1889 until the 1950s and demolished in 1960. A deed recorded 30 November 1979 (WA 3844/396) falls inside the rebuild window and may record a city acquisition rather than an internal transfer. The lot remains city-owned and is operated today as the 'Waverly Lot.' Box 10 folders 24-26, 36; Box 10B folder 41.

summary: The 32nd Street Farmers Market opened on 30 May 1980, conceived the previous year by a city housing employee who walked past the Waverly Shop & Park Lot while the revitalization program was rebuilding it. The market has operated continuously ever since, outlasting the Waverly Merchants Association, the urban renewal plan that authorised the lot's reconstruction, and every other institution involved in the 1976-1983 program. It is the most durable thing the Waverly System produced, and it was not in the plan.

summary: A DHCD folder titled 'Subway Shop, Greenmount and Calvin, 1979' records program attention to a sandwich shop at the corner of Greenmount Avenue and Calvin Avenue, the former name of the frontage consolidated into today's 3400 Greenmount Avenue (a 1978 Shell Oil assignment described five former Calvin Avenue lots as 'now known as 3400 Greenmount Ave'). The operator and trade name are unrecovered from any source: this predates the Subway franchise's Baltimore presence and refers to a sub shop of unknown ownership. A single photograph or drawing in the folder would settle a tenant that no keyless research could recover. Box 10, folder 21.

summary: A Kodak Safety Film 5062 contact sheet labelled 'WAVERLY A+P' (negative sleeve 1763) records twenty frames circling the supermarket block at 33rd Street and Gorsuch Avenue / Old York Road and its parking frontage, storefront by storefront. A companion measured elevation drawing titled 'Gorsuch Avenue A&P' renders the same building with a proposed canopy, signage band and painted produce mural. The store anchored the district for six decades: opened in the late 1930s as half A&P and half Acme with Stadium Bowling Lanes upstairs, doubled when A&P absorbed the Acme half around 1959, and closed as a Super Fresh on 30 January 1999. The shell stood until spring 2003 and the Waverly Crossroads Giant opened on the 4.46-acre assembly in July 2004.

summary: George J. Bluso (1920-2009, buried Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens, Timonium; wife Angelina 1924-2004) purchased 3223 Greenmount Avenue on 16 March 1977 and signed the July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter as president sixteen months later, announcing the city's commercial revitalization program and its capital schedule. He held the property into the 1990s. Newspaper research records a George J. Bluso of the same city with a 1953 gambling conviction (given as age 34, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue), a September 1960 federal arrest for bookmaking without a federal gambling stamp, a May 1961 appearance in reporting on a case connected to an East Baltimore Street club (given as age 42, same Purdue Avenue address), a Baltimore Sun description in 1970 as 'a major gambling figure in the area' who served a year in 1964, and a reported federal decision vacating a wagering-tax conviction (Bluso v. United States, 375 F. Supp. 1085, D. Md. 1974). CAUTION: the two newspaper ages agree with each other at a birth of about 1918-19, while the memorial gives 1920; year-only memorial dates are frequently approximate, but the identification is NOT yet confirmed. The decisive test is the grantee clause of the 16 March 1977 deed (RHB 3457/824-830): if it names a grantee residing in the 5600 block of Purdue Avenue, the merchants' president and the gambling defendant are the same man.

summary: Preservation documentation was not performed decades after the revitalization program as an unrelated exercise; it was intertwined with it. The Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation's City of Baltimore Neighborhood Survey covered Waverly in 1977, surveyed by Michelle Belco, generating Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties forms in a wave running roughly B-2776 to B-2817, with the Greenmount corridor's forms at B-2785 through B-2791. The DHCD program files carry a parallel 'Waverly Historic Survey' folder for 1977-1978, and a Maryland Historical Trust inventory form for 3021-3031 Greenmount Avenue citing the 1977 city survey was filed alongside the merchants' newsletter. The buildings' architectural character was becoming part of the district's economic strategy thirty-six years before the National Register district was listed.

summary: The revitalization program's lending arm is documented on this block: in January 1980 the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, through the Department of Housing and Community Development, lent the Adlers $67,000 against 3220 Greenmount Avenue as a city rehabilitation loan, mid-program. A comparable stack appears one block north in December 1981, where a $75,000 City of Baltimore / DHCD loan combined with a $125,000 SBA loan was expressly 'applied to the rehabilitation of properties known as Nos. 3202-05-07-09 Greenmount Avenue' for the retail tenant The Princess Shops. Together these establish that the Commercial Revitalization Division's public money was rebuilding Greenmount retail blocks, not merely drawing them.

summary: Every HOLC zone at the Waverly four-corners - A1 (Guilford), B16, C9, D6, and the ballpark's own C4 - was appraised by the same man on the same day: Louis Kroner, property review appraiser, H.O.L.C., May 4, 1937. His sheets (verbatim, Mapping Inequality transcriptions) span a sevenfold income gradient across ~150 m: A1 "Executives, Professional men," income "Over $5,000," Negro "No," trend upward, favorable influence "Close to business area on Greenmount Ave."; D6 "Laborers," income "$700-1,000," "Negro: Yes, 35" (35% foreign-born), "Houses in very bad condition. Many alley properties"; remarks "Vandalism in this section" - and, as D6's listed FAVORABLE influence: "Near desirable properties." C4 (the Oriole Park V ground): population "Mixture," income $2,000, favorable "Goucher college located in the section. Desirable location," detrimental "Industrial plants. Continuing obsolescence of old property," trend static. The four-corners was not four judgments that collided; it was one administrative act - executed three weeks after the ballpark's Negro National League opening day (April 10, 1937).

summary: The Waverly study Survey Influence section quantified the survey itself as a market intervention, in the year ending June 1, 1940: HOLC loans repaid in full nearly doubled; borrowers in default dropped by more than half; for-sale signs fell about 50 percent and for-rent signs over 90 percent; HOLC sales of foreclosed Waverly properties jumped from 24 percent (prior three years) to 57 percent in one year - while Maryland overall FELL from 37 to 34 percent. The measurement was the medicine. The same chapter found definite evidence of overzoning on Greenmount Avenue between Thirty-fifth and Forty-second Streets (also Old York Rd 34th-35th and 33rd St), and recorded early Master Plan wins: the old junk yard and unsightly frame tabernacle at the NW corner of Venable Ave and Old York Rd removed and the lot paved; the first of 12 planned interior play areas (block 3903-A) approved by the Park Commission at 1,286.25 dollars - an assessment of 36.75 dollars per property.
